Aspergillus alboluteus.Cardinal temperatures: Aspergillus alboluteus grows veryrestrictedly at 10 °C, and the optimum growth temperature is30 °C. This species is able to grow at 37 °C but not at 40 °C(Fig. 7).
Aspergillus alboluteus.Micromorphology: Ascomata absent. Hülle cells present instrains CCF 5695 and CCF 4916 and absent in strains CCF 6201and DTO 410-I8, elongated, branched, 20–30 μm long, formingyellow clumps. Conidial heads globose to radiate (remainingcompact). Stipes smooth, brown (always hyaline under thevesicle), (500–)800–1 200(–2 000) × 4–7(–10) μm; vesicleshyaline, subglobose, (6–)9–17(–20) μm diam; metulae hyaline,cylindrical, 5–7 μm long, covering two thirds to entire surface ofthe vesicle; phialides hyaline, ﬂask-shaped, 6–8 μm long.Conidia globose to subglobose, smooth, hyaline 2.5–3.5 (2.9 ±0.1) × 2–2.5 (2.4 ± 0.1) μm. Accessory conidia absent or rare,globose to subglobose, on short, hyaline micro- to semi-macronematous conidiophores.
Aspergillus alboluteus.Distinguishing characters: Aspergillus alboluteus is most closelyrelated to A. inusitatus, but the latter is strikingly different from allrelated species by its green colonies and higher maximumgrowth temperature (40 °C). Phylogenetically, the next closestclade consists of A. alboviridis, A. lanuginosus and A. movilensis.AspergillusalboluteusisphenotypicallymostsimilartoA. movilensis, that has similar colonies and also produces Hüllecells and accessory conidia with analogous morphology. How-ever, these two species can be differentiated based on theirconidiophore stipe lengths, vesicle diameters and colony sizes at10 and 37 °C. The conidiophore stipes of A. movilensis rarelyexceeds 400 μm, while stipes of A. alboluteus are (500–)800–1200(–2 000) μm long. The diameter of vesicles of A. movilensisrarely exceeds 13 μm, (5–)9–13(–16) μm, while vesicles ofA. alboluteus are frequently larger, (6–)9–17(–20) μm. Thecolony diameters at 10 and 37 °C (on MEA, 14 d) slightly differbetween these two species: at 10 °C, the colonies ofA. movilensis attained 7 mm on average (the whole range was6–8 mm), while colonies of A. alboluteus attained only 2 mm onaverage (1–2 mm); at 37 °C, A. alboluteus attained 18 mm onaverage (10–23 mm), while those of A. movilensis only 11 mmon average (6–19 mm).

In contrast to A. movilensis, production ofaccessory conidia was not observed in A. alboviridis.

Metulae covering virtually the entire surface of the vesicle, measuring 22–30 × 3–6 µm. Phialides flask shaped, 7–9 × 3–4 µm. Conidia subglobose,
Aspergillus brasiliensis.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus brasiliensis.Similar species: Aspergillus brasiliensis is quite similar to A. niger, A. tubingensis and A. neoniger, but differs by its echinulate conidia.
Aspergillus brasiliensis.Chemical markers: Naphtho-?-pyrones (including au- rasperone B), pyrophen, tensidol A & B, oxalic acid, citric acid. Dihydrocarolic acid, 14-epi-14-hydroxy-10,23-dihy- dro-24,25-dehydro-aflavinine and 10,23-dihydro-24,25- dehydro-aflavinine are produced in strains producing sclerotia.
Aspergillus brasiliensis.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus brasiliensis occurs worldwide and has been isolated from (dried) fruits in Brazil, Portugal, Turkey, USA) and soil.
Aspergillus brasiliensis.Biotechnological applications: ATCC 16404 (=CBS 733.88) is used as a reference strain in fungal resistance testing and was incorrectly identified as A. niger.
Aspergillus brasiliensis.References: Varga et al. (2007), Manikandan et al. (2010)

Aspergillus campestris.Species description: Aspergillus campestris M. Chr., Mycologia 74: 212. 1982. MycoBank MB110495.
Aspergillus campestris.Holotype: NY ST 2–3–1 (catalogue number 00936735). Culture ex-type: CBS 348.81 = NRRL 13001 = IBT 13382 = IBT 28561 = IMI 259009 = ATCC 44563 = IFM 50931 = CCF 5596.
Aspergillus campestris.Diagnosis: Aspergillus campestris is most closely related to A. candidus, A. dobrogensis and A. magnus. Strains of A. campestris are usually easily differentiated from other members of section Candidi by their bright yellow colonies. Conidiophores of A. magnus have longer and wider stipes and broader vesicles compared to A. campestris, while the stipes of A. candidus are shorter. In comparison with A. dobrogensis, A. campestris isolates produce dark soluble pigments and grow more restricted on all cultivation media. The remaining species in sect. Candidi, i.e., A. neotritici, A. pragensis, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus have shorter stipes than A. campestris. These species, except for A. neotritici, have also narrower stipes and smaller vesicles (Table 5). Aspergillus campestris colonies have a smaller diameter than A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. neotritici on all media, but larger than A. pragensis (Table 4). In addition, the majority of strains of A. subalbidus, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. neotritici grow at 35 °C or higher temperatures (Table 6) in contrast to A. campestris where only one strain germinated at 35 °C (CBS 348.81T).
Aspergillus campestris.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus campestris is able to grow at 10 °C (4–10 mm) and its optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (16–28 mm). Some strains did not grow or only germinate at 30 °C (IBT 17867, IBT 23172), while all other strains grew well at this temperature (12–22 mm). The only strain capable of growing at 35 °C was CBS 348.81T (3–4 mm). No growth at 37 °C.
Aspergillus campestris.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA pale yellow (2A3), light yellow (3A5), yellowish white (2A2) or greyish yellow (4B4) with pale yellow margins (2A3), flat, texture granular or floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse yellow (3A6), light yellow (4A5) or greyish yellow (4B5). Colonies on CYA yellowish white (3A2), pale yellow (3A3), light yellow (3A5) or yellowish grey (4B2) with pale yellow margins (2A3), flat or centrally raised, usually radially wrinkled, texture granular or floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire or delicately undulate, reverse yellowish brown (5D5), greyish yellow (4B5), brownish orange (5C5) or dark blond (5D4), exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown after 4 wk in some strains with varying intensity or location: 4–5 mm large circle around colonies in CBS 348.81T and CCF 5641; 1–3 mm large circle around colonies in FMR 15226 and IMI 344489; pigment in central area between colonies in FMR 15224. Colonies on CZA yellowish white (3A2), yellow (3A6) or light yellow (2A5), flat, texture granular or floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire or irregular, reverse pale yellow (3A3), light yellow (3A5) or greyish yellow (3B5), exudate absent, soluble pigment present in some strains after 4 wk: dark brown to black in CBS 348.81T and IMI 344489 (3–5 mm large circle around colonies), greenish grey in FMR 15226 (6–7 mm around colonies) and brown in IBT 17867, FMR 15224 and IBT 23172 (2 mm large circle around colonies). Colonies on CY20S yellowish white (3A2), pale yellow (3A3) or pastel yellow (3A4) with bluish grey margins (23D2), flat, centrally raised or umbonate, texture floccose, granular or downy, sporulation abundant, margins entire, less frequently undulate or irregular, reverse olive (2E5), olive yellow (3C8) or yellowish brown (5E4) with greyish yellow margins (3B5, 4B4), exudate absent, soluble pigment present in some strains after 4 wk: dark green to black in CBS 348.81T (3 mm large circle around colonies), dark brown to black in FMR 15224 (5 mm around colonies), and brown in IBT 17867 and CCF 5641 (only central area between colonies). Sclerotia produced superficially after 4 wk of cultivation, in IBT 17867, CCF 5641, FMR 15226 and FMR 15224. Sclerotia absent in CBS 348.81T, IBT 23172 and IMI 344489. Dark grey or black sclerotia were observed on CZA (IBT 17867, CCF 5641) and CYA (FMR 15224), dark brown sclerotia were present on CYA in strain FMR 15226. No sclerotia were observed in any strain on MEA and CY20S.

Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, undulate in CBS 348.81T, usually non-septate, (90–)250–850(–1  300) × (4–)5–7.5(–9) μm, vesicles globose or subglobose, (10.5–)14–22(–31.5) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (7–)8–14(–17) μm long, covering three quarters to entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (4.5–)5–7(–9) μm long. Conidia subglobose to globose, ovate or limoniform, (2.5–)3–4.5(–5) (3.8 ± 0.5 μm) × (2.5–)3–4.5(–5) (3.4 ± 0.4 μm), smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened. In IMI 344489 conidia wider and broader, subglobose or ovate, (3.5–)4–4.5(–5) (4.4 ± 0.3 μm) × (3–)4–4.5(–5) (4.2 ± 0.3 μm).

Aspergillus candidus.Literature: Link, Mag. Ges. Naturf. Freunde Berlin 3: 16. 1809.
Aspergillus candidus.EX_TYPUS: CBS 566.65 = NRRL 303 = ATCC 1002 = IMI 16264 = IMI 91889 = IBT 28566 = CCF 5594 = LSHBA c.27 = NCTC 595 = QM 1995 = Thom 106 = WB 303
Aspergillus candidus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 13–20 mm after 7 days), usually thin with some aerial mycelium, intermixed with conidiophores arising from the agar or from the aerial mycelium. Conidial heads white, later cream, in fresh isolates often wet. The colony reverse is uncoloured to pale yellow. Colony diameter on MEA 8–14 mm and on YES 19–33 mm after 7 days, colony reverse cream yellow. On CREA poor growth and no acid production.
Aspergillus candidus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores 500–1000 × 5–10 (–20) µm. Conidial heads variable in size, globose to ra- diate, 200–500 µm in diameter. Conidiophores smooth, vesicles globose to subglobose, 10–40 µm, metulae wedge shaped 5–8 × 2.5–3.5 µm to 25–30 × 10–12 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short distinct neck, 5–8 × 2–2.5(–3) µm. Conidia colourless, globose, 3.0–3.5(–4) µm, smooth-walled.
Aspergillus candidus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus candidus.Similar species: Aspergillus candidus is related to A. tritici. The latter can grow at 37 °C, while the former cannot. Aspergillus dobrogensis differs from A. candidus by its longer and broader stipes and smaller vesicles. Almost all isolates of A. dobrogensis produce sclerotia on MEA and CYA, while the majority of A. candidus strains did not produce sclerotia on CYA and none of the isolates produced them on MEA. The following related species are rather common in foods:
Aspergillus candidus.Chemical markers: Aspergillazine A, chloroflavonins, dechlorochlorflavonin, 3-hydroxyterphenyllin, terphe- nyllin and the related candidusin A & B and terprenins, xanthoascins. Odour weak.
Aspergillus candidus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus candidus is common world-wide. It occurs on corn, wheat and other cereals and has also been found in peanuts and on other foods and in soil. Aspergillus tritici is also common in cereals and can cause active heating. Both are good lipase producers.
Aspergillus candidus.Physiology: Aspergillus candidus is halo-tolerant. It can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities.
Aspergillus candidus.Biotechnological applications: Several “A. candidus” used in biotechnology proved to be white mutants of A. flavus or A. oryzae.
Aspergillus candidus.Fig: 62. Aspergillus candidus. Conidiophores and conidia; reduced head and well developed head.
Aspergillus candidus.Neotype: Neotype (designated by Samson & Gams 1985): CBS 566.65. Culture ex-type: CBS 566.65 = NRRL 303 = IMI 091889 = ATCC 1002 = IBT 28566 = CCF 5594.
Aspergillus candidus.Diagnosis: Aspergillus candidus is sister to A. dobrogensis and closely related to A. campestris and A. magnus. In general, A. candidus has smaller vesicles, shorter and narrower stipes and also shorter phialides and metulae compared to A. dobrogensis (Table 5). Aspergillus dobrogensis colonies also have a larger diameter than A. candidus on MEA, CYA and CY20S (Table 4). However, most of these differences can be interpreted as a trend across the whole species, while some isolates show identical dimensions to A. dobrogensis strains (Fig. 7). Thus, distinguishing between them can be problematic in practice. Aspergillus magnus colonies have a smaller diameter and it has wider and longer stipes, vesicles and metulae than A. candidus. Aspergillus campestris has usually bright yellow colonies and produces stipes, vesicles and metulae which are longer/wider than in A. candidus. Aspergillus pragensis grows more restricted on all media while A. neotritici, A. tenebricus and A. taichungensis colonies have a larger diameter on MEA, CYA and CY20S. The latter three species grow at 35 °C or higher temperatures (Table 6). Aspergillus taichungensis and A. tenebricus produce shorter stipes and A. tenebricus has longer phialides and metulae compared to A. candidus.
Aspergillus candidus.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus candidus is able to grow at 10 °C (8−11 mm), the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (20−27 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (18−25 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Aspergillus candidus.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (3A1) with a tint of yellowish white (4A2), flat, texture granular to floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, reverse light yellow (4A4) or pale yellow (4A3). Colonies on CYA white (3A1) with a tint of yellowish white (4A2) or orange white (5A2), flat or slightly centrally raised, texture granular to floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire or slightly undulate, exudate absent, reverse light yellow (4A5) or brownish orange (5C3). Colonies on CZA white (3A1) to pale yellow (1A3, 3A3), flat, texture waxy to granular, sporulation weak, margins entire or irregular, exudate absent, reverse pale yellow (3A3) or light yellow (4A4). Colonies on CY20S white (3A1), flat or slightly centrally raised, texture floccose, granular or velvety, radially or irregularly folded, sporulation abundant, margins entire to diffuse or slightly erose, exudate absent, reverse light yellow (4A4, 4A5). Soluble pigment production after 4 wk was examined in nine strains: five of them (CCF 488, CCF 5172, CCF 6200, CCF 3996, NRRL 58959) were able to produce it and four (CBS 566.65T, CCF 4659, CCF 4713, CCF 6195) not. Dark brown to black soluble pigment (3−4 mm around colonies) was observed on CZA in strains CCF 488 and CCF 6200. Brown soluble pigment was observed on CZA in strains CCF 5172 and CCF 3996 (2−4 mm around colonies) and on CYA in strain CCF 3996. Brownish yellow soluble pigment was observed on CZA in strain NRRL 58959. No soluble pigment was observed on MEA and CY20S in any strain. Sclerotia production after 4 wk was examined in nine strains. Five of them (CCF 488, CCF 5172, CCF 6200, CCF 3996, NRRL 58959) were able to produce sclerotia, while no sclerotia were observed in the remaining strains (CBS 566.65T, CCF 4659, CCF 4713, CCF 6195). Brown to black sclerotia covered by mycelium were present on CZA in five mentioned strains. No sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S in any examined strain.
Aspergillus candidus.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from indoor environments (air, dust), caves, soil, dung, clinical samples, food, metal duct, tunnels of bark beetles, the red flour beetle (Tribolium castaneum) and egg-mass of Arctoscopus japonicus. Aspergillus candidus has been isolated in Canada, Czech Republic, Italy, the Netherlands, Romania, South Korea, Spain and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Aspergillus carbonarius.EX_TYPUS: CBS 111.26 = CCF 5600 = NRRL 369 = ATCC 1025 = IMI 16136 = LSHBA c11 = NCTC 1325 = NRRL 1987 = QM 331 = Thom 4030.1 = WB 369
Aspergillus carbonarius.Macromorphology: Colonies growing relatively fast CYA at 25 °C (diameter 45–70 mm after 7 days), producing black conidia. The colony reverse is coloured creamish dull yellow to yellow. On CREA poor growth but with rather strong acid production.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Micromorphology: Conidiophores 0.5–2.5 mm × 16– 22(–30) µm. Conidial heads globose to radiate, 300–500 (–1000) µm in diameter. Conidiophores smooth, long and coarse, vesicles globose, 40–80 µm, metulae cylindri- cal, 20–40(–75) × 6–8 µm. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 7–10 × 3–3.5 µm. Conidia globose, 7–9 µm, rough-walled, with black bars.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Similar species: Aspergillus ibericus (NRRL 35644; CaM: EF661163), A. sclerotiicarbonarius (CBS 121057; CaM: EU159235), and A. sclerotioniger (CBS 115572; CaM: FN594557) resemble A. carbonarius. The two former do not produce ochratoxins. Aspergillus niger produces some or all of the extrolites kotanins, fumonisins and ochra- toxins, while A. tubingensis produces none of those, but asperazine consistently. Aspergillus carbonarius has larger conidia, grows better on boscolide, and produce less acid on CREA than A. niger, A. tubingensis and A. luchuensis.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Chemical markers: Carbonarins, naphtho-?-pyrones, ochratoxin A & B, oxalic acid, pyranonigrin A. Odour weak.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus carbonarius is common world-wide. It occurs on grapes, coffee, and many other foods.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Physiology: Aspergillus carbonarius is halo-tolerant, but less so than A. niger. It grows rather well at high temperatures; it can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities. The black conidia are very radiation resistant and hence often found on sun-dried products.
Aspergillus carbonarius.Biodeterioration and pathology: Black rot of grapes (together with A. niger).

Aspergillus chevalieri.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diam. 10–18 mm after 7 days), usually thin with some sporulation and ascoma formation. Colonies on CY20 or CY40 usually developing fast, producing numerous aspergilla and yellow ascomata. Colonies on M40 growing and sporulating well, consisting of a dense felt of grey-green conidiophores, arising from the agar or the scanty aerial mycelium and numerous yellow ascomata. The colony reverse is uncoloured to pale green. On CREA, poor growth and no acid production.
Aspergillus chevalieri.Micromorphology: Ascomata yellow, diam. 100–140 (–150) µm. Asci globose to subglobose, diam. 9–10 µm. Ascospores lenticular, smooth or faintly roughened, with a conspicuous furrow, 4.6–5 × 3.4–3.8 µm and prominent equatorial crests. Conidiophores hyaline, smooth walled, 700–850 × 5–10(–20) µm. Conidial heads radiate 125– 175 µm diam. Conidiophore vesicles subglobose, 25–35 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 5–7 × 3–3.5 µm. Conidia colourless, ovate to elliptical, 4.5–5.5 µm, spinulose.
Aspergillus chevalieri.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph produced on low wateracti- vity media, eurotium-type, homothallic.
Aspergillus chevalieri.Similar species: Aspergillus chevalieri is closely related to A. montevidensis, but the latter has rough walled asco- spores and less prominent ridges.
Aspergillus chevalieri.Chemical markers: Asperflavin, auroglaucin, bisan- throns, dihydroauroglaucin, echinulins, emodin, epi- heveadride, eurocristatin, flavoglaucin, isoechinulins, neoechinulins, physcion, questin, questinol, tetrahydro- auroglaucin.
Aspergillus chevalieri.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus chevalieri has a worldwide distribution and is more common in tropical and subtropical regions than in temperate regions. Furthermore, common in indoor air, house dust, cereals, dried fruit, peas, rice, dried foods, including herbs, spices, and salami.
Aspergillus chevalieri.Physiology: Aspergillus chevalieri is osmo-, xero- and halo-tolerant and grows well at 37 °C. It can tolerate low water activities, and grows quite poorly at high water activities.

Theshape of the vesicles is usually spatulate to clavate in contrast toall other members of the A. penicillioides clade that have at leastin part pyriform vesicles. Isolates of this species can grow onM60Y at 37 °C.

Aspergillus clavatus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing quite fast on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 28–45 mm after 7 days), mostly consisting of a dense felt of blue-green conidial heads. The colony reverse is uncoloured to light brown. Colonies on MEA show similar growth, conidiophores less abundant than on CYA (diameter 25–44 mm after 7 days) and on YES diameter 29–45 mm after 7 days, reverse cream yellow. Colonies on CYA at 37 °C are 9–26 mm in diameter. On CREA good growth and usually moderate to strong acid production.
Aspergillus clavatus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores 1500–3000 × 20–30 µm. Conidial heads large, clavate, 300–400 × 150–200 µm in diameter. Conidiophores hyaline and smooth-walled, vesicles typically clavate, 200–250 × 40–60 µm. Phialides borne directly on the vesicle, with a short distinct neck, 6–9 × 2–3 µm. Conidia light green, ellipsoid, 3.0–4.5 ×
Aspergillus clavatus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph can be induced on OA incubated between 25 and 30 °C, neocarpenteles-type (hard, sclerotioid, fawn coloured), heterothallic.

Aspergillus clavatus.Chemical markers: Antafumicins, ascladiol, cytocha- lasins E and K, kotanins, patulin, tryptoquivalines, tryp- toquivalones. Odour can be strong, suggesting trime- thylamine.
Aspergillus clavatus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus clavatus is common world-wide. It occurs on malting barley, decaying vegetation, soil and dung.
Aspergillus clavatus.Physiology: Aspergillus clavatus is alkali-tolerant, and it can tolerate low and high pH values and rather low water activities.

Aspergillus conicus.Distinguishing characters: Aspergillus conicus is most closelyrelated to A. domesticus and A. destruens. The colour of spor-ulating colonies on M40Y is pale turquoise in A. conicus, while myrtle green in A. destruens; reverse of A. conicus is olive greyin the centre, but apricot greyish orange in A. destruens. Thesethree species share almost identical micromorphology, but dif-ferences can be found in their response to the osmotic stress.Aspergillus conicus grows fastest on MEA + 5 % NaCl andMEA + 10 % NaCl, while A. domesticus grows slowest (seeFig. 12E). Aspergillus gracilis and A. pseudogracilis differ fromthese three species by their inability to grow on MEA and CYA at25 °C (several strains of A. gracilis exhibited very restrictedgrowth on CYA) and more rapid growth on M60Y at 25 °C and30 °C. In contrast to A. domesticus, isolates of A. conicus cangrow on MEA and grow slightly faster on CYA. Aspergillus vil-losus can be distinguished from A. conicus, A. domesticus andA. destruens by its faster growth on CY20S, ability to grow onCY20S at 30 °C and on M60Y at 37 °C.

Aspergillus creber.Literature: Jurjevi?, S.W. Peterson & B.W. Horn, IMA Fungus 3: 69. 2012.
Aspergillus creber.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C and attaining a diameter of 15–30 mm. Sporula- tion is moderate, first white, then changing to yellow, orange-yellow to yellow-green, often intermixed with flesh to pink colours. Reverse mostly pale yellow, orange, olive drab or orange-brown. Colonies diameter on MEA slightly smaller than on CYA (8–25 mm). On CREA good growth, but no acid production.
Aspergillus creber.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline or slightly pigmented, smooth-walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm, vesicles globose to ellipsoidal, 12–16 µm diam, conidial heads bi- seriate. Metulae 5–7.5 × 2–2.5 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 5.5–8 × 2.5–3 µm. Conidia globose, 2–3.5 µm, with roughened wall. Reduced conidial heads consisting of solitary phialides or in small whorls can oc- cur as well.
Aspergillus creber.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus creber.Similar species: Aspergillus creber resembles A. protuberus and A. versicolor. Aspergillus protuberus produces Hülle cells and conidiophore stipes with protuberances, while A. creber and A. versicolor have smooth or finely roughened stipes and do not (or rarely) produce Hülle cells. Aspergillus creber.Chemical markers: Diorcinol, sterigmatocystin, peni- gequinolon, psychrophilins, versicolamide, violaceols.
Aspergillus creber.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus creber has a worldwide distribution. This species is a common species in indoor environments (e.g. air, dust, building materials), but also isolated from cheese, cereals, soil.

Aspergillus dobrogensis.Diagnosis: See section “Diagnosis” of A. candidus for more details. Aspergillus dobrogensis differs from A. candidus, A. pragensis, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus by its longer and broader stipes and larger vesicles (Table 5, Fig. 6). Aspergillus campestris can be differentiated by its yellow colonies. Aspergillus dobrogensis colonies have a larger diameter than A. campestris, A. candidus, A. pragensis, A. magnus and A. subalbidus on MEA, CYA and CY20S, while A. neotritici and A. taichungensis colonies have a larger diameter than A. dobrogensis on these media (Table 4). Aspergillus subalbidus, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. neotritici can be differentiated by their ability to grow at 35 °C or even higher temperatures (Table 6).
Aspergillus dobrogensis.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus dobrogensis is able to grow at 10 °C (9–13 mm) and the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (23–32 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (17–24 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Aspergillus dobrogensis.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (4A1), sometimes with a tint of yellowish white (4A2), flat or slightly centrally raised, texture floccose, downy or granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse pale yellow (4A3) or light yellow (4A4). Colonies on CYA white (4A1), sometimes with a tint of yellowish white (4A2), flat, centrally raised or umbonate, texture floccose, downy or granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4, 4A5). Colonies on CZA white (3A1) to yellowish white (3A2, 4A2), flat, texture waxy to granular, sporulation weak and located in a small area in the colony, margins entire or irregular, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse yellowish white (4A2, 3A2) or pale yellow (3A3, 4A3). Colonies on CY20S white (3A1), flat, centrally raised or umbonate, texture floccose, granular or downy, velvety margins in some strains, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4, 4A5). Sclerotia production after 4 wk was examined in 10 strains, two of them (CCF 4651T, CCF 5570) were able to produce sclerotia and eight of them (CCF 5567, CCF 5568, CCF 4650, CCF 5844, IBT 29476, CCF 5575, CCF 5569 and CCF 5572) not. They were produced superficially, less commonly covered by felt of mycelium. Strain CCF 4651T was able to produce sclerotia on all four media; dark brown sclerotia on MEA, CZA and CY20S and brown sclerotia on CYA. Dark brown sclerotia covered by felt of mycelium were present on CZA in CCF 5570. No sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S in remaining examined strains.
Aspergillus dobrogensis.Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores occasionally present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, usually non-septate, rarely septate, (100–)150–1 150(–2 000) × (3.5–)5–7(–14) μm, vesicles predominantly globose, sometimes subglobose or elongated, (9–)10–30(–39.5) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or Glässnerová et al. wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (5–)5.5–12(–14) μm long, usually covering the entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (5–) 5.5–7.5(–8.5) μm long. Conidia globose to subglobose, (3–)3.5–4(–4.5) (3.7 ± 0.3) μm × (2.5–)3–4(–4.5) (3.5 ± 0.3 μm), smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened.
Aspergillus dobrogensis.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from caves (bat droppings and guano, sediment, air), indoor environments (air, dust, carpet), mouse dung, herbivore dung and clinical material. It has been isolated in the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1). Glässnerová et al.

Aspergillus fischeri.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C (diam. 45–68 mm after 7 days), consisting of a dense felt mycelium intermixed with ascomata and aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar. Reverse mostly in shades of cream yellow, and in some strains dark green. Diameter on MEA 66–80 mm after 7 days, colonies white to creamish, granular appea- rance caused by a continuous layer of ascomata; reverse creamish or slightly pinkish. On CREA, poor growth and no acid production.
Aspergillus fischeri.Micromorphology: Ascomata single or borne in small clusters within loose white-creamish hyphae, globose, 80–150(–400) µm in diam, with a 2–3 layers thick wall of flattened cells. Asci 8-spored, globose to somewhat flattened, 8–10 × 10–12 µm. Ascospores biconvex, colourless, 6–7 × 4 µm (including crests), with two equatorial crests and irregular surface ridges. Conidial heads in olive-grey shades, columnar, uniseriate, 100– 150 µm diam. Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, 300–500 µm tall and 4–7 µm diam, smooth-walled. Conidiophore vesicles more or less elongated, 12–18 µm in diam, particularly in the upper part, smooth walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm. Phialides with a short neck, 6–7 × 2–2.5 µm. Conidia colourless, (sub)globose to ellipsoidal, with slightly roughened walls, 2–2.5 µm in diam or up to 3 µm when globose. The fungus is homothallic.
Aspergillus fischeri.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph known, neosartorya-type, homothallic.
Aspergillus fischeri.Similar species: Aspergillus neoglaber (CBS 111.55; CaM: EU014120), A. spinosus (CBS 483.65; CaM: EF669914)
Aspergillus fischeri.Chemical markers: Aszonalenins, fischerins, fumitre- morgins, fumagillins, helvolic acids, neosartorin, trypa- cidin, tryptoquivalines.
Aspergillus fischeri.Important mycotoxins: Fumitremorgin A, B & C, ver- ruculogen.
Aspergillus fischeri.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus fischeri is quite common world-wide and isolated from soil, rice, cotton, potatoes, groundnuts, leather, paper products. Aspergillus section Fumigati strains with ascospores are heat resistant and cause spoilage in pasteurized products, such as fruit and fruit juices, and yoghurts.
Aspergillus fischeri.Physiology: Aspergillus fischeri is thermotolerant. Minimum temperature 11–13 °C, optimum 26–45 °C and maximum 51–52 °C. At 24 °C the ascigerous state is predominant, while the conidial state is predominant at 37 °C. The ascospores are heat-resistant, but less than those of A. glaber and A. spinosus.
Aspergillus fischeri.Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus fischeri strains produce fiscalins, which effectively inhibit the binding of substance P to the human neurokinin receptor.
Aspergillus fischeri.Biodeterioration and pathology: Sometimes patho- genic to animals and man, but A. fumigatus, A. thermomu- tatus (formerly Neosartorya pseudofischeri) (CBS 208.92; CaM: EF669874) and A. lentulus (CBS 117885; CaM: EF669895) are more common as causes of mycoses.
Aspergillus fischeri.References: Samson et al. (2007a), Samson et al. (2014), Tamiya et al. (2015), Houbraken et al. (2016), Frisvad & Larsen (2016), Hubka et al. (2017)

Aspergillus flavus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced, petromy- ces-type, heterothallic.
Aspergillus flavus.Similar species: There are many species resembling A. flavus sensu stricto, e.g. its domesticated form A. oryzae. The latter is more floccose, less strongly sporulating, has smoother, larger and more brownish conidia. Aspergillus flavus.Important mycotoxins: Aflatoxins (only the B type), cyclopiazonic acid and 3-nitropropionic acid.
Aspergillus flavus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus flavus is common world-wide. It occurs on peanuts, maize, oilseeds, cereals, nuts, dates and many other foods.
Aspergillus flavus.Physiology: Aspergillus flavus is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate rather low water activities.

Aspergillus fumigatus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 60–75 mm after 7 days), consisting of a dense velvety felt of dark green conidiophores intermixed with aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar. Reverse mostly in shades of cream yellow, and in some strains dark green. Diameter on MEA 45–55 mm after 7 days. On CREA poor growth and no acid production. Growth on CYA at 37 °C, even better than at 25 °C.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, short, green, particularly in the upper part, smooth walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm. Conidial heads radiate to nearly globose, 100–150 µm in diameter, uniseriate. Conidiophore vesicles broadly clavate, 20–30 µm. Phialides with a short neck, often greenish pigmented, 6–8 × 2–3 µm. Conidia colourless, globose to subglobose, 2.5–3 µm, green, rough-walled to echinulate. The sexual morph is produced after crossing.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, neosartorya-type, heterothallic.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Similar species: Aspergillus fumigatus is closely related to A. fischeri. The latter species produce ascomata much more easily. Further species are mentioned under A. fischeri.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Chemical markers: Fumagillins, fumigaclavines, fu- migatin, fumiquinazolines, fumitremorgins, gliotoxins, helvolic acids, pseurotins, pyripyropens, trypacidins, tryptoquivalines, verruculogen. Odour weak.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Important mycotoxins: Gliotoxin, fumigaclavine A & B, fumitremorgin A, B & C, verruculogen.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus fumigatus is common world-wide, especially in warm environments: heated cereals, garbage, compost, humidifier systems, it is often found in indoor air.
Aspergillus fumigatus.Biodeterioration and pathology: Aspergillus fumigatus is the most important human pathogen causing fungal ball formation in lungs.

However, the characteristics are various according to strains, and some stains have exceptional characteristics. The species grows at 50 °C, no growth at 10 °C.

Aspergillus glaucus.Synonym: Aspergillus testaceocolorans Eurotium herbariorum E. minus
Aspergillus glaucus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diam. 10–18 mm after 7 days), usually thin with some sporulation and ascoma formation. Colonies on CY20 or CY40 usually developing fast, producing numerous aspergilla and yellow ascomata. Colonies on MY40 growing and sporulating quite well, consisting of a dense felt of grey-green conidiophores, arising from the agar or the scanty aerial mycelium and numerous yellow ascomata. The colony reverse brown on CY20 and CY40. On CREA, extremely poor growth, no acid production.
Aspergillus glaucus.Micromorphology: Ascomata yellow, diam. 75–100 (–125) µm. Asci globose to subglobose, diam. 10–12 µm. Ascospores lenticular, smooth, with a rather inconspicuous furrow, 4.8–5.6 × 3.8–4.5 µm. Conidiophores hyaline, smooth walled, 500–1000 × 5–10(–20) µm. Conidial heads radiate 500–1000 µm diam. Conidiophore vesicles subglobose, 25–40 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 7–10 × 3.5–4.5 µm. Conidia colourless, ovate to subglobose, 4.5–7(–8) µm, spinulose.
Aspergillus glaucus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced on low wateractivity media, eurotium-type, homothallic.
Aspergillus glaucus.Similar species: Aspergillus glaucus is closely related to A. pseudoglaucus (CBS 123.28; CaM: EF652007) and A. ruber, but grows slower and does not produce asperentins or mycophenolic acid. Strains of A. pseudo- glaucus consistently produce mycophenolic acid and asperentins (Chen et al. 2017, Mouhamadou et al. 2017).
Aspergillus glaucus.Chemical markers: Asperflavin, auroglaucin, bisan- throns, dihydroauroglaucin, echinulins, emodin, epihe- veadrides, erythroglaucin flavoglaucin, isoechinulins, neoechinulins, physcion questin, questinol, tetrahydro- aurioglaucin.
Aspergillus glaucus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus glaucus has a world wide distribution, more common in tropical and subtropical regions than in temperate regions, common in indoor air, house dust, cereals, dried fruit, peas, rice, dried foods, including herbs, spices, dried ham and salami.
Aspergillus glaucus.Physiology: Aspergillus glaucus is osmo-, xero- and halo- tolerant and does not or grows poorly at 37 °C. It can tolerate low water activities, and grows quite poorly at high water activities.
Aspergillus glaucus.References: Raper & Fennell (1965), Slack et al. (2009), Hubka et al. (2013), Chen et al. (2017), Mouhamadou et al. (2017)

Aspergillus pseu-dogracilis can be distinguished from A. gracilis by its widerstipes, larger vesicles and longer phialides. Growth parametersof both species in the osmotic gradient are identical (seeFig. 12D). Notes: Aspergillus gracilis var. exiguus was proposed basedon slight differences in physiological characters and treated assynonym of A. gracilis by Raper & Fennell (1965). Aspergillus hiratsukae.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slow on CYA at 25 °C (10–20 mm) and faster at 37 °C (25–35 mm) after 7 days, consisting of dense mycelium intermixed with ascomata and aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar; reverse colourless or light brown. Diameter on MEA 25–40 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, colonies white to pale yellow with granular appearance caused by a continuous layer of ascomata. On CREA poor growth and no acid production.
Aspergillus hiratsukae.Micromorphology: Ascomata single or borne in small clusters within loose white-creamish hyphae, globose, 100–250 µm in diam, with a multi-layered cell wall. Asci 8-spored, globose to subglobose, sometimes broadly pyriform, 12–16 µm. Ascospores lenticular measuring 6–7 × 4–5 µm (including crests; spore body 4.5–5 µm) with two closely appressed equatorial crests and a finely reticulate convex surface. Conidiophores columnar, uniseriate, 120–380 µm tall and 4–7 µm diam, smooth walled. Vesicles globose to subclavate, 10–25 µm diam. Phialides with a short neck, 6–8 × 2–2.5 µm covering the upper part of the vesicle. Conidia en masse blue-green coloured, globose to subglobose shaped, 2–2.5 µm in diam, with a delicately roughened wall.

Aspergillus hiratsukae.Similar species: The ascospores of A. hiratsukae resemble those of A. fischeri, but the ascospore surface ornamentation of A. hiratsukae is more finely reticulate due to close-anastomosing ridges. Furthermore, A. hiratsukae grows slower on CYA that A. fischeri. Aspergillus spinosus and A. hiratsukae are related foodborne species and have different ascospores ornamentations. For more details, see A. fischeri.
Aspergillus hiratsukae.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, with a preference to (sub)tropic regions. It occurs in pasteurised foods (juices, dairy), soil, cardboard and gypsum board.
Aspergillus hiratsukae.Physiology: Thermotolerant; good growth 37 °C. Asper- gillus hiratsukae produces heat resistant ascospores that are able to survive a heat treatment.

Aspergillus luchuensis.Synonym: Aspergillus acidus A. coreanus A. foetidus var. acidus
Aspergillus luchuensis.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 50–70 mm after 7 days), producing greyish black brown to black conidia. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is cream dull yellow to yellow. On CREA poor growth but with strong acid production.
Aspergillus luchuensis.Micromorphology: Conidiophores 2–3(–5) mm × 15– 20(–30) µm. Conidial heads globose to radiate, 200–500 µm in diameter. Conidiophores smooth, long and coarse, vesicles globose, 20–80 µm, metulae cylindrical, 15–30 (–50) × 3.5–4.0 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short distinct neck, 7.5–10 × 2.8–3.3 µm. Conidia globose, 3.0–3.5 µm, rough-walled, with black bars.
Aspergillus luchuensis.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus luchuensis.Similar species: Aspergillus niger produces some or all of the extrolites kotanins, fumonisins and ochratoxins, while A. luchuensis produces none of those, but asperazine consistently. Many strains of A. luchuensis also produce antafumicins. The two species and A. tubingensis can also be separated by their different calmodulin and ?-tubulin sequences. Aspergillus luchuensis grows slower than A. niger and A. tubingensis.
Aspergillus luchuensis.Chemical markers: Antafumicins, asperazine, funa- lenone, naphtho-?-pyrones, pyranonigrin A, tensidol B. Odour weak.
Aspergillus luchuensis.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus luchuensis is common world-wide. It occurs on grapes, coffee, tea and many other foods.
Aspergillus luchuensis.Physiology: Aspergillus luchuensis is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures. It can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities.
Aspergillus luchuensis.References: Samson et al. (2004, 2007b), Yu et al. (2004) (listed as A. foetidus in those papers, but the type strain of A. foetidus belongs to A. niger), Bragulat & Cabanes (2008), Hong et al. (2013)

Aspergillus magnus.Species description: Aspergillus magnus Glässnerová & Hubka, sp. nov. MycoBank MB 844202.
Aspergillus magnus.Etymology: Latin adj. magnus -a -um, referring to its larger conidiophores (stipe length and width, metulae length and vesicle diameter) compared to related species.
Aspergillus magnus.Diagnosis: Aspergillus magnus differs from other section Candidi members by its larger vesicles, longer and wider stipes and longer metulae (Table 5, Fig. 6). Some strains of A. dobrogensis reach similar stipe lengths but they differ from A. magnus by other characters, especially its white colony colour. Aspergillus magnus grows more restricted than other species on all media except for A. pragensis (Table 4). Aspergillus neotritici, A. tenebricus, A. taichungensis and A. subalbidus can be differentiated by their ability to grow at 35 °C or even higher temperatures.
Aspergillus magnus.Typus: Canada, Alberta, Edmonton, mouse collected on horse farm, 1962, J.W. Carmichael (holotype PRM 956934 (dried culture, metabolically inactive), isotypes PRM 956935–956937 (dried culture, metabolically inactive), culture ex-type UAMH 1324 = IBT 14560).
Aspergillus magnus.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus magnus is able to grow at 10 °C (9–10 mm) and the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (20–22 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (5–7 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Aspergillus magnus.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA yellowish grey to pale yellow (3C2–3A3) in the centre, yellowish white (3A2) on the margins, flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4). Colonies on CYA pale yellow (3A3) in the centre, yellowish grey (4B2) on the margins, flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown (3 mm around colonies after 4 wk), reverse greyish yellow to dark blond (4B4-5D4). Colonies on CZA pale yellow (3A3), flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse pale yellow (3A3). Colonies on CY20S pale yellow (3A3), centrally raised, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow to dark blond (4B4–5D4). Sclerotia production after 4 wk was not observed on any medium.
Aspergillus magnus.Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores usually present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, non-septate or occasionally septate, (540–)810–1 150(–1 600) × (6–)9–13(–16) μm, vesicles globose to subglobose, (18–)33–39(–45) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (7.5–)9–14(–17) μm long, covering the entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (4.5–)5.5–7(–8) μm long. Conidia subglobose to globose, (3–)3.4–3.6(–4) (3.5 ± 0.2 μm) × (2.5–)3.1–3.3(–3.5) (3.2 ± 0.2 μm), occasionally broadly ellipsoidal, smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened.
Aspergillus magnus.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known only from a single strain, isolated from a mouse collected on a horse farm in Canada.

Conidial heads radiate to columnar 120–150 µm diam. Conidiophore vesicles subglobose, 25–35 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 5–6.5 × 2.5–3.5 µm. Conidia colourless, subglobose to elliptical, 4.5–5.5 µm, finely spinulose.

Aspergillus neotritici.Species description: Aspergillus neotritici Glässnerová & Hubka, sp. nov. MycoBank MB 844204. = Aspergillus tritici [as triticus] B.S. Mehrotra & M. Basu, Nova Hedwigia 27 (3-4): 599. 1976. MycoBank MB309248. Not validly published [Art. 8.1, Art. 8.4, Art 40.1, Art. 40.4 (Turland et al. 2018)].
Aspergillus neotritici.Etymology: Latin preposition neo- referring to a new description of previously invalidly described species A. tritici.
Aspergillus neotritici.Diagnosis: Aspergillus neotritici colonies have a larger diameter than A. campestris, A. candidus, A. magnus and A. pragensis on all media at 25 °C (Table 4). It grows better than any other species at 30–40 °C and its optimum growth temperature is 30 °C, while in other species, except for A. subalbidus, it is 25 °C (Table 6). It is also the only species which is not able to grow or at least germinate at 10 °C and can grow at 40 °C. Aspergillus pragensis, A. dobrogensis, A. candidus, A. campestris and A. magnus can be differentiated from A. neotritici by their inability to grow at 37 °C. The stipe length and vesicle diameter of A. neotritici is generally longer when compared to A. subalbidus, A. pragensis, A. tenebricus and A. taichungensis (Fig. 7), noting that this omits strains with atypical or uniseriate conidiophores.
Aspergillus neotritici.Typus: Czech Republic, Prague, toenail of 62-year-old man, 2008, isolated by M. Skořepová (holotype PRM 956940 (dried culture, metabolically inactive), isotypes PRM 956938, PRM 956939 and PRM 956941 (metabolically inactive), culture ex-type CCF 3853 = IBT 32725).
Aspergillus neotritici.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus neotritici does not grow at 10 °C, and its minimum growth temperature is 15 °C (4–13 mm). The optimum growth temperature is 30 °C (32–51 mm) and the maximum growth temperature is 40 °C (4–22 mm). No growth at 45 °C.
Aspergillus neotritici.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (3A1) to yellowish white (2A2, 3A2), flat, texture floccose to granular, less commonly velvety (in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659), sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4), greyish yellow to golden yellow (4B5–5B7). Colonies on CYA white (3A1) to yellowish white (3A2), flat to centrally raised, usually radially wrinkled, texture floccose, velvety or floccose in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659, margins entire or diffuse, sporulation abundant, exudate usually absent, minute yellow droplets present in CCF 6202, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4B5), reddish yellow (4A6) or brownish orange (5B4) in the centre, light yellow (4A4) on margins. Colonies on CZA white (3A1) to yellowish white (3A2), flat to centrally raised, texture granular, floccose or downy, sporulation abundant, margins entire or irregular, exudate usually absent, minute yellow droplets present in CCF 6202, soluble pigment present in some strains after 4 wk, dark brown soluble pigment (1–2 mm around colonies) present in strains CCF 4030 and CCF 6397, dark green soluble pigment present in strain CCF 4653 (2 mm around colonies), yellow soluble pigment present in strains CCF 3314, CCF 3853T and CCF 4914 (1–5 mm around or between colonies), reverse greyish yellow to pale orange (4B5–5A3). Colonies on CY20S white to yellowish white (1A1–2A2) or pale yellow in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659 (2A2–2A3), flat or centrally raised, radially wrinkled in some strains (CBS 266.81, CCF 4914 and IBT 12659), texture floccose, downy to velvety in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659, sporulation abundant, margins entire or diffuse, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse yellow to reddish yellow (3A6–4A6) or greyish yellow (4C5). Sporulation was abundant in all strains on all tested media except for strains NRRL 4847 (ex-type of A. albus var. thermophilus) and CCF 1649 which were sterile. Sclerotia were present on the colony surface after 4 wk of cultivation in strains CBS 266.81, CCF 3314, CCF 4914 and IBT 12659, absent in CCF 4030, CCF 4653, CCF 3853T, CCF 4658, CCF 6202, CCF 1649 and CCF 6397. Purple sclerotia were present only on CZA in all mentioned strains, no sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S. Purple sclerotia were present in both strains on CZA only.
Aspergillus neotritici.Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, predominantly biseriate, uniseriate in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659 (dimensions of micromorphological features are given separately in the next paragraph). Diminutive conidiophores occasionally present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled or finely roughened, usually non-septate, occasionally with septa (extensively septate in CBS 266.81), (140–)200–500(–700) × (3.5–)4–8(–9) μm, vesicles globose, subglobose or elongated, (11–)14–24(–28) μm diam, (5–) 6–8(–11) μm diam in CBS 266.81, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (4–)7–17(–21) μm long, (3.5–)4–5(–5.5) μm long in CBS 266.81, usually covering the entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (2.5–)3.5–6(–8) μm long. Conidia (including Glässnerová et al. CCF 4914 and IBT 12659) globose to subglobose or ellipsoidal, (2.5–)3–4.5(–5) (3.5 ± 0.5) μm × (2.5–)3–4(–4.5) (3.2 ± 0.5) μm, smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened. Conidiophores in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659 short, uniseriate, stipes (6–)18–45(–85) × (2–)2.5–4(–5) μm, vesicles (3.5–)4–7(–8.5) μm, phialides (3–)3.5–4.5(–6) μm long, conidia had similar dimension to other strain, (3–)3.5–4(–4.5) (3.6 ± 0.3) μm × (3–) 3–3.5(–4) (3.4 ± 0.3) μm.
Aspergillus neotritici.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from clinical samples, food (flour, corn, sunflower seed, cave cheese rind, grains of Triticum sativum), soil, indoor environments, outdoor air, vermicompost, and deep litter for pig raising. It has been reported in Brazil, China, Cuba, Czech Republic, India, Iran, Italy, South Africa, and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Aspergillus nidulans.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced, emericella-type, homothallic.
Aspergillus nidulans.Similar species: Aspergillus nidulans is closely related to other species in Aspergillus section Nidulantes, in particular the former varieties of it. These varieties now have species status (Hubka et al. 2015, Chen et al. 2016).
Aspergillus nidulans.Chemical markers: Asperthecin, austinol, emerin, penicillin, shamixanthone, sterigmatocystin. Asperugins, aspochinolones, aspyridones, emodin, monodictyphenone, terrequinone A and other extrolites were later found, using genome mining and different growth conditions or chromatin remodelling of A. nidulans.
Aspergillus nidulans.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus nidulans has a worldwide distribution and is more common in tropical and subtropical regions than in temperate regions. Also common in indoor air, house dust, cereals, dried fruit, peas, rice, dried foods, including herbs, spices and salami.
Aspergillus nidulans.Physiology: Aspergillus nidulans is less halotolerant than species belonging to Aspergillus section Aspergillus and Restricti. Good growth at 37 °C.
Aspergillus nidulans.Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus nidulans is a genetical model organism and has been used as trans- formation host for genes or gene clusters from other mi- croorganisms.
Aspergillus nidulans.Biodeterioration and pathology: May deteriorate cereals, leather etc., and may cause sinusitis in horses and other diseases in animals.

Aspergillus niger.Synonym: Aspergillus awamori A. foetidus A. phoenicis
Aspergillus niger.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 70–85 mm after 7 days), producing purple-black, brown-black or black conidia. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is cream- coloured dull yellow to yellow but may is some cases be dark brown to black. On CREA poor growth but with strong acid production. Sclerotia occasionally produced if raisins are added to an agar medium (Frisvad et al. 2014).
Aspergillus niger.Micromorphology: Conidiophores 0.5–2 mm × 16– 22(–30) µm. Conidial heads globose to radiate, 300–500 (–1000) µm in diameter. Conidiophores smooth, long and coarse, vesicles globose, 25–75 µm, metulae cylin- drical, (10–)20–40(–75) × 6–8 µm. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 7–10 × 3–3.5 µm. Conidia globose, 3.5–4.5 µm, rough-walled, with black bars.
Aspergillus niger.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus niger.Similar species: Aspergillus niger has a sibling species
Aspergillus niger.Chemical markers: Atromentins, fumonisins B2 and B4, funalenone, kotanin, malformins, naphtho- ?-pyrones, ochratoxin A (only 6–10 % of all strains examined), orlandin, pyranonigrin A-E, tensidol A &
Aspergillus niger.Important mycotoxins: Fumonisins B2 and B4, ochratoxin A (Frisvad et al. 2007, 2011, 2018).
Aspergillus niger.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus niger is common world-wide. It occurs on grapes, coffee, corn, onions, and many other foods. It also occurs in indoor air and in soils of potted plants.
Aspergillus niger.Physiology: Aspergillus niger is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities. The black conidia are very radiation resistant and hence often found on sun-dried products.
Aspergillus niger.Biotechnological applications: Production of citric acid, gluconic acid and oxalic acid. Used as a transformation host, especially for production of recombinant proteins. Production of amylases, lipases, pectinases, amyloglucosidases and many other enzymes. Used for production of awamori aquavit and Kuro- koji. Biotransformation of chemical compounds, waste handling, metal leaching and several other applications.
Aspergillus niger.Biodeterioration and pathology: Produce a rot in grapes (black rot), onions and other fruits and vegetables. May degrade plastics, textiles and other materials. Opportunistic human pathogen (especially otomycosis).

Aspergillus oryzae.Synonym: Aspergillus gymnosardae A. oryzae var. effusus and several other varieties (see Frisvad et al. 2019)
Aspergillus oryzae.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diam. 70–85 mm after 7 days), producing pale greenish yellow conidia, later becoming light to dull brown. Colony texture floccose or rarely velutinous. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is coloured creamish dull yellow to yellow. Sclerotia large, 400–700 µm, first white, then becoming black, often covered by exudate droplets, but only in few isolates. On CREA, poor growth and poor or no acid production. On AFPA a cream-coloured reverse.
Aspergillus oryzae.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, long and mostly rough-walled, 1–5 mm × 10–20 µm. Conidial heads globose to radiate, 300–500(–1000) µm diam. Conidiophore vesicles subglobose, 40–80 µm, metulae, if present, cylindrical, 8–12 × 4–5 µm. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 10–15 × 3–5 µm. Conidial heads often biseriate, but heads with only phialides also common. Conidia ellipsoidal when young, globose to subglobose when mature, 4.5–8 µm, green, smooth to finely rough-walled. Some strains produce conidial columns.
Aspergillus oryzae.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus oryzae.Similar species: Aspergillus oryzae resembles A. flavus. The former is more floccose, less strongly sporulating, has more smooth, larger and more brownish conidia. Aspergillus arachidicola differs by producing type B and G aflatoxins, while A. minisclerotigenes produces small
Aspergillus oryzae.Chemical markers: Asperfuran, asprirochlorin, cyclo- piazonic acid, kojic acid, 3-nitropropionic acid, penicillin, sporogen AO1. Odour usually weak.
Aspergillus oryzae.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus oryzae has only been found in industrial factories and is probably a domesticated form of A. flavus.
Aspergillus oryzae.Physiology: Aspergillus oryzae is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate rather low water activities.
Aspergillus oryzae.Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus oryzae is used for fermentation of tuna fish (katsuobushi), production of soy sauce, production of sake, enzymes, especially amylases, as transformation host and several other purposes.
Aspergillus oryzae.References: Machida et al. (2005), Varga et al. (2011), Frisvad et al. (2018), Frisvad et al. (2019)

Aspergillus parasiticus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores, hyaline, long, smooth and rough-walled, 300–700(–1000) × 10–20 µm. Conidial heads globose to radiate, 300–500 µm in diameter. Conidiophore vesicles globose, 20–35 µm, metulae, if present, cylindrical or apically swollen, 6–10(– 16) × 4–5.5 µm. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 7–9 × 3–4 µm, hyaline to pale green. Conidial heads often biseriate, but heads with only phialides also common. Conidia globose to subglobose, 3.5–5.5 µm, yellow green, conspicously rough-walled. Most conidial heads are uniseriate, but strains referred to A. toxicarius have predominantly biseriate conidial heads.
Aspergillus parasiticus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, petromyces-type, heterothallic.
Aspergillus parasiticus.Similar species: Aspergillus parasiticus resembles its domesticated form A. sojae. The latter is more floccose,

Aspergillus parasiticus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus parasiticus is quite common world-wide. It occurs on peanuts, cereals, nuts other foods.
Aspergillus parasiticus.Physiology: Aspergillus parasiticus is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate rather low water activities.

Aspergillus penicillioides.Macromorphology: Colonies growing very slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 1–2 mm after 7 days), usually thin with no sporulation. Colonies on CY20 or CY40 developing slowly, sometimes sporulating after 14 days. Colonies on M40 growing and sporulating well, consisting of a dense felt of dark to dull green conidiophores, arising from the agar or the scanty aerial mycelium. The colony reverse is uncoloured to pale green. On CREA no growth. No growth at 37 °C.
Aspergillus penicillioides.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, smooth walled, 500–1000 × 5–10(–20) µm. Conidial heads radiate when young, becoming loosely columnar, 80–90 (later 300–350) µm in diameter. Conidiophore vesicles pear shaped to subglobose, (6–)10–20(–25) µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 6–9 × 2.5–3 µm. Conidia colourless, ovate to truncate-elliptical when young, later becoming barrel shaped, 3.0–4.5(–5) µm, rough-walled or echinulate.
Aspergillus penicillioides.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus penicillioides.Similar species: Aspergillus penicillioides is closely related to A. restrictus, which has by dark green colonies. The phialides of A. restrictus are situated only on the upper half of the vesicles, which gives the conidial head a typical columnar feature. The conidia are born cylindrical to barrel shaped, whereas the conidia of A. penicillioides are more ellipsoidal in the beginning. A large number of new species have recently been described from the section Restricti (Sklenár et al. 2017). The species A. caesiellus,
Aspergillus penicillioides.Chemical markers: Asperglaucide, aurantiami- de, cristatin A, echinulin, mycophenolic acid (trace amounts). Odour weak.
Aspergillus penicillioides.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus penicillioides has a world-wide occurrence and can be found on cereals, indoor air, house dust, archives, probably associated to bed mites.
Aspergillus penicillioides.Physiology: Aspergillus penicillioides is osmo-, xero- and halo-tolerant. It can tolerate low water activities, and grows very poorly at high water activities.

Aspergillus pragensis.Holotype: PRM 922702. Culture ex-type: CCF 3962 = CBS 135591 = NRRL 62491 = IBT 32274.
Aspergillus pragensis.Diagnosis: Aspergillus pragensis is phylogenetically basal to A. subalbidus, A. tenebricus and A. taichungensis. Together with A. magnus, it is unique by its small colony diameters on all media, especially on CZA. Aspergillus pragensis and A. magnus can be easily distinguished by colony colour and strikingly different micromorphology (Fig. 5, Fig. 6). Aspergillus subalbidus, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. neotritici can be differentiated from A. pragensis by their ability to grow at 35 °C or higher temperatures (Table 6). Aspergillus pragensis differs from A. dobrogensis, A. magnus and A. campestris by its shorter and narrower stipes, shorter metulae and smaller vesicles (Table 5).
Aspergillus pragensis.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus pragensis grows restrictedly at 10 °C (5–6 mm, colonies having character of minimally sporulating waxy drops) and the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (15–18 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (3–14 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Aspergillus pragensis.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (3A1), slightly raised, crateriform in the centre, radially sulcate, texture velvety to downy, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse brownish yellow (5C6) in the centre, orange white (5A2) on the margins. Colonies on CYA white (3A1), centrally raised to umbonate, texture floccose to granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire or slightly undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown in CCF 3962T, CCF 4654, CCF 5693, CCF 5847 after 4 wk (4–6 mm wide circle around colonies or in the area between colonies), reverse light brown to brownish orange (5D5–5C4). Colonies on CZA white (3A1) or brownish grey (4D2), flat, texture waxy to floccose, sporulation weak and located only in the colony centre, margins irregular or submerged, exudate absent, soluble pigment intense dark green to greyish blue in all strains after 4 wk (3–6 mm around colonies), reverse yellowish grey (3D2). Colonies on CY20S white (3A1) with a tint of yellowish white (3A2), flat to slightly raised, texture downy, granular or floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A5). Sclerotia were present after 4 wk of cultivation in NRRL 58614 and CCF 5847, absent in CCF 3962T, CCF 4654 and CCF 5693. Dark brown to purple sclerotia covered by felt of mycelium were observed on CYA in NRRL 58614 and CCF 5847, and on MEA in CCF 5847. No sclerotia were observed on CZA and CY20S.
Aspergillus pragensis.Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores occasionally present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, usually non-septate, occasionally with septa, (40–)110–260(–380) × (3–)3.5–5(–6) μm, vesicles predominantly globose, sometimes subglobose, (7–)10–17(–23) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (4–)5–6.5(–8) μm long, covering three quarters to entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (4–)5–6(–6.5) μm long. Conidia globose to subglobose, (3–)3.5–4(–4.5) (3.7.± 0.3 μm) × (3–)3.5–4(–4.5) (3.5 ± 0.2 μm), smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened.
Aspergillus pragensis.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from indoor environments (indoor air, carpet, dust), food (rice bran), clinical samples and outdoor air. It has been isolated in Canada, Czech Republic, South Korea and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Aspergillus pseudoglaucus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing moderately fast on CYA at 25 °C, diam. 20–35 mm after 7 days, usually thin with some sporulation and ascoma formation. Colonies on CYA20 developing fast (38–60 mm, 25 °C, 7 d), sporulation sparse to moderately dense, yellow ascomata present, mycelium sulphur yellow or orange and white. Colonies on M40 growing well (65–>75 mm, 25 °C, 7 d), mycelium sulphur yellow or orange, sporulation sparse to moderately dense; conidia en masse pale green, yellow ascomata present. Colony reverse uncoloured, luteous or fulvous on M40, sulphur yellow or ochreous on DG18.
Aspergillus pseudoglaucus.Micromorphology: Ascomata eurotium-like, yellow, globose to subglobose, 75–200 µm. Asci globose to subglobose, diam. 10–12 µm. Ascospores in side view lenticular, furrow absent or showing as a trace, crests absent, 4–6.5 × 3–4.5 µm. Conidiophores hyaline or light brown, 500–1000 × (7–)11–22 µm, stipes smooth. Vesicles globose to subglobose, generally (25–)35–65 µm wide (smaller vesicles occur in degenerated strains, 10–25 µm), fertile over two thirds to entire surface. Phialides flask- shaped, 6–11 × 4–6.5 µm. Conidia globose to subglobose, in most strains tuberculate; microtuberculate in atypical strains, (3.5–)6–9 × (3–)5.5–7.5 µm.
Aspergillus pseudoglaucus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced on low wateractivity media, eurotium-type, homothallic.

Aspergillus pseudoglaucus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus pseudoglaucus has a worldwide distribution and is common in indoor air, house dust, feed, cereals, dried fruit, bakery products, spices, ham.

Aspergillus pseudoglaucus.Distinguishing characters: Morphologically A. pseudoglaucusresembles A. proliferans and A. ruber in ascospore size andornamentation, however the ascospores of A. pseudoglaucus donot have or have indeﬁnite furrow, while A. proliferans andA. ruber have more pronounced furrow on ascospores. Thegrowth proﬁle characters on M60Y at 37 °C can be used todistinguish A. pseudoglaucus and A. proliferans, the latter spe-cies cannot grow under this condition (Table 5). Aspergilluspseudoglaucus belongs to the A. ruber clade (Fig. 1). Otherspecies in the A. ruber clade such as A. cumulatus,A. appendiculatus and A. mallochii can be differentiated by presence of crests, while A. tonophilus and A. sloanii do not growon MEA and CYA at 25 °C and A. zutongqii has larger asco-spores measuring 6–7.5 × 4.5–6 μm.

Aspergillus quadrilineatus.Notes: Phylogenetically Aspergillus acristatus, A. ﬂoriformis,A.parvatheciusandA.miyajiiareidenticalwithA. quadrilineatus and are considered as synonyms as didHubka et al. (2016). Morphologically these species have minordifferences in ascospore crests. Aspergillus acristatus wasintroduced as a crest-free variety of A. nidulans (Fig. 42I),Fennell and Raper (1955) suggested a close relationship be-tween A. acristatus and A. quadrilineatus, because a number ofA. quadrilineatus strains also show reduced four crests.Aspergillus ﬂoriformis was described as a anamorphic species,only Hülle cells were mentioned in the original description(Samson & Mouchacca 1975), but the ex-type (CBS 937.73) ofA. ﬂoriformis is now degenerated and does not produce anyanamorphic or teleomorphic structures. Also the ex-type (CBS493.65) of A. parvathecius which was described with asco-spores does not produce the teleomorph. Hubka et al. (2016)speculated that both A. parvathecius and A. miyajii representatypical A. quadrilineatus strains characterized by smallerascomata with delayed maturation in the ﬁrst and ascosporeswith aberrant development and shape in the latter. We agreewith their opinion, one strain (CBS 853.96) collected from Spainfurther conﬁrms the diversity of ascospore phenotype inA. quadrilineatus, the ascospore crests in this isolate areirregularly protuberate (Fig. 3G, H), phylogenetically it is iden-tical in ITS, CaM and BenA with other A. quadrilineatus strains,but shows seven bp differences in RPB2 (99.2 % similarity, 907/914 bp).

In contrast toA. salinicola, isolates of A. reticulatus can grow on M60Y at37 °C, grow faster on CY20S at 25 °C and 30 °C and usuallyhave wider stipes and larger vesicles. Aspergillus ruber.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diam. 10–18 mm after 7 days), usually thin with some sporulation and ascoma formation. Colonies on CY20 or CY40 developing fast, producing numerous as- pergilla and yellow ascomata, covered with red hyphae. Colonies on MY40 growing and sporulating well, con- sisting of a dense felt of pale grey-green conidial heads, arising from the agar or the scanty aerial mycelium and numerous yellow to orange ascomata. Colony reverse is uncoloured to pale green. On CREA, extremely poor growth, no acid production.
Aspergillus ruber.Micromorphology: Ascomata yellow, diam. 75–100 (–125) µm. Asci globose to subglobose, diam. 10–12 µm. Ascospores lenticular, smooth, with a conspicuous furrow, 4.8–5.6 × 3.8–4.4 µm. Conidiophores hyaline, smooth walled, 500–750 × 5–10(–20) µm. Conidial heads radiate 500–1000 µm diam. Conidiophore vesicles subglobose, 25–35 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 7–9 × 4–5 µm. Conidia colourless, elliptical, ovate to subglobose or globose, 4.5–7(–8) µm, spinulose.
Aspergillus ruber.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced on low wateractivity media, eurotium-type, homothallic.

Aspergillus ruber.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus ruber has a worldwide distribution, but is more common in tropical and subtropical regions than in temperate regions. Furthermore, A. ruber is common in indoor air, house dust, cereals, dried fruit, peas, rice, dried foods, including herbs, spices, and salami.

Aspergillus rugulosus.Notes: The ascospore colour in A. rugulosus varies from greyishred to dark greyish red or reddish purple (Benjamin 1955, Raper& Fennell 1965). In this study, the type strain CBS 133.60 pro-duces orange red ascospores, which turn to reddish purple aftermonths. Emericella rugulosa var. lazulina was described basedon its greyish magenta to greyish violet ascospores (Horie et al.1996b), since it is identical in morphology (except the asco-spores colour) and phylogeny with A. rugulosus, we treat it as asynonym as did Hubka et al. (2016). According to Mehrotra &Prasad (1969) Emericella cleistominuta differed from A. rugulo-sus in producing much smaller ascomata (15–50 μm). However,weobservedascomatameasuring200–300μmin E. cleistominuta, the ascospores of these two species areidentical too (Fig. 5E–H). Based on morphological and molecularresults, E. cleistominuta is treated as a synonym.

Aspergillus spinosus.Synonym: Neosartorya fischeri var. spinosa N. spinosa
Aspergillus spinosus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (40–70 mm and 67–85 mm after 7 days, resp.), consisting of dense mycelium intermixed with ascomata and aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar; reverse colourless to light pink. Diameter on MEA 50–75 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, colonies white to pale yellow with granular appearance caused by a continuous layer of ascomata. On CREA poor growth and no acid production.
Aspergillus spinosus.Micromorphology: Ascomata single or borne in small clusters within loose white-creamish hyphae, globose, 200–300 µm in diam, with a multi-layered cell wall. Asci 8-spored, globose, 8–12 µm. Ascospores lenticular measuring 4.5–7.5 × 4.5–5 µm (including crests), with two widely separted equatorial crests of 1–2 µm and convex surface decorated with spinelike projections, ranging from less than 0.5 µm to as much as 2.0 µm. Conidiophores columnar, uniseriate, 200–400 µm tall and 4–7 µm diam, smooth walled. Vesicles globose to subclavate, 12–18 µm diam. Phialides with a short neck, 6–8 × 2–2.5 µm covering the upper part of the vesicle. Conidia en masse blue-green coloured, globose to subglobose shaped, 2–3 ?m in diam, with a finely roughened wall.
Aspergillus spinosus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph known, neosartorya-type, homothallic.
Aspergillus spinosus.Similar species: Aspergillus fischeri, A. hiratsukae and A. neoglaber are related foodborne species. For more details, see A. fischeri.
Aspergillus spinosus.Physiology: Thermotolerant; good growth 37 °C. Aspergillus spinosus produces heat resistant ascospores that are able to survive a heat treatment.

Aspergillus subalbidus.Holotype: CBS H-21807. Culture ex-type: CBS 567.65T = NRRL 312 = IMI 230752 = ATCC 16871 = CCF 5822.
Aspergillus subalbidus.Diagnosis: Aspergillus subalbidus is closely related to A. taichungensis and A. tenebricus. Aspergillus taichungensis differs from A. subalbidus by its larger colony diameters on MEA, CYA, CY20S, and by its pastel yellow colonies and yellow soluble pigment produced by some strains on CYA and MEA (Table 4). Aspergillus tenebricus has longer phialides and metulae than A. subalbidus. Aspergillus subalbidus differs from A. dobrogensis, A. magnus, A. neotritici, A. candidus and A. campestris by its shorter and narrower stipes and smaller vesicles (Table 5, Fig. 6). Aspergillus pragensis and A. magnus colonies have a smaller diameter compared to A. subalbidus. Aspergillus taichungensis and A. neotritici can be differentiated by their larger colony diameters at 37 °C and by their ability to grow at 40 °C (Table 6).
Aspergillus subalbidus.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus subalbidus germinates or grows restrictedly at 10 °C (3–9 mm). The optimum growth temperature is between 25 °C (18–30 mm) and 30 °C (9–29 mm). Only eight out of 12 tested strains (CBS 567.65T, FMR 15736, NRRL 58123, FMR 15733, CCF 5643, NRRL 4809, CCF 5697, CCF 6197) were able to grow at 35 °C (2–22 mm) and only three out of 12 tested strains (CCF 5643, CCF 5697 and FMR 15733) were able to grow at 37 °C (3–9 mm). No growth at 40 °C.
Aspergillus subalbidus.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (4A1) to yellowish white (2A2, 3A2, 4A2), greyish yellow (4B3) in CBS 112449 and orange grey (5B2) in FMR 15877, flat, slightly raised to crateriform, texture floccose to granular, downy or fluffy, sporulation abundant, margins entire, less frequently slightly irregular or erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4B5), light yellow (4A5) or reddish orange (7B8) in the centre, pale yellow (4A3) or light orange (5A4) on margins. Colonies on CYA white (4A1), yellowish white (2A2, 3A2, 4A2), yellowish grey (4B2), brownish grey (8C2) or greyish brown (8E3) with white (8A1) margins, flat or centrally raised, texture granular, floccose, velvety or downy, sporulation abundant, margins entire, less frequently delicately undulate or erose, reverse brownish orange (5C4, 5C5), greyish yellow Glässnerová et al. (4B4, 4B5, 4B6) or dark blond (5D4) in the centre, light yellow (4A4, 4A5) or golden brown (5D7) on margins, exudate absent, soluble pigment brown in some strains with varying intensity or location after 4 wk: central area between colonies in CCF 4913, CBS 112449, CCF 5697 and CBS 567.65T; 3–4 mm large circle around colonies in NRRL 58123 and CCF 5698; 5–6 mm large circle around colonies in CCF 5643; slightly pigmented areas around sclerotia in strain CCF 6199; rusty brown soluble pigment was present in strain CCF 6197 (6–7 mm around colonies). Colonies on CZA white (4A1), yellowish white (1A2, 2A2, 3A2), greyish yellow (4B3) or reddish grey (7B2) in strain DTO 196-E4, flat or submerged, floccose, waxy or granular, sporulation usually abundant, weak in CCF 5696, CCF 6199, CCF 5642 and CCF 6197, margins entire, less frequently delicately undulate or erose, reverse pale yellow (3A3, 4A3), greyish brown (5E3, 5F3) or greyish yellow (4B3), exudate absent, soluble pigment present in some strains after 4 wk: dark green to black in FMR 15736, NRRL 58123, CCF 5643 (all over the Petri dish), in the central area between colonies in CBS 567.65T, weak greyish green soluble pigment was present in the central area between colonies and Glässnerová et al. slightly around colonies in NRRL 5214, and dark brown soluble pigment was present in DTO 196-E4 (3 mm around colonies). Colonies on CY20S white (4A1), yellowish white (2A2, 3A2, 4A2) or yellowish grey (4B2), flat or centrally raised, irregularly folded, texture floccose, less frequently granular, downy or fluffy, sporulation abundant, margins entire, less frequently erose or undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse brownish orange (5C5, 5C6), light yellow (4A5), greyish yellow (4B4, 4B5, 4B6) or reddish yellow (4A6) in the centre, light yellow (4A4, 4A5) on margins. Sclerotia were produced superficially, less commonly covered by felt of mycelium (NRRL 4809 and CCF 6199 on CZA). After 4 wk of cultivation, they were observed in CBS 567.65T, NRRL 4809, FMR 15877, CCF 6197, CCF 6911, NRRL 5214 and CBS 112449, absent in CCF 5642, CCF 5696, DTO 196-E4, FMR 15733, CCF 4913, CCF 5848, CCF 5697, CCF 6205, CCF 5643, CCF 5698, NRRL 58123 and FMR 15736. Dark brown sclerotia were observed on MEA in FMR 15877, CCF 6197 and CCF 6199, on CYA in CBS 567.65T, CCF 6197, CCF 6199, NRRL 5214 and CBS 112449, on CZA in CCF 6197 and on CY20S in CCF 6197. Brown sclerotia on CZA were observed in CBS 112449, on CY20S in FMR 15877, and sclerotia in various shades of brown were observed on CZA in FMR 15877.
