Aspergillus sydowii.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 18–26 mm after 7 days), velvety, sometimes somewhat floccose, usually consisting of a dense felt of intensely blue green (“Delft blue”) conidiophores. Conidial heads blue green, radiate, exudate reddish brown often abundant. Reverse mostly in shades of reddish brown to dark red (maroon). On CREA good growth, but no acid production. Colonies on CYA at 37 °C: 2–16 mm in diameter after 7 days.
Aspergillus sydowii.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, smooth walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm. Conidial heads radiate to nearly globose, 100–150 µm in diameter, biseriate. Conidiophore vesicles spathulate to subclavate, hyaline, 10–20 µm. Metulae 4–6(–7) × 2–3.5 µm, Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 5–7(–10) × 2–3.5 µm. Conidia colourless, globose to subglobose, (2.5–)3–4 µm, hyaline, conspicuously spinose. Reduced conidial heads on short stipes present in the aerial mycelium.
Aspergillus sydowii.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus sydowii.Similar species: Aspergillus sydowii is closely related to A. versicolor. The former species has blue green conidia and larger rougher walled conidia. Small reduced penicillate conidial heads are common in A. sydowii, but can also occur in A. versicolor. These structures may occur in other members of the Aspergillus versicolor clade.
Aspergillus sydowii.Chemical markers: Aspergillosenes, aspergillusones, aspermutarubrol, diorcinol, 4-hydroxy benzoic acid, expansols, fischeacid, fischexanthone, orcinol, sydo- nic acids, sydowinin A & B, sydowins, WIN64821, WIN 64745. Odour weak.
Aspergillus sydowii.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus sydowii is common world-wide, especially as a marine organism. However it has been found in foods, soil cotton, beans, nuts, straw, cotton fabrics, leather, paper, archives and in indoor air.
Aspergillus sydowii.Physiology: Aspergillus sydowii is halo-tolerant and tolerates low pH.
Aspergillus sydowii.Biodeterioration and pathology: Can cause sea fan disease and human mycoses.

Aspergillus taichungensis.Species description: Aspergillus taichungensis Yaguchi, Someya & Udagawa, Mycoscience 36: 421. 1995. MycoBank MB 434473.
Aspergillus taichungensis.Holotype: PF1167. Culture ex-type: IBT 19404 = CCF 5597 = DTO 031-C6.
Aspergillus taichungensis.Diagnosis: Aspergillus taichungensis has the shortest and narrowest stipes and smallest vesicles in section Candidi (Table 5, Fig. 6). It is micromorphologically most similar to A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus, but differs from these by its pastel yellow colonies, production of yellow soluble pigment by some strains on CYA and MEA, and by its shorter stipes, metulae and phialides, and smaller vesicles. In addition, colonies of A. taichungensis have a larger diameter on CYA and CY20S compared to A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus (Table 4). Aspergillus candidus, A. dobrogensis, A. magnus and A. pragensis can be differentiated by their inability to grow at 37 °C. Colonies of A. neotritici have a larger diameter than A. taichungensis at 37 °C and 40 °C (Table 6).
Aspergillus taichungensis.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus taichungensis germinates or grows restrictedly at 10 °C (4–7 mm). The optimum growth temperature is between 20 °C (20–32 mm) and 25 °C (25–29 mm). Aspergillus taichungensis is able to grow at 37 °C (12–20 mm) and the maximum growth temperature is 40 °C (1–7 mm), but the strain IBT 19404T only germinates at this temperature (1–2 mm).
Aspergillus taichungensis.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA pastel yellow (1A4), flat, texture floccose to granular or velvety, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment yellow (all over the Petri dish, predominantly around colonies) present in DTO 266-G2 and IBT 19404T, reverse yellow (2A8, 3A6) or light yellow (2A5). Colonies on CYA pastel yellow (1A4) or pale yellow (1A3), flat, texture granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment yellow (all over the Petri dish) present in IBT 19404T and DTO 266-G2, reverse yellow (3B8) or deep yellow (4B8) with vivid yellow margins (3A8) or yellowish brown (5D5) with reddish yellow (4A6) margins. Colonies on CZA pastel yellow (1A4), flat, texture granular or waxy, sporulation weak and located in irregular zones, margins irregular, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse pastel yellow (1A4, 2A4). Colonies on CY20S white (2A1) with a tint of yellowish white (2A2), flat to centrally raised, texture granular, downy or floccose, irregularly folded, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A5) or reddish yellow (4A6). Sclerotia produced superficially, less commonly covered by felt of mycelium (DTO 270-C9 on CY20S). After 4 wk of cultivation, they were observed in strains DTO 270-C9 and IBT 19404T, absent in DTO 266-G2. Brown sclerotia were observed on CZA in strain IBT 19404T, and dark brown to black sclerotia on CY20S in strain DTO 270-C9. No sclerotia were observed on MEA and CYA.
Aspergillus taichungensis.Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, usually non-septate, occasionally with septa, (15–)40–90(–215) × (2–)3–4(–5) μm, vesicles hemispherical, elongated, subglobose or globose, (5–)7–11(–15) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (4–)5.5–7(–9.5) μm long, covering three quarters to entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (3.5–)4.5–5.5(–6.5) μm long. Conidia globose to subglobose, (2.5–)3–3.5(–4) (3.4 ± 0.3 μm) × (2.5–)3–3.5(–4) (3.2 ± 0.3 μm), smooth-walled, rarely finely verrucose.
Aspergillus taichungensis.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from soil, agriculture products, caves and house dust. It has been isolated in Iran, Mexico and Taiwan (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Aspergillus tamarii.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 65–85 mm after 7 days), mostly sporulating densely, forming a dense felt of yellow-brown conidiophores, which rapidly turn dark green-brown. Colony texture is velutinous or more often with floccose tufts. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is cream dull yellow to yellow to pinkish drab, but may in some cases be brown, especially in sclerotial strains. Sclerotia produced by some strains, brownish to purplish to black, large, 1–1.2 mm × 1.5–2 mm. On CREA poor growth and no or poor acid production. On AFPA a dark brown to maroon reverse.
Aspergillus tamarii.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, long and coarse, 0.5–2 mm × 10–20 µm. Conidial heads radiate, splitting into separate columns, 500–600 µm in diameter. Conidiophore vesicles globose, 25–50 µm, metulae present, cylindrical 7–10 × 4–6 µm. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 10–15 × 4–8 µm. Conidial heads often biseriate, but heads with only phialides also present. Conidia cylindrical to pyriform when young, later globose to subglobose, 5–6.5(–8) µm, conspicuously roughened from prominent tubercles and bars of brownish yellow colouring matter, the outer and inner conidial wall visible.
Aspergillus tamarii.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus tamarii.Similar species: Aspergillus tamarii resembles A. bertholletius (CBS 143687; CaM: JX198674), A. caelatus (CBS 763.97; CaM: MG518018), A. pseudocaelatus (CBS 117616; CaM: MG517995) and A. pseudotamarii (CBS 766.97; CaM: EF661521). The latter two species produce aflatoxins, while aflatoxins have never been found in A. caelatus and A. tamarii.
Aspergillus tamarii.Chemical markers: Aspirochlorin, (-)-canadensolide, cyclopiazonic acid, speradines, kojic acid. Odour usually weak.
Aspergillus tamarii.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus tamarii is pantropical. It occurs on amaranth, cacao, corn, spices, and other tropical raw material and products.
Aspergillus tamarii.Physiology: Aspergillus tamarii is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate rather low water activities.

Aspergillus tenebricus.Species description: Aspergillus tenebricus Houbraken, Glässnerová & Hubka, sp. nov. MycoBank MB 844203.
Aspergillus tenebricus.Etymology: Latin adj. tenebricus -a -um, referring to dark soluble pigment which is produced on CYA and CZA unlike its close relative A. taichungensis. Glässnerová et al.
Aspergillus tenebricus.Diagnosis: Aspergillus tenebricus is closely related to A. taichungensis and A. subalbidus. It has larger vesicles and longer phialides and metulae than A. taichungensis. Aspergillus tenebricus also produces a dark brown soluble pigment on CYA and CZA after 4 wk compared to A. taichungensis, which can produce a yellow soluble pigment on CYA and MEA. The length of phialides and metulae of A. tenebricus is comparable to A. dobrogensis, A. campestris and A. magnus but longer than other species (Table 5, Fig. 6). The colonies of A. taichungensis have a larger diameter than A. tenebricus on CYA and CY20S (Table 4). Aspergillus candidus, A. dobrogensis, A. magnus and A. pragensis can be differentiated by their inability to grow at 35–37 °C while colonies of A. neotritici and A. taichungensis have a larger diameter than A. tenebricus at 37 °C (Table 6).
Aspergillus tenebricus.Typus: South Africa, Robben Island, soil, 2015, collected by P.W. Crous and isolated by M. Meijer (holotype PRM 957108 (dried culture, metabolically inactive), isotypes PRM 957109–957110, culture ex-type DTO 337-H7 = CBS 147048).
Aspergillus tenebricus.Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus tenebricus is able to grow at 10 °C (9–11 mm). The optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (26–33 mm). Strains DTO 337-H7T and DTO 440-E2 are able to grow at 37 °C (7–12 mm) in contrast to strain DTO 440-E1. No growth at 40 °C.
Aspergillus tenebricus.Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (4A1) to yellowish white (4A2, 2A2), flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins slightly erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4B4). Colonies on CYA yellowish white (4A2), flat with slight radial folding, texture granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown after 4 wk (3–6 mm large circle around colonies), reverse light yellow (4A5, 4A4) or dark blond (5D4). Colonies on CZA white (2A1) to yellowish white (2A2), flat, texture granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown after 4 wk (3–5 mm large circle around colonies), reverse pale yellow (3A3). Colonies on CY20S white (2A1), flat, texture granular to floccose, irregularly folded, sporulation abundant, margins slightly erose or entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4C6) with pastel yellow (3A4) margins. Sclerotia were produced superficially and only on CZA after 4 wk of cultivation. Brown sclerotia were observed in strains DTO 440-E1 and DTO 337-H7T, and absent in DTO 440-E2. No sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S in any of the examined isolates.
Aspergillus tenebricus.Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, usually non-septate, occasionally with septa, (30–)80–140(–310) × (2.5–)3.5–5(–6.5) μm, vesicles subglobose to globose, (8.5–)11–18(–27) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (7–)8–12(–14) μm long, covering three quarters to entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (5.5–)6–7(–8.5) μm long. Conidia subglobose to globose, (3–)3.5–4(–4.5) (3.8 ± 0.2 μm) × (3–)3.5–4(–4.5) (3.6 ± 0.2 μm), smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened.
Aspergillus tenebricus.Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known only from soil. It has been isolated in Australia and South Africa (Fig. 12, Table 1).

Aspergillus terreus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 40–65 mm after 7 days), consisting of a dense velvety felt of yellow brown conidiophores intermixed with aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar. Reverse mostly in shades of cream yellow. Diameter on MEA 45–55 mm after 7 days. On CREA poor growth and no acid production. Growth on CYA at 37 °C even better than at 25 °C.
Aspergillus terreus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, short, green, particularly in the upper part, smooth walled, 150–500 × 5–8 µm. Conidial heads radiate to nearly globose, 100–150 µm in diameter, biseriate, becoming columnar. Conidiophore vesicles globose to subglobose, 10–20 µm. Metulae 5–7 × 2–2.5 µm. Phialides with a short neck, 5–7 × 1.5–2 µm. Conidia colourless, globose to ellipsoidal, 1.5–2.5 µm, hyaline to light yellow, smooth.
Aspergillus terreus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, fennellia-type, heterothallic.
Aspergillus terreus.Similar species: Aspergillus terreus is closely related to A. alabamensis (CBS 125693; CaM: EU147583),
Aspergillus terreus.Chemical markers: Acetylaranotin, aspulvinones, as- terric acid, asterriquinones, butyrolactones, citreoiso- coumarin (only some strains), citreoviridin (only some strains), erdin, geodin, geodoxin, itaconic acid, terrein, terreulactone, terrequinone A, terretonin, territrems (only some strains). Odour weak.
Aspergillus terreus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus terreus is common world-wide, especially in soil.
Aspergillus terreus.Biotechnological applications: Production of mevi- nolin and itaconic acid.
Aspergillus terreus.Biodeterioration and pathology: Aspergillus terreus is an important human pathogen.
Aspergillus terreus.References: Samson et al. (2007, 2011), Balajee et al

Aspergillus versicolor.Species description: Aspergillus versicolor (Vuill.) Tirab., Ann.Bot.(Roma) 7: 9. 1908 ≡Sterigmatocystis versicolor Vuill., Erreur Det. Asp. Paras. Homme: 15.1903. [MB172159].
Aspergillus versicolor.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 13–27 mm after 7 days), velvety, sometimes somewhat floccose, either consisting of a dense felt of conidiophores or of aerial hyphae and closely interwoven mycelium bearing the conidiophores. Colony colour at first white, then changing to yellow, orange-yellow to yellow green, often intermixed with flesh to pink colours. Reverse mostly in shades of cream yellow to reddish brown. Diameter on MEA 9–17(–22) mm after 7 days. On CREA good growth, but no acid production. Growth on CYA at 37 °C: 0(–6) mm diam. after 7 days.
Aspergillus versicolor.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, smooth walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm. Conidial heads radiate to nearly globose, 100–150 µm in diameter, biseriate. Conidiophore vesicles subglobose to ellipsoidal, 12–16 µm. Metulae 5–7.5 × 2–2.5 µm, Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 5.5–8 × 2.5–3 µm. Conidia colourless, globose, 2–3.5 µm, hyaline, echinulate. (Hülle cells present in A. fructus).
Aspergillus versicolor.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Aspergillus versicolor.Similar species: Aspergillus versicolor is closely related to A. sydowii. This species has recently been subdivided into several species. The latter species has blue green conidia and larger rougher walled conidia. Also small reduced conidial heads are common in A. sydowii, but usually absent in A. versicolor.
Aspergillus versicolor.Chemical markers: Aspergillus versicolor sensu lato produces anthcolins, aspercolins, aspergillitine, aspergillones, asperolactones, asperones, calbistrins A and C, cyclopiamin B, diorcinol, mycoversilin, rheoemodin, sterigmatocystin, versicolorins, versimide, versiol. Odour weak or earthy.
Aspergillus versicolor.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus versicolor is common world-wide. Common on cheese, cereals, soil, peanuts, nuts, spices, dry meat products. This species is common in indoor environments.
Aspergillus versicolor.Physiology: Aspergillus versicolor is halo-tolerant and tolerates low pH. It can grow at lower temperatures than most other Aspergillus species.

Aspergillus wentii.Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus wentii is used for katsuo-bushi production.

Monascus ruber.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or OAT at 25
Monascus ruber.Micromorphology: Ascomata are borne terminally on a pedicel, which is commonly up to 150 µm long (occasionally up to 1000 µm). The ascomata wall consists of hyphae and the ascomata are globose, 20–70 µm in diameter, subhyaline to brownish-red. Asci are globose to subglobose, 7.5–10 µm in diameter and the ascospores are yellowish ovate-ellipsoidal, often with a hyaline smooth wall, (4–)5–6 × 3–4 µm. The conidia are borne in basipetal succession in chains from undifferentiated conidiogenous cells. The conidia are ovate to pyriform with a broadly truncate base, 6–8(–11) × 5.5(–10) µm, mostly thin-walled, functioning as chlamydospores when thick-walled.
Monascus ruber.Similar species: Many similar species are described by differences in pigmentation and conidial size, but are insignificant for differentiation at species level (Li & Gou 2004, Stchigel et al. 2004). In the present concept, we regard these species to be synonyms of M. ruber. Monascus ruber is closely related to M. purpureus (Barbosa et al. 2017).
Monascus ruber.Chemical markers: Citrinin, monacolins, monankarins, monascorubramine, rubropunctatin, monascin, moans- codilone, ankaflavin, monascopyridine.
Monascus ruber.Habitats and distribution: This species is cosmopolitan and typically found starch-rich food and feed, such as cooked potatoes, rice, seeds of oat, soya, sorghum, tobacco, olives, bread, silage, but also isolated from soil.
Monascus ruber.Physiology: This species can grow in a wide temperature range between 18 and 40 °C, and does tolerate low oxygen levels and low pH.
Monascus ruber.Biotechnological applications: Monascus has been used for fermentation and as food colouring agent for centuries in Asia. Monascus fermented rice products are sold as cholesterol-lowering agents due to the content of monacolins.

Paecilomyces divaricatus.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA attaining 25–45 mm at 25 °C after 7 days, consisting of a dense felt of numerous conidiophores The colony edge more or less feathery and the texture is velvety or floccose; conidium colour olive-brown; exudates and soluble pigments ab- sent. Colonies on CYA more restricted 8–20 mm (25 °C, 7 days), with no to weak sporulation. Growth on CREA moderate, acid production absent.
Paecilomyces divaricatus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores irregularly or regularly branched, 150–300 µm, at multiple levels; phialides with a broad base and a long narrow neck, 10–20 µm in length; conidia ellipsoidal to cylindrical with truncated ends, measuring 3.5–4.5 × 1.5–2 µm; chlamydospores absent. Ascomata absent on agar media, though ascomatal initials, arising as coils, can be observed. Ascospores are rarely produced and if present
Paecilomyces divaricatus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic co- nidiogenesis, basipetal; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, possibly heterothallic.
Paecilomyces divaricatus.Similar species: See Paecilomyces key. Paecilomyces divaricatus can be differentiated from other food- and airborne Paecilomyces species by a slower growth on MEA and CYA.
Paecilomyces divaricatus.Chemical markers: Cornexistin and/or byssochlamic acid, ascofuranone, emodin and other anthraquinones.
Paecilomyces divaricatus.Habitats and distribution: Isolated heat treated in- gredients (e.g. fruit concentrates, pectin) and pasteu- rised foods (e.g. blueberries, apples).
Paecilomyces divaricatus.Physiology: This species probably produces heat- resistant ascospores and is able to growth at 37 °C.

Paecilomyces formosus.EX_TYPUS: CBS 990.73B = DTO 093-D2 = ATCC 10865 = IMI 58427 = LSHB Pa31 = LSHB X26 = NRRL 1282

Paecilomyces fulvus.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or CYA at 30 °C reach a diameter of 50–90 mm in 7 days, composed of a basal felt with white ascomata, occasionally in localized sectors, covered by a velvety or floccose overgrowth of the conidial morph, which gives the colonies a yellowish brown appearance. Reverse colour is inconspicuous.
Paecilomyces fulvus.Micromorphology: Ascomata are white and up to 150 µm in diameter and ripening in 7 to 10 days at 30 °C. Wall lacking or very scanty, composed of loose wefts of hyaline, thin hyphae of about 1 µm in diameter. Asci are globose to subglobose, 9–12.5 µm in diameter and the ascospores are smooth walled, ellipsoidal and measure 5.0–7.0 × 3.0–4.5. Conidiophores up to 150 µm tall, smooth with phialides born in groups of two to five on short metulae and single phialides are occasionally born directly on the aerial hyphae. Phialides have a cylindrical basal portion, 12.5–17 × 2.5–3.5, and tapering abruptly to a long thin neck, 3–8.5 µm long and 1–1.2 µm in width. Conidia are produced in dry chains and usually cylindrical with flattened ends, 3.7–7.5 × 1.4–2.5 µm. Chlamydospores are usually absent, though occasionally detected in older cultures.
Paecilomyces fulvus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph produced in culture, homo- thallic.
Paecilomyces fulvus.Similar species: Paecilomyces niveus and P. lagunculariae are similar species, but differ in size and shape of the conidia.
Paecilomyces fulvus.Important mycotoxins: Paecilomyces fulvus is claimed to be a patulin producer, though Houbraken et al. (2006) showed that this mycotoxin is not produced by this spe- cies.
Paecilomyces fulvus.Habitats and distribution: This species is cosmopolitan and causes spoilage in pasteurized food products, such as fruit juices and canned strawberries. Paecilomyces fulvus is also commonly occurring in soil and this is often the primary source of spoilage incidents.
Paecilomyces fulvus.Physiology: The ascospores of this species are heat resistant (D90=4–36 minutes, Bayne and Michener 1979). Furthermore, P. fulvus grows well in atmospheres of 20– 60 % CO2 with 0.5 % O2 (Taniwaki et al. 2009) and is able to grow between 10 and 45 °C.

Paecilomyces variotii.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or OA at 30 °C attaining a diameter of 60–90 mm in 7 days, consisting of a dense felt of numerous conidiophores giving the colonies a powdery yellow brown appearance. Reverse colour is inconspicuous.
Paecilomyces variotii.Micromorphology: Conidiophores consist of dense whorls of verticillately arranged branches, each bearing 2 to 7 phialides. Phialides are formed solitary or in whorls, variable in size but mostly 12–20 × 2.5–5.0 µm. Phialides consist of a cylindrical to ellipsoidal basal portion, tapering abruptly to a long, cylindrical, 1–2 µm wide neck. Conidia are one-celled and produced in long divergent chains, hyaline to yellow, smooth walled, predominantly ellipsoidal and ellipsoidal with truncate ends, measuring 3.0–6.0 × 1.5–4.5 µm. Chlamydospores usually present, single or in short chains, brown to dark brown, smooth to slightly rough, subglobose to pyriform, thick walled, 4–8 µm.
Paecilomyces variotii.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, heterothallic.
Paecilomyces variotii.Similar species: The taxonomy of P. variotii has been revised by Samson et al. (2009) and this species was splitted into five species (P. variotii, P. dactylethromorphus (= P. saturatus), P. formosus, P. divaricatus, P. brunneolus). These species can be distinguished on morphological characters, such as acid production on CREA, growth ratios between 30 and 37 or 40 °C, and size and shape of conidia (see also page 206–209). Paecilomyces formosus and P. variotii are to our experience the two most commonly occurring species, followed by P. dactylethromorphus and subsequently P. brunneolus and
Paecilomyces variotii.Habitats and distribution: Paecilomyces variotii is a common contaminant in air and often isolated from substrates originating from higher temperatures e.g. compost. Furthermore, P. variotii also occurs in indoor environments, soil, heat treated products and is able to grow in the preservatives containing foodstuffs.
Paecilomyces variotii.Physiology: The ascospores of P. variotii are heat resistant and have a D85-value between 40–75 minutes (in ACES buffer). Furthermore, this species is thermophilic, growing at a maximum of about 50 °C.

Penicillium alogum.Notes: Penicillium alogum belong to section Stolkia and is closely related to P. stolkiae, P. subarcticum, P. boreae, P. pul- lum and P. canariense (Fig. 4). These species all produce coni- diophores with some brown pigmentation. Penicillium boreae and P. canariense typically produce biverticillate conidiophores, while the others mainly have monoverticillate/simple conidio­phore branching patterns. Penicillium pullum produces large, conspicuously rough walled conidia (3.5–4.5 μm) that turn dark with age, which easily distinguish it from P. alogum. On the other hand, P. subarcticum produces bigger conidia than the new species (3–4 μm) (Peterson & Sigler 2002). From a mor-phological perspective, P. alogum is most similar to P. stolkiae, having similar colony colours, growth rates and conidiophore branching patterns. However, P. stolkiae produces longer phialides (7–10 μm) and slightly larger conidia (2.8–3.5 µm) ﬁde Pitt (1980).

The new species can easily be distinguished from its close relatives by its poor growth on CYA at 37 °C, in contrast to the strong growth of P. singorense (40–43 mm diam) (Visagie et al. 2014a). Also, P. amphipolaria has a more complex con-idiophore branching pattern compared to the generally simple conidiophores of P. singorense (Visagie et al. 2014a).

Penicillium aurantiogriseum.Macromorphology: Colonies growing rather restrictedly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 11–32 mm after 7 days), producing blue green to grey green or dark dull green conidia and granular to fasciculate colonies, with clear to brown exudate droplets. The colony reverse is coloured orange brown yellow with the colour often diffusing into the medium. Strains that are maintained for a long time on agar will often have a yellow to orange reverse colour. On MEA the conidia are blue green with a strong blue element and the velutinous colonies have a distinct yellow reverse, often with the yellow colour diffusing into the agar. On YES agar the degree of sporulation varies, reverse colour distinct yellow. The colonies are growing moderately fast (diameter 24–46 mm after 7 days). On CREA weak growth but strong acid production (few isolates have poor acid production).

Penicillium bissettii.Etymology: Latin, bissettii, named after John Bissett, recently retired mycologist, AAFC Ottawa, who collected and isolated the strains, in honour of his contributions to soil fungus ecology.
Penicillium bissettii.Type specimen: Canada, Quebec, near Lacolle, soil from Spruce forest, 5 Apr. 1977, J. Bissett (holotype DAOM 695761, culture ex-type DAOMC 167011 = CBS 140972 = KAS 1951).
Penicillium bissettii.Molecular markers: ITS barcode: KT887845. Alternative identiﬁcation markers: BenA = KT887806, CaM = KT887767.
Penicillium bissettii.Colony morphology: Colony diam, 7 d, in mm: CYA 42–43; CYA 37 °C no growth; MEAbl 35–43; YES 47–52; OA 45–48; CREA 23–26.
Penicillium bissettii.CYA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderately deep, radially sulcate; margins low, wide, entire; mycelia white; texture floccose; sporu-lation moderately dense, sparse in DAOMC 167033, conidia en masse greyish green to dull green (26C3–D4), greenish grey (26B2); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse brown to dark brown (7E6–F6), yellowish white to greyish yel-low (4A2–B4). MEA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies low, plane, pinkish red underneath mycelial and sporulating areas; margins low, wide, entire; mycelia white, red submerged in media; texture floccose and velutinous; sporulation absent, sparse in some colonies, conidia en masse greyish green to dull green (26D4–E5), greenish grey (26B2); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse greyish red to reddish brown (8B6–D6). YES 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderately deep, radially and concentri-cally sulcate, some strains sporulating in concentrical rings; margins low, wide, entire; mycelia white; texture floccose; sporulation moderately dense, absent in some strains, conidia en masse dull green (26D4–E4), greenish white (26B2); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse brownish orange (6C5), light yellow to greyish yellow (4A3–B5). OA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies low, plane; margins low, wide, entire; mycelia white; texture velutinous and floccose; sporulation sparse, conidia en masse greenish grey to greyish green (26B2–3); soluble pigments pink, absent in DAOMC 167033; exudates absent. CREA 25 °C, 7 d: Weak growth, acid not produced.
Penicillium bissettii.Conidiophores: biverticillate, terverticillate, minor proportion di- varicate; stipes rough, 190–670 × 2.5–3.5 μm; branches 14–25 μm; metulae divergent, 3–4 per stipe or branch, 11–15.5 × 2.5–3.5 μm; phialides ampulliform, 3–6 per metula, 6.5–9 × 2.5–3 μm (7.5 ± 0.7 × 2.6 ± 0.2); average length metula/phialide 1.8; conidia smooth walled, globose to subglobose, 2–3 × 2–3 μm (2.6 ± 0.2 × 2.4 ± 0.1), average width/length = 0.92, n = 72. Extrolites — DAOMC 167033: penicillic acid, uncharacteri­sed C14H19O4N. DAOMC 167011: aurantioclavine, dehydrohis-tidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine, glandicoline B, meleagrin, oxalicine B, roquefortine C, roquefortine M, roquefortine N.
Penicillium bissettii.Extrolites: DAOMC 167033: penicillic acid, uncharacteri­sed C14H19O4N. DAOMC 167011: aurantioclavine, dehydrohis-tidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine, glandicoline B, meleagrin, oxalicine B, roquefortine C, roquefortine M, roquefortine N.
Penicillium bissettii.Additional material examined: Canada, Quebec near Lacolle, soil from Spruce forest, 5 Apr. 1977, J. Bissett, culture DAOMC 167033 (= CBS 140971 = KAS 1949).
Penicillium bissettii.Notes: Penicillium bissettii is classiﬁed in section Lanata-Divaricata in a clade distantly related to all other species in the section. The multigene phylogeny places it closest to P. vas­coniae and P. annulatum (Fig. 7, 8), but on a poorly supported backbone. Penicillium bissettii and P. vasconiae share the production of red mycelia submerged in the media (Ramírez & Martinez 1980). However, P. vasconiae has smooth walled conidiophores, in comparison with the roughened conidiophores of the new species. Penicillium annulatum grows well on CYA at 37 °C in contrast to P. bissettii, which does not grow at this temperature.

Penicillium brevicompactum.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter (8–)14–30 mm after 7 days), consisting of a dense felt of large compact conidiophores. Conidium colour grey green, dull green or yellow green. Colonies are velutinous, often with clear or light yellow exudate droplets. The colony reverse is cream often with a brown centre. On MEA the conidia are grey green to yellow green, velutinous and less dense. On YES agar the degree of sporulation is strong, reverse colour cream-coloured to beige, rarely bright red with the colour diffusing into the medium. The colonies are growing slowly to moderately fast (diameter 20–36 mm after 7 days). On CREA, poor growth and no acid production, however occasionally there is a weak or moderate acid production.
Penicillium brevicompactum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores 300–700 × 4–6 µm, hyaline to light yellow, terverticillate, with all elements appressed, stipes smooth-walled, metulae usually inflated, 9–12 × 4–7 µm, bearing 5–10 phialides. Phialides are cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 7–10 × 3.5 µm. Conidia are globose to subglobose, 2.5–3.2 µm, greenish, smooth-walled or slightly roughened.
Penicillium brevicompactum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Penicillium brevicompactum.Chemical markers: Asperphenamate, botryodiploidin, brevianamides A and B, brevigellin, macrophorin analoge, mycochromenic acid, mycophenolic acid, mycophenolic acid diol lactone, pebrolides, penifulvins, Raistrick phenols, silvatins, xanthoepocin (brevioxim, breviones and compactins are not produced by P. brevicompactum).
Penicillium brevicompactum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Penicil- lium brevicompactum occurs in arctic, temperate and sub- tropical regions. It can be found on cereals, coffee beans, dried salami and other meat products, tomatoes, pota- toes and mushrooms. It often spoils refrigerated pro- ducts, such as meat, cheese and margarine. It also occurs in soil, and is common in indoor air and water-damaged building materials.
Penicillium brevicompactum.Physiology: Penicillium brevicompactum is psychro- and halotolerant. It grows well at low temperatures, but cannot grow at 30 °C. It can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities.

Penicillium camemberti.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 19–27 mm after 7 days), consisting of a raised floccose aerial mycelium usually up to 1 cm high, at first white, remaining so or changing to yellowish, pinkish (rare) or greenish grey, the latter shade usually appearing rather late. Exudate rarely present as colourless drops. The colony reverse is coloured cream or dull yellow. On MEA colonies growing faster, the conidia are grey green, colonies have a pale or light yellow reverse, and are velutinous to granular, rarely fasciculate. Colonies on YES are growing moderately fast (diameter 25–39 mm after 7 days) with weak or moderate conidium production, and colonies have cream yellow reverse. On CREA strong growth with moderate to good acid, followed by base production.
Penicillium camemberti.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, bi- to terverticillate, with all elements appressed, stipes rough-walled, rarely smooth-walled, sometimes becoming ornamented, metulae cylindrical, 8–14 × 2.5– 3 µm, bearing 3–6 phialides. Phialides are cylindrical tapering to a short distinct neck, 10–13 × 2.5 µm. Conidia in tangled chains, globose to subglobose, or broadly ellipsoidal, 4–5 × 3–4.5 µm, hyaline or slightly greenish, smooth-walled. On MEA, conidiophores more abundant and more roughened than on CYA.
Penicillium camemberti.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.

On MEA colonies are mostly growing faster, the conidia are blue green to green with flat velvety or slightly floccose colonies having a pale or yellow reverse. Penicillium chrysogenum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, mono- nematous, terverticillate to quarterverticillate, or even more complicated, 250–500 × 2.5–3.5(–4) µm, stipes smooth, branches somewhat divergent, metulae more or less cylindrical, 8–15 × 2–2.5 µm, bearing 3–6 phialides. Phialides are cylindrical tapering to a short neck, often with a thickened wall, 7–10 × 2–2.5 µm. Conidia in loose columns, at first subglobose to ellipsoidal, remaining so or later becoming globose, hyaline or slightly greenish, smooth-walled, 3.0–4.0 × 2.8–3.8 µm.
Penicillium chrysogenum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely observed in culture, heterothallic.

Penicillium chrysogenum.Physiology: Penicillium chrysogenum is halotolerant and psychrotolerant. It grows well from 5 to 30 °C. Some isolates are able to grow up to 5 mm on CYA in 7 days at 37 °C.

Penicillium corvianum.Notes: Penicillium corvianum is classiﬁed in section Ca­nescentia. Phylogenies (Fig. 3) resolve it in a larger clade with P. canescens, P. jensenii and P. janczewskii. Colonies of the new species are dominated by the presence of abundant cream to brown sclerotia. Sclerotia in the section are not a common feature and are only known from P. coralligerum and P. novae-zeelandiae. However, sclerotia generally do not dominate colony appearance in the latter two species. Also, their conidio­phores are consistently symmetrically biverticillate compared to the more diverse range of conidiophore branching observed in P. corvianum.

Colonies on MEA less dense growing faster, though the sporulation is stronger, grey green colonies. On YES agar moderate sporulation. Reverse cream coloured or occa- sionally distinct blackish green. Penicillium costaricense.Notes: Penicillium costaricense is known from only the one isolate and forms a subbasal branch distinct from the main body of section Charlesia and P. georgiense, the basal species in the section (Fig. 4). The new species produces monoverticillate conidiophores, readily distinguished from the biverticillate to divaricate conidiophores of P. georgiense. The same character also distinguishes it from P. charlesii and P. fellutanum. The remaining species, P. coffeae, P. phoeniceum and P. indicum all produce monoverticillate conidiophores. However, P. indicum (20–30 mm diam) and P. phoeniceum (5–8 mm diam) are able to grow on CYA at 37 °C, in contrast to P. costaricense, which does not grow at 37 °C. Microscopically, P. costaricense most closely resembles P. coffeae, but the latter grows much slower on CYA and MEA (11–17 mm, 11–13 mm diam) than the new species.

Penicillium fimorum.Description: Colony diam, 7 d, in mm: CYA 20–26; CYA15°C 15–20; CYA30°C 8–12; CYA37°C no growth; MEA 20–25; YES 30–37; CYAS 18–22; creatine agar 3–10, weak growth, acid production absent.CYA, 25 °C: Colonies elevated in centre; sporulation strong; co- lony texture velvety, slightly fasciculate in centre; mycelium white; exudate present as large pale brown droplets; soluble pigments present, poor, pale brown; radial sulcate, deep; margin entire to slightly irregular; conidia grey-green; reverse brown. YES, 25 °C: Sporulation moderate to good, mycelium white; exudate absent; soluble pigments present, brown; conidia dull green, grey-green in centre; reverse brown. MEA, 25 °C: Sporulation strong; colony texture velvety, slightly fasciculate in centre; mycelium white; exudate present, large, brown drop- lets; soluble pigments absent; conidia dull green to dark green; reverse brown. DG18, 25 °C: Sporulation strong; colony texture velvety to slightly floccose; mycelium white, conidia dull green; reverse brown in centre, edge pale brown. Ehrlich reaction negative.Sclerotia absent. Synnemata absent. Conidiophores 40–120 µm long, with rough-walled stipes, predominantly terverticillate, occasionally bi- or quarterverticillate, stipe 3.0–4.0 µm wide. Rami 1–3 per stipe, slightly appressed, 10–20 × 3.0–4.5 μm. Metulae (2–)3–5, 9.5–11.5 × 2.5–4.0 µm. Phialides ampulli­form, 3–9 per metula, 8–10 × 2.0–3.0 µm. Conidia in long, deﬁned chains, smooth-walled, ellipsoid, 3.7–4.5 × 3.0–4.0 µm. Extrolites — andrastin A, citreoisocoumarin, palitantin, xan-thoepocin.
Penicillium fimorum.Additional material examined: Denmark, Høve Strand, ex mouse dung, 2009, J.C. Frisvad, cultures CBS 140576 = DTO 159-E9 = IBT 31262 and DTO 159-F1 = IBT 29495.
Penicillium fimorum.Notes: Penicillium fimorum is phylogenetically closely re- lated to P. robsamsonii. Colonies of P. fimorum are velvety on CYA and have a brown reverse, and P. robsamsonii has fasciculate colonies and a pale brown reverse. Furthermore, P. robsamsonii has a violet reaction with Ehrlich reagent (due to the production of chaetoglobosins), while the examined P. fi- morum cultures are negative. Both species also differ in their extrolite proﬁles (also see Table 4). It is interesting to note that P. robsamsonii, P. glandicola, P. vulpinum and P. fimorum were all present on the same sample of mouse dung pellets. No synnemata production by P. robsamsonii and P. fimorum was observed on the mouse dung pellets. It should, however, be noted that the pellets were dry at time of collection, and this might have prevented the production of synnemata on the mouse dung pellets.

Penicillium fundyense.CYA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderately deep, radially sulcate, crateriform; margins low, narrow, entire; mycelia white; texture velutinous; sporulation moderately dense, conidia en masse dull green to greyish green (25E4–5); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse olive (3D4), yellowish white (2A2). MEA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies low, lightly sulcate centrally; margins low, narrow, entire; mycelia white; texture velutinous; sporula-tion moderately dense, conidia en masse dull green to greyish green (25E4–5); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse olive (3E4), greyish yellow (3B4–C4). YES 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderately deep, radially and concentrically sulcate, crateriform; margins low, narrow, entire; mycelia white; texture velutinous; sporulation sparse to moderately dense, conidia en masse greyish green (25B3–C4); soluble pigments absent; exudates deep yellow, inconspicuous; reverse brownish orange (5C6), light yellow to greyish yellow (4A4–B5). OA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies low, plane; margins low, wide, entire; mycelia white; texture velutinous; sporulation sparse to moderately dense, conidia en masse greyish green to dull green (26C3–D3); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent. CREA 25 °C, 7 d: Strong growth, acid not produced.
Penicillium fundyense.Conidiophores: monoverticillate, biverticillate and divaricate both common, often difﬁcult to distinguish between branches and metulae; stipes smooth, 15–200(–400) × 2–2.5 μm; branches 16–30(–47) μm; metulae divergent, 2–4 per stipe, 16–30 × 2–2.5 μm; phialides ampulliform, 8–16 per metula, 6–8.5 × 2–2.5 μm (7.4 ± 0.7 × 2.4 ± 0.2); average length metula/phialide 3.3; conidia smooth walled, globose, 2–3 × 2–3 μm (2.4 ± 0.2 × 2.4 ± 0.2), average width/length = 0.96, n = 46. Extrolites — dehydrohistidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine, meleagrin, N6-formyl-roquefortine C, neoxaline, oxaline, roque-fortine C, roquefortine M.
Penicillium fundyense.Extrolites: dehydrohistidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine, meleagrin, N6-formyl-roquefortine C, neoxaline, oxaline, roque-fortine C, roquefortine M.
Penicillium fundyense.Notes: Penicillium fundyense is classiﬁed in section Exili­caulis, with phylogenies resolving it in a clade with P. cineras-cens, P. citreonigrum and P. citreosulfuratum. The species of this complex are almost impossible to distinguish morpho-logically, but chemically they represent distinct species, which resulted in Visagie et al. (2016b) suggesting the use of ITS and BenA sequences for identiﬁcations of strains in this clade. This approach is followed here, because P. fundyense shows only minor morphological differences from its close relatives, but is phylogenetically distinct from the other three.

Penicillium improvisum.Notes: Phylogenetic analyses resolved P. improvisum, classiﬁed in section Aspergilloides, in a unique clade distinct from the 12 clades recognised by Houbraken et al. (2014) (Fig. 1, 2). Section Aspergilloides species are typically mono-verticillate, but some do produce extra subterminal branches as observed in some conidiophores of P. glabrum, P. armarii, P. athertonense and P. bussumense. In addition, more complex patterns occur in P. saturniforme (biverticillate), P. verhagenii (biverticillate and divaricate) and P. ranomafanaense (divari-cate). In common with the latter two, P. improvisum produces divaricate conidiophores. However, P. ranomafanaense and P. verhagenii produce rough-walled conidia in contrast to the smooth-walled conidia of P. improvisum. Additionally, P. ver-hagenii produces larger conidia (3.5–4 µm) than P. improvisum, while P. ranomafanaense has more ellipsoidal conidia in com-parison to the globose conidia of the new species.

Penicillium nalgiovense.Macromorphology: Colonies growing relatively slow on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 15–35 mm after 7 days), producing white or pale green conidia, mostly consisting of a dense felt of conidiophores giving velvety colonies. On MEA colonies are mostly growing faster, the conidia are white or pale green and flat velvety or slightly floccose colonies having a pale or yellow reverse. Penicillium nucicola.Notes: Classiﬁed in section Canescentia, P. nucicola sits on a well-supported branch distinct from all other species (Fig. 3). Morphologically it resembles P. atrovenetum, P. antarcticum, P. coralligerum, P. novae-zeelandiae and P. herquei (the latter classiﬁed in section Sclerotiora). These species commonly pro-duce broad, symmetrical biverticillate conidiophores with bright yellow and green colours often evident in colonies, as observed for P. nucicola on OA (Fig. 12). However, the restricted growth on MEA (12–14 mm diam) easily distinguishes P. nucicola from all of these morphologically similar species.

Penicillium rubens.Macromorphology: Colonies are growing rapidly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 28–50 mm after 7 days); conidium colour variable: yellow-green, blue green or dull green. Colony texture velvety, sometimes slightly floccose, resembling sectors. Exudates absent or generally present as yellow droplets, occasionally hyaline. Soluble pigments, if produced, yellow. The colony reverse is strong yellow, beige or pale cream. On MEA colonies rapidly growing with blue-green to green conidia, texture velvety and sometimes slightly floccose. On YES agar the degree of sporulation is strong, reverse colour yellow. The colonies are growing rapidly (diameter 40–65 mm, 7 days). On CREA poor to moderate growth with poor acid production.
Penicillium rubens.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, terverticil- late to quarterverticillate, or even more complex branched, 200–300 × 3–4 µm, stipes smooth, branches divergent, metulae cylindrical, 8–12 × 2.5–4 µm, bearing 3–7 phialides. Phialides cylindrical, with short neck, 7–9 × 2–2.5 µm. Conidia in loose columns, globose to subglobose to broadly ellipsoidal, hyaline to slightly greenish, smooth, 2.5–4 × 2–2.5 µm.
Penicillium rubens.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, heterothallic.
Penicillium rubens.Similar species: Penicillium chrysogenum is phenotypically similar to P. rubens and these species are difficult to differentiate phenotypically. They can be differentiated using ?-tubulin sequencing, preferably in combination with calmodulin gene sequencing. Penicillium rubens differs from P. chrysogenum in its extrolite profile: P. rubens produces PR-toxin and a red anthraquinone, while P. chrysogenum produces secalonic acid D & F and haenamindole. For information on other related species that have been found in foods and indoor air: see P. chrysogenum.
Penicillium rubens.Chemical markers: Andrastin A & B, chrysogines (chrysogine, 2-pyruvoylaminobenzamide, 2-acetyl-quin- azolin-4(3H)-one & 2-(2-hydroxypropionylamino)-ben- zamide), citreoisocoumarins, 7-deacetoxyyanuthone, meleagrin, penicillins, PR-toxin, roquefortine C & D, sorbicillins (including bisorbibutenolide, bisorbicillinol, bisvertinoquinol, bisvertinolone, 2’,3’-dihydrosorbicil- lin, oxosorbicillinol tautomer, sorhinones A–C, rezisha- nones A–D, sorbicillin), xanthocillins.
Penicillium rubens.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. This species is, like P. chrysogenum, common in damp buildings and occurs frequently in indoor air, (house) dust and water-damaged building materials. Penicillium rubens has been isolated from various (processed) foods, such as fruit and fruit juices, margarine.
Penicillium rubens.Physiology: Penicillium rubens is halotolerant and psy- chrotolerant. It grows well from 5 to 30 °C and some isolates are able to grow slowly at 37 °C. The minimum water activity supporting growth of P. rubens is 0.82 and the optimum aw is between 0.96 and 0.98.
Penicillium rubens.Biotechnological applications: Penicillium rubens is used for the production of penicillin.

Penicillium salamii.Macromorphology: Colonies growing rather fast on CYA at 25 °C (diameter (14–)25–35 mm after 7 days), with a velvety texture; exudates, when present, in small droplets, clear. Conidium colour grey-green, soluble pigments absent. The colony reverse is in shades of brown: crème-brown, yellow-brown, orange-brown or beige. On MEA, the colonies attain (9–)22–33 mm after 7 days with a velvety texture, sometimes slightly floccose in centre and with grey-green conidia. On YES agar there is strong sporulation, reverse variable: cream-yellow, crème with (crème-) brown center or brown. The colonies are growing fast (diameter (23–)37–50 mm after 7 days). On CREA, poor growth and no or weak acid production. Some isolates produce large greyish brown coloured sclerotia on CYA and MEA.

Penicillium salamii.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Penicillium salamii.Similar species: Penicillium salamii is phenotypically and phylogenetically closely related to P. olsonii. Besides the ecological difference, P. salamii also has a slower growth rate on CYA incubated at 25 and 30 °C.
Penicillium salamii.Chemical markers: Asperphenamate, chrysogine (and precursors), indole alkaloids, xanthoepocin and deriva- tives.
Penicillium salamii.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, isolated from meat (salami, air dried ham, liver pate), factory environ- ments, tea leaves.
Penicillium salamii.Physiology: Optimum growth temperature between 21 and 24 °C and maximum around 30 °C.
Penicillium salamii.Biotechnological applications: Penicillium salamii is a potential candidate to be used as a starter for the fer- mentation of meat.

Penicillium samsonianum.Description: Colony diam, 7 d, in mm: CYA 20–26; CYA15°C 21–28; CYA30°C 5–12; CYA37°C no growth; MEA 16–23; YES 23–32; CYAS 20–27; creatine agar 7–15, poor growth, moder-ate acid production.CYA, 25 °C: Colonies elevated in centre; sporulation moder-ate, mainly in centre; colony texture lanose; mycelium white, occasionally pale brown; exudate absent or present as large pale droplets; soluble pigments absent; radial sulcate; margin entire; conidia dull green, reverse brown. YES, 25 °C: Sporula-tion absent; mycelium white; exudate absent; soluble pigment production absent; reverse yellow. MEA, 25 °C: Sporulation variable; weak, moderate or good; colony texture lanose; my-celium white; exudate absent or present, large droplets, clear; soluble pigments absent; conidia bluish grey-green; reverse brown. DG18, 25 °C: Sporulation moderate to strong; colony texture floccose; mycelium white; conidia grey-green or grey to dull green; reverse pale or pale to pale yellow. Ehrlich reac-tion negative.Sclerotia absent. Conidiophores arising from agar surface, (300–)400–600(–700) μm long, smooth-walled, terverticillate, occasionally bi- or quarterverticillate, stipe 3.5–4 μm wide. Rami 1–3 per stipe, (11–)14–18 × 3–3.5 μm. Metulae (2–)4–6 per ramus, (7–)9–14 × 2–2.5 μm. Phialides 4–6 per metula, ampulliform with distinguishable collula, 9–11 × 2–2.5 μm. Conidia born in short irregularly tangled chains, smooth-walled, globose, 3–3.5 μm. Extrolites — Penitrem A, penitremone A, penitremone B, mycophenolic acid, patulin, roquefortine C.

Penicillium samsonianum.Notes: Penicillium samsonianum is phylogenetically most closely related to P. osmophilum. Penicillium solitum.Macromorphology: Colonies attaining on CYA at 25 °C a diameter of 15–28(–35) mm after 7 days, producing dark green to dark bluish green conidia and velutinous to slightly granular colonies, with clear to dark brown exudate droplets. The colony reverse is coloured cream dull yellow to brown yellow often with a brown centre. On MEA the conidia are green and the velutinous colonies have a pale to sun yellow reverse. Colonies on YES have a diameter of 25–39 mm after 7 days, often with some or none conidium production, and colonies have a bright yellow to yellowish orange reverse. On CREA, moderate or strong growth with acid and often subsequent base production.
Penicillium solitum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, terverticil- late, with all elements appressed, stipes rough-walled, metulae cylindrical, 11–15 × 3–3.5 µm, bearing 5–8 phialides. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 9–11 × 2.5–3 µm. Conidia subglobose, 3.5–4.5 µm, greenish, smooth to slightly rough-walled.
Penicillium solitum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Penicillium solitum.Similar species: Penicillium commune grows slower, has a cream yellow reverse on YES, sporulates poorly on YES, and has grey green conidum colour. Penicillium palitans has less dark conidia, grows faster on all media, and a less vividly yellow colony reverse on YES agar. Penicillium cavernicola, P. echinulatum and P. discolor have rough- walled conidia.
Penicillium solitum.Chemical markers: Compactin, cyclopenin, cyclopenol, cyclopeptin, dehydrocompactin, dehydrocyclopeptin, solistatin, solistatinol, viridicatin, viridicatol.
Penicillium solitum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Penicil- lium solitum is common in arctic and temperate regions. It occurs on refrigerated dried meat, cheese, pate, apples berries, and nuts. It produces a minor rot in apples, pears, plums, cherries and other pomaceous and stone fruits. It also occurs in soil, indoor air and sometimes on water-damaged building materials.
Penicillium solitum.Physiology: Penicillium solitum is halo- and psychro- tolerant. It grows well at low temperatures, and does not or grow poorly at 30 °C. It can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities.
Penicillium solitum.Biotechnological applications: Penicillium solitum is the main producer of the cholesterol-lowering agent compactin (= mevistatin) and is used to produce mevistatin industrially. It is also found to be the dominating surface covering mould on specialities from the Faroe Island, such as naturally fermented wind-dried mutton meat (skærpekød) and lipids (garnatalg, i.e. fat from intestine of mutton).

Penicillium tanzanicum.Notes: Penicillium tanzanicum is classiﬁed in section La­nata-Divaricata. The phylogeny assigns it to a clade of species typically having roughened conidiophores, i.e. P. simplicissi­mum, P. araracuaraense and P. wotroi (Fig. 7, 8). Penicillium tanzanicum does not grow on CYA at 37 °C, in contrast with P. wotroi and P. simplicissimum, which grow at 37 °C. It should be noted that this character has been considered unstable for delineating species in the P. simplicissimum complex (Pitt 1980, Houbraken et al. 2011b). Additionally, P. tanzanicum also grows more restrictedly than P. simplicissimum. Penicillium araracuaraense produces a weak acid on CREA, whereas acid production is absent in P. tanzanicum. The main character distinguishing the new species from all three of its close rela-tives, is the abundant yellowish sclerotia on MEA, which are absent in close relatives.

Penicillium verrucosum.Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 9–24 mm after 7 days), producing pure green conidia and granular to fasciculate colonies, with large clear exudate droplets. The colony reverse is cream often with a brown center. On MEA the conidia are green and the granular to fasciculate colonies have a cream coloured reverse. On YES agar the degree of sporulation is weak, reverse colour red-brown to terracotta. The colonies are growing slowly to moderately fast (diameter 14–32 mm after 7 days). On CREA, poor growth and no acid production.
Penicillium verrucosum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, terver- ticillate, with all elements appressed, stipes rough- walled, metulae cylindrical, 8–13 × 3–4 µm, bearing 5–8 phialides. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 7–9 × 2.2–2.8 µm. Conidia globose to subglobose,
Penicillium verrucosum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Penicillium verrucosum.Similar species: Penicillium nordicum has a cream coloured reverse on YES agar.

Penicillium verrucosum.Habitats and distribution: Food. Penicillium verrucosum is common in arctic and temperate regions. It occurs on cereals, including barley, wheat, rye, oat, and occasionally in flour and on beans and cheese. Discolouration of cheese with red brown spots.
Penicillium verrucosum.Physiology: Penicillium verrucosum is psychro- and halo- tolerant. It grows well at low temperatures, but does not or poorly grow at 30 °C. It can tolerate low pH values and low water activities.

Talaromyces amestolkiae.Macromorphology: Colonies growing rapidly on MEA at 25 °C (30–45 mm, 7 days), consisting of a dense felt of conidiophores, slightly raised at centre, plane, in some colonies black sclerotia produced during longer incuba- tion; margins low, plane, entire (3–5 mm); mycelia white and pastel red; texture floccose in centre with overlaying loosely funiculose; sporulation moderately dense to dense, conidia en masse greyish to dull green; soluble pig- ments absent; exudates absent; reverse dark brown cen- tre fading into reddish brown and greyish yellow to grey- ish orange at margins. Colonies on CYA raised at centre, slightly sulcate; mycelia white, pastel yellow and pastel red; texture floccose in the centre and loosely funiculose; sporulation moderately dense to dense, conidia en masse greyish green; soluble pigments very weak brownish red, in some strains absent (at 37 °C yellowish red); exudates absent; reverse violet brown. On CREA poor growth and weak acid production.
Talaromyces amestolkiae.Micromorphology: Conidiophores biverticillate with a minor proportion having subterminal branches; stipes smooth walled, 90–180 × 2.5–3 µm; branches 15–50 µm; metulae three to six, divergent, 9–15 × 3–4 µm; phiali- des acerose, three to six per metulae, 9.5–12 × 2.5–3 µm; conidia smooth and sometimes finely rough, ellipsoidal, 2–3 × 1.5–2.5 µm.
Talaromyces amestolkiae.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph known but rarely produced in culture, heterothallic.
Talaromyces amestolkiae.Similar species: Talaromyces amestolkiae resembles T. purpurogenus and is distinguished by production of acid on CREA.

Talaromyces amestolkiae.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide and more common in tropic and subtropic regions. Isolated from various food- and feedstuffs (e.g. corn, coffee beans, pineapples), soil and house dust.
Talaromyces amestolkiae.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species is occasionally associated with human infections.

Talaromyces macrosporus.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA are spreading broadly and attain a diameter of 60 to 80 mm after 2 weeks at 25 °C, consisting of a basal felt in which conspicuous yellow numerous ascomata are embedded near the agar surface; usually forming a continuous, thick layer. Asexual morph is scanty formed, usually not affecting the colony appearance.
Talaromyces macrosporus.Micromorphology: Ascomata are usually yellow, but sometimes buff or pinkish to purple-red, globose and measuring 200–700 µm in diameter, ripening within 2 weeks. Covering of the ascomata consist of a few layers of well-developed networks of yellow- pigmented hyphae, surrounded by loose wefts of yellow, often heavily encrusted. Initials consist of club-shaped ascogonia, around which thin antheridia coil tightly several times. Asci are 8-spored, ellipsoidal to subglobose 13–18 × 11–14.5 µm. Ascospores are yellow, ovoidal to broadly ellipsoidal 5–6.5 × 4.0–5 µm, with walls up to 0.5 µm thick and spines up to 1 µm in length. The conidiophores are arising primarily from the substratum, especially in marginal areas, occasionally borne also as short branches from aerial hyphae overgrowing the ascomata, usually erect, 24– 250 × 1.5–2.5 µm. Metulae 2–3(–6) in the verticil, 10–15 × 1.7–2 µm, occasionally lacking. Phialides in whorls of 2 to 7, lanceolate, 8–12 × 1.7–2.5 µm, in
Talaromyces macrosporus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced in culture, homothallic.
Talaromyces macrosporus.Similar species: Talaromyces flavus resembles T. ma- crosporus and has similar growth rates on various agar media. The main difference is the size of the ascospores, which are measuring 3.5–5.0 × 2.5–3.2 µm for T. flavus.

Talaromyces trachyspermus.Micromorphology: Ascomata white at first and become creamish to yellowish in age, globose, 50–350 µm in diameter, usually confluent, ripening within 2 weeks. These structures are have a distinct covering and consist of a network of closely interwoven hyphae, simulating a pseudoparenchymatous wall, surrounded by a loose weft of radiating hyphae, usually encrusted with granules,
Talaromyces trachyspermus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced in culture, homothallic.

Talaromyces trachyspermus.Physiology: This species produces heat resistant asco- spores, which have a D85 of 45 seconds.

Xerochrysium xerophilum.Macromorphology: Colonies on CYA or MEA absent or very restricted (3 mm in diameter). Colour white, becoming pale grey in age.
Xerochrysium xerophilum.Micromorphology: Chlamydospores borne on hyphal tips or in short side-chains of cells (which may themselves be transformed subsequently into arthroconidia) or occasionally on pedicles. Terminal conidia globose, 10–11 µm diameter. Conidia in side-chains smaller, ovate or pyriform, 5–7 × 7–8 µm. Vegetative hyphae rare in mature areas, having formed chlamydospores and arthroconidia, variable in size and shape and intergrading with each other. Chlamydospores globose, 6–9 µm, arthroconidia 4–5 × 3–9 µm, width sometimes exceeding length. All spores are hyaline, thick-walled, and without surface markings.
Xerochrysium xerophilum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic and thallic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Xerochrysium xerophilum.Habitats and distribution: Food. Xerochrysium xerophilum has been isolated from dried fruit and chocolate. It has been reported from USA, UK and Australia.
Xerochrysium xerophilum.Physiology: Xerophilic: minimum water activity for growth is 0.71.

Xeromyces bisporus.Literature: L.R. Fraser, Proc. Linn. Soc. New South Wales 78: 245. 1953.
Xeromyces bisporus.Macromorphology: Colonies on Malt Yeast 50 % Glucose (MY50G) growing slowly reaching about 15 mm in diameter, after two weeks, low, whitish to translucent, more or less shiny. No growth on standard agar media, such as MEA, DG18 or OA.
Xeromyces bisporus.Micromorphology: Development of cleistothecia after 2 weeks; cleistothecia (almost) sessile, maturing after a prolonged incubation period of 4–6 weeks, about 45–125 µm in diam, walls thin, hyaline; asci evanescent containing 2 ascospores. Ascospores more or less lunate, plano-convex, 10–12 × 4–5 µm. Aleurioconidia thick- walled, smooth, 15–20 × 12–15 µm, rounded at the top and with a flattened base.
Xeromyces bisporus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, blastic retrogressive conidiogenesis; sexual morph present on media with low wateractivity.
Xeromyces bisporus.Habitats and distribution: Food. Isolated from low wateractivity products, like tobacco, dried prunes, candied fruits, chocolate, licorice, spices. The fungus often will be visible after a long-term storage and on products with long shelf lives (6 months and longer).
Xeromyces bisporus.Physiology: Extremely xerophilic, is able to growth at aw 0.61, with an optimum aw for growth at 0.85 (Pitt & Hocking, 1997). No or very slow growth on MEA, DG18 or other general isolation media. Good growth and sporulation at 25–30 °C; optimum growth at 30 °C.

Aspergillus nomius.Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (>55 mm at 7 d), producing yellow- green conidia. Colony texture velutinous, sometimes with floccose areas, or floccose, consisting of white or light orange-brown mycelium, and sparse to moderately abundant conidial structures. The colony reverse is dull yellow or in pink or brown shades. Sclerotia large, dark brown to black, vertically elongate, 500–1200 µm, up to 6000 µm in length. On CREA poor growth and poor acid production.
Aspergillus nomius.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, rough walled, variable in length and generally 300–1100 µm, but up to 3000 µm. Conidial heads globose, uni- or biseriate, radiate, often splitting in columns, 150–600 µm in diameter. Vesicles globose to subglobose, 25–65 µm diameter. Metulae, if present, 4–8 × 8–18 µm. Phialides cylindrical, tapering to a distinct neck, 4–7
Aspergillus nomius.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced, petromy- ces-type, heterothallic.
Aspergillus nomius.Similar species: Aspergillus nomius produces yellow- green conidia on MEA and CYA, and in that respect resembles various other commonly occurring, food borne section Flavi members such as A. aflatoxiformans,
Aspergillus nomius.Chemical markers: Aflatoxin B1, B2, G1, G2, anominine, aspergillic acid, aspernomine, kojic acid, a miyakamide, 3-O-methylsterigmatocystin, parasiticol, paspaline, pas- palinine, pseurotin A, tenuazonic acid, versicolorins and other aflatoxin precursors.
Aspergillus nomius.Important mycotoxins: Aflatoxin B1, B2, G1, G2, tenu- azonic acid.
Aspergillus nomius.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus nomius has a worldwide distribution, but is more common tropical and subtropical regions. This species has been isolated from cereals, nuts, cocoa, cassava, house dust and soil.
Aspergillus nomius.Physiology: Aspergillus nomius grows well at 37 °C and it can tolerate rather low water activities.

Aspergillus protuberus.Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus protuberus is common worldwide. This species is common in indoor environments (e.g. air, dust, building materials), but also isolated from cheese, soil and (sewage) water.

Acrostalagmus luteoalbus.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA reaching a diameter of 24–34 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, on OA growing slightly smaller 18–30 mm. The colonies are in orange or red shades (dull orange, orange-brown, brick red) due to the pigmented conidiophores and conidia. Colony texture on OA flat and occasionally hairy in centre; on MEA funiculose. Reverse colour is orange, red or red- brown. Colonies on DG18 restricted, often less than 10 mm after 7 days at 25 °C.
Acrostalagmus luteoalbus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores consisting of dense whorls of verticillately arranged branches, arising from submerged or aerial hyphae, erect and more or less straight. Phialides arising in whorls of 2–5(–7) along the main stipe and its branches, slender, flask-shaped, hyaline to light orange, smooth-walled, 10–14 µm long, 2–3 µm wide at the base, with an inconspicuous collarette. Conidia ellipsoidal, orange to reddish brown
Acrostalagmus luteoalbus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Acrostalagmus luteoalbus.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide. Isolated from indoor environment (air, plaster), water, decaying timber, various soil types, including alkaline soils, a variety of types of plant debris, as well as dung. Acrostalagmus. luteoalbus is also known as a mycoparasite.
