Alternaria alternariae.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES at 25 °C attaining a diameter of 32–34 mm in 7 days, appearing folded and green with a thin, white rim. Reverse is black. Colonies on PCA are 42–46 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/ darkness with a yellow extracellular pigment. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 24–26 mm in 7 days at 25
Alternaria alternariae.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are simple, branched and/or geniculate with several conidiogenous loci, 6–30 × 3–4 µm, mostly smooth, orange brown and arise from the agar surface or from aerial mycelium. Conidia are solitary, broadly elipsoidal to obovoid, 20–33 × 13–15 µm, finely verrucose, becoming verrucose to tuberculate with age, 2–4 transverse, 0–3 oblique or longitudinal septa and are chestnut brown with darker septa and outer walls.
Alternaria alternariae.Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic, acropetal conidiogenesis (poroconidia); sexual morph not known.
Alternaria alternariae.Similar species: Alternaria oudemansii (= Ulocladium oudemansii) has a similar morphology on PCA as A. alternariae, but also produce geniculate secondary conidiophores with solitary conidia. Alternaria chartarum (= Ulocladium chartarum) differs from A. alternariae by also producing conidia in short unbranched chains
Alternaria alternariae.Molecular markers: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AY376329; ITS: AY376642 (section level identification).
Alternaria alternariae.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Alternaria alternariae has been isolated from bean, nuts and seeds, and very common in dust, wallpaper, gypsum wallboard and plaster from water damaged building materials. It is often found growing on damp materials, but rarely gets airborne. Reported from Europe and North America.
Alternaria alternariae.Biotechnological applications: Used as a biological control agent against Botrytis spp. in grape, tomato and strawberries and a potential biological control agent against rice blast disease.
Alternaria alternariae.References: Simmons (1969, 1998), Andersen & Hollensted (2008), Pedersen et al. (2009), Andersen et al. (2011, 2016), Woudenberg et al. (2013)
Alternaria alternariae.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Alternaria alternata.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 38–40 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing light green, velvety and sulcate. Reverse is brownish- green. Colonies on PCA are 70 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/darkness. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing dark green, flat and velvety. Reverse is blackish-green. No sporulation on DG18 and DRYES and sparingly on MEA.
Alternaria alternata.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are short, 20–40 × 3–4 µm, and arise either from the agar surface or from aerial mycelium. They are smooth, dark and occasionally branched. Conidia are produced in long, unbranched chains via short, apical secondary co- nidiophores, 3–20 × 3–4 µm. Commonly chains contain between 10–15 conidia. Conidium body is ovoid to long- ellipsoid, sometimes tapering into a true beak, 7–60 × 5–15 µm, with 1–8 transverse septa, of which 1–2 are constricted, and 0–2 longitudinal septa. Conidium surf- ace is punctate to verrucose and golden to brown in co- lour with darker septa. Sometimes side branches of 2–4 conidia are produced via short, secondary conidiopho- res, 6–12 × 3–4 µm, originating from a basal or central cell of an older conidium.
Alternaria alternata.Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic acropetal conidiogenesis (poroconidia); sexual morph not known.
Alternaria alternata.Similar species: Alternaria alternata belongs to the A. alternata species complex in sect. Alternaria. Some species, like A. tomaticola and A. interrupta have sporulation patterns similar to A. tenuissima (CBS 918.96 and CBS 124277) and are reported in the literature as belonging to the A. alternata species complex together with A. tenuissima. Other species, like A. longipes and A. gaisen also have similar sporulation patterns are distinct species. These species are plant pathogens and produce host specific toxins
Alternaria alternata.Molecular markers: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AY278808, KP124225; ITS: AF347031,
Alternaria alternata.Chemical markers: Alternaria alternata (CBS 124277) produce altenuenes, alternariols, altertoxins, tentoxin and tenuazonic acid.
Alternaria alternata.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Alterna- ria alternata has been isolated from black cereal grain, nuts, mouldy solanaceous vegetables, citrus, pomacea- ous and stone fruit. Alternaria tenuissima is sometimes found in water damaged buildings in wet insulation ma- terials, on plywood, gypsum wallboard and wallpaper. Reported worldwide.
Alternaria alternata.References: Andersen et al. (2005, 2009), Simmons (2007), Woudenberg et al. (2013), Ariyawansa et al. (2015), Lawrence et al. (2016)
Alternaria alternata.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Alternaria arborescens.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 35–38 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing dark green, velvety and sulcate. Reverse is blackish- green. Colonies on PCA are 70 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/darkness. The long arborescent conidiophores are produced in the darker concentric rings. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 30–34 mm in 7 days at 25
Alternaria arborescens.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are long, mostly 200–300 × 3–4 µm, but can be up to 900 µm in the dark rings. They are erect and branching at the top resembling a tree trunk. The first couple of conidia in a cluster usually have a large conidium body, up to 50 × 20 µm, and long, geniculate secondary conidiophores, up to 100 × 3–4 µm, with several conidiogenous loci. These ellipsoidal or obpyriform conidia with 2–5 transverse septa and 0–3 longitudinal septa start the characteristic compact branching pattern. The later conidia are smal- ler and produce short, apical secondary conidiophores, 3–15 × 3–4 µm, with 1 or 2 conidiogenous loci. Conidium body is ovoid to ellipsoid, 12–30 × 7–11 µm, with 1–4 transverse septa and 0–2 longitudinal septa. Conidia are finely rough to verrucose, while both types of conidiop- hores are smooth and septate, except for the shortest of the secondary conidiophores. Conidia and conidiophores are straw to brown in colour with very dark septa and wall.
Alternaria arborescens.Morphs: Asexual morph present,enteroblastic, acro- petal conidiogenesis (poroconidia); sexual morph not known.
Alternaria arborescens.Similar species: Alternaria arborescens belongs to the A. arborescens species complex in sect. Alternaria. Several species (e.g. A. cerealis and A. senecionicola) and undescribed taxa have sporulation patterns similar to
Alternaria arborescens.Molecular markers: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase AY278810, KP124264; ITS: AF347033,
Alternaria arborescens.Chemical markers: Members in the A. arborescens species complex produce alternariols, altenuene, altenusin, tentoxin and tenuazonic acid. Alternaria arborescens (CBS 102605) is the only isolate in the species complex that produces AAL toxins.
Alternaria arborescens.Habitats and distribution: Food. Members of the A. arborescens species complex have been isolated from ber- ries, nuts, apples and solanaceous vegetables. Reported worldwide.
Alternaria arborescens.References: Simmons (2007), Woudenberg et al. (2013), Andersen et al. (2015), Lawrence et al. (2016)
Alternaria arborescens.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Alternaria atra.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 37–40 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing folded, deep green with a whitish centre. Reverse is black. Colonies on PCA are 49–51 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/darkness. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 25–27 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing downy with a deep green colour. Reverse is blackish green.
Alternaria atra.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are simple, branched and/or geniculate with many conidiogenous loci, 6–70 × 3–5 µm, smooth and golden brown and arise from the agar surface or from aerial mycelium. Conidia are globose 16–18 µm in diameter and have 1 transverse and 0–1 longitudinal septa or obovoid, 20–24 × 14–16 µm and have 3–4 transverse and 1–2 longitudinal septa, verrucolose and golden to brown in colour with darker septa and outer wall, becoming opaque and verrucose with age. They are solitary and are produced either directly on primary conidiophores or rarely on an obovoid conidium via a long, 10–20 × 3–4 µm, apical and geniculate secondary conidiophore with many conidiogenous loci.
Alternaria atra.Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic, acropetal conidiogenesis (poroconidia); sexual morph not known.
Alternaria atra.Similar species: Alternaria terricola (= U. tuberculatum) has grossly tuberculate conidia on PCA, whereas A. atra has verrucose conidia.
Alternaria atra.Molecular markers: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AY562418; ITS: FJ266483 (section level identification).
Alternaria atra.Habitats and distribution: Food. Alternaria atra has been isolated from fruit and vegetables. Reported from Europe, North America and New Zealand.
Alternaria atra.References: Simmons (1969, 1998), Andersen & Hollensted (2008), Pedersen et al. (2009), Woudenberg et al. (2013)
Alternaria atra.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Alternaria cucurbitae.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 28–31 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing folded, deep green with a lighter green centre. Reverse is black. Colonies on PCA are 56–59 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/darkness. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 19–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing downy with a deep green colour. Reverse is black.
Alternaria cucurbitae.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are simple, branched and/or geniculate with many conidiogenous loci, 6–60 × 3–4 µm, smooth and golden brown and arise from the agar surface or from aerial mycelium. Two types of conidia are formed. The first type to be produced is the alternarioid ones, which are evident in cultures 2–3 days old. These conidia are long ellipsoidal, 28–47 × 11–15 µm and smooth. They are pale brown with 2–6 transverse and 0–3 longitudinal darker septa and outer wall. The second type, the ulocladioid one, appears after 3–4 days, either on primary conidiophores or on secondary conidiophores produced by an alternarioid conidium. The secondary conidiophores are 28–70 × 3–4 µm, apical and geniculate with many conidiogenous loci. The ulocladioid conidia are solitary, globose, 14–17 µm in diameter with 1 transverse and 0–1 longitudinal septa. They are densely verrucolose, golden to brown in colour with darker septa and outer wall, becoming opaque and verrucose with age.
Alternaria cucurbitae.Morphs: Asexual morph present,enteroblastic, acropetal conidiogenesis (poroconidia); sexual morph not known.
Alternaria cucurbitae.Similar species: Alternaria consortiale (= U. consortiale) has a similar morphology on PCA as A. cucurbitae, but differs in having ulocladioid conidia that are smoother and obovoid with a narrowing basal end. Alternaria oudemansii (= U. oudemansii) also differs from A. cucurbitae on PCA by having ulocladioid conidia that are smoother and obovoid with a rounded basal end.
Alternaria cucurbitae.Molecular markers: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AY562418; ITS: FJ266483 (section level identification).
Alternaria cucurbitae.Habitats and distribution: Food. Alternaria cucurbitae has been isolated from cereals, onion, pomaceaous and stone fruit, especially apple. Reported from Europe and New Zealand.
Alternaria cucurbitae.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Alternaria infectoria.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 30–35 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing white and hairy. Reverse is reddish brown. Colonies on PCA are 70 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/darkness, producing conidia in tufts. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 15–17 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing greyish white and downy. No sporulation on DRYES or MEA.
Alternaria infectoria.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are short, 20–80 × 3–4 µm, and arise either from the agar surface or from aerial mycelium. They are smooth, dark and geniculate with 0–3 conidiogenous loci. Conidia are produced in chains that often branch via long, 3–130
Alternaria infectoria.Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic, acro- petal conidiogenesis (poroconidia); sexual morph not known.
Alternaria infectoria.Similar species: Alternaria infectoria belongs to sect. Infectoriae. Several other species (e.g. A. arbusti, A. oregonensis, A. triticina and A. triticimaculans) and undescribed taxa have sporulation patterns similar to
Alternaria infectoria.Molecular markers: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AY278793; ITS: AF347034 (section level identification).
Alternaria infectoria.Chemical markers: Members in sect. Infectoriae produ- ce infectopyrones, and many produce novae-zelandines and altertoxin derivatives.
Alternaria infectoria.Habitats and distribution: Food. Members of sect. Infectoriae have mostly been isolated from poaceaeous grasses, like barley, oat, rye, wheat and maize, but have also been isolated from human and animal skin lesions. Can be detected in indoor air and dust due to outdoor air. Reported worldwide.
Alternaria infectoria.Physiology: Members of sect. Infectoriae are sensitive to cyclohexamide and some isolates are able to grow at 35–37 °C on PDA.
Alternaria infectoria.Biodeterioration and pathology: Alternaria triticina is pathogenic to wheat plants. Some members of sect. Infectoriae can cause cutaneous infections in humans and animals.
Alternaria infectoria.References: Simmons (2007), Labuda et al. (2008), Andersen et al. (2009), Lawrence et al. (2014, 2016)
Alternaria infectoria.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Arthrinium.Macromorphology: Colonies flat, spreading, with mod- erate aerial mycelium. On PDA surface pale luteous with patches of olivaceous-grey, reverse pale luteous. On OA surface dirty white, reverse pale luteous. On MEA sur- face pale luteous, reverse luteous.
Arthrinium.Micromorphology: Conidiophores reduced to conidiogenous cells. Conidiogenous cells aggregated in clusters on hyphae, brown, verruculose, globose to clavate to doliiform, 5–7 × 4–5 µm. Conidia brown, smooth, guttulate, globose to somewhat ellipsoid in surface view, lenticular in side view, with pale equatorial slit, (7–)9–10(–11) µm diam in surface view, 6–7 µm diam in side view, with central scar, 1.5–2 µm diam. Setae erect, brown, smooth, subcylindrical, tapering in apical cell to subobtuse or obtuse apex, 1-septate, base truncate, to 100 µm tall, 5–8 µm diam. Mycelium consisting of smooth to finely verruculose, hyaline to pale brown, branched, septate, 3–5 µm diam hyphae.
Arthrinium.Morphs: Asexual morph present, hololastic, basipetal, basauxic conidopogenesis,; sexual morph known but not produced in cuture.
Arthrinium.Chemical markers: (Arthinium spp.): Arthichitine, arthione, bostrycin, decarboxyhydroxyhydroxycitrinone, echinocandin A, (-)-hexylitaconic acid, libertellone E & F, 3-nitropropionic acid, papulaspordin A & B, terpestacin.
Arthrinium.Important mycotoxins: Arthrinium aureum, A. phaeo- spermum, A. sacchari, A. saccharicola, A. serenense and
Arthrinium.Habitats and distribution: Arthrinium spp. is wide- spread in commonly occurs as a saprobe on grasses, and also on leaves, stems and roots of a range of different plant substrates (Agut & Calvo 2004).
Arthrinium.Biodeterioration and pathology: Arthrinium is ecologically diverse and has been reported as a plant pathogen, with A. arundinis causing kernel blight of barley (Martínez-Cano et al. 1992), and A. sacchari causing damping-off of wheat (Mavragani et al. 2007). It also causes moulding of sugarcane.
Arthrinium.References: Ellis (1965, 1971), Samuels et al. (1981), Wei et al. (1994), Ming (1995), Agut & Calvo (2004), Seifert et al. (2011), Crous & Groenewald (2013), Wang et al. (2017)
Arthrinium.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Aureobasidium melanogenum.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 24 °C attaining a diameter of 40 mm in 7 days, smooth, soon covered with a slimy mass of spores, yellow, cream, pink, brown or black. Aerial mycelium sometimes formed, scanty, thinly floccose.
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Micromorphology: Hyphae 2–16 µm in diam, hyaline, smooth- and thin-walled. In older cultures dark brown, thick-walled hyphae may be formed. These thick-walled hyphae may act as chlamydospores or often fall apart into separate cells (arthroconidia). Conidiogenous cells undifferentiated, intercalary or terminal on subhyaline hyphae or arising as short lateral branches. Blastic conidia produced synchronously in dense groups from indistinct scars or denticles (they can be produced all over the cell surface). Conidia one-celled, (7.5–)9–11(–16) × (3.5–)4–5.5(–7) µm, often with an indistinct hilum (= a mark or scar at the point of attachment), hyaline, smooth- walled. Secondary smaller conidia often produced. Endoconidia not common, but formed by an intercalary cell and released into a neighbouring empty cell.
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal conidiogene- sis; sexual morph not known.
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Similar species: Aureobasidium pullulans is closely related with A. melanogenum. The colonies of the former species remain pink, light brown, or yellow for at least three weeks, while the colonies A. melanogenum become black or greenish-black quickly. The dark hyphae in A. melanogenum often fall apart into separate cells.
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Molecular markers: Aureobasidium melanogenum, ITS: FJ150886; ?-tubulin: FJ157858. Aureobasidium pullu- lans, ITS: FJ150906; ?-tubulin: FJ157869.
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Typical cultures: Aureobasidium melanogenum: CBS 105.22; A. pullulans: CBS 100524
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Aureo- basidium species are saprophytes with a world-wide distribution. They have been isolated from soil, leaf surfaces of trees, such as oak, beech, maple and poplar and from rocks and monuments. They have been recorded from various foodstuffs, such as wheat-, barley- and oat grain, from flour, tomato, fresh harvested pecans, pears, grapes, fruit-juices and frozen fruit-cakes. Furthermore, they are also common in wet or water-damaged indoor environments, such as bathrooms, window frames, and have been isolated from human skin and nails.
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Physiology: Aureobasidium melanogenum has a mini- mum at 10 °C, optimum at 30 °C, maximum at 35 °C. The maximum tolerated salt concentration is 10 %; Aureobasidium pullulans has other growth characteristics: minimum growth temperature of 4 °C, an optimum at 25
Aureobasidium melanogenum.Biotechnological applications: Aureobasidium melano- genum is used a biofinish on wood; A. pullulans is known for its biotechnological significance as a producer of the biodegradable extracellular polysaccharide (EPS) pullu- lan (poly-?-1,6-maltotriose).
Aureobasidium melanogenum.References: Zalar et al. (2008), Slepecky & Starmer (2009), van Nieuwenhuijzen et al. (2016)

Botryosporium pulchrum.Macromorphology: Colonies growing restricted on MEA at 25 °C, attaining a diameter of 8–25 mm, producing white colored conidia. Colony texture floccose and mycelium white. Exudate occasionally produced as clear droplets.
Botryosporium pulchrum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores, (75–)200–800(– 1600) × (8–)10–15(–21) µm, stipes smooth or with a limited surface granulation just below the vesicle, hyaline or pigmented just below the vesicle. Vesicles globose to elipsoidal, (30–) 35–70 (–90) µm diam. Conidial heads
Botryosporium pulchrum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic synchro- nous conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Botryosporium pulchrum.Similar species: Several species have been described in the genus Botryosporium and a recent taxonomic
Botryosporium pulchrum.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, isolated from indoor air, fruit (tomato) decaying plant material.

Botrytis cinerea.Macromorphology: Colonies at 20 °C attaining a diameter of 60 mm or more in 10 days on most media. Colonies are hyaline at first, later becoming grey to greyish brown. Sclerotia are black, consisting of a medulla and a dark brown to black cortical layer of cells and are extremely variable in shape and size.
Botrytis cinerea.Micromorphology: Conidiophores are frequently up to 2 mm and 16–30 µm wide, brown below, smooth-walled and with an apical head of alternate branches. Conidia are obovoid, 8–14 × 6–9 µm, usually with a protuberant hilum. They are pale brown, hydrophobic and smooth- walled. Microconidia produced on sporodochia (spermo- dochia), flask-shaped phialides often present, globose and 2.5–3 µm in diameter.
Botrytis cinerea.Morphs: Asexual morph present holoblastic synchronous conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced on natural substrates, but not in culture.
Botrytis cinerea.Molecular markers: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase subunit II: AJ745676; glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AJ705004; ITS: AJ745676.
Botrytis cinerea.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Botrytis cinerea has a world-wide distribution, but is mainly occurring in humid temperate and subtropical regions. It can be facultative parasitic on a wide range of plants. This so-called “grey-mould” can damage flowers, leaves, stems and causes fruit- and leaf-rot in grapes, strawberries, cabbage and lettuce. Also isolated from soils as well as stored and transported fruit and vegetables, contamination probably occurred already in the field.
Botrytis cinerea.Physiology: Conidium production can be stimulated growing the cultures on PCA and hay-infusion agar in near-UV (“black”) light. Optimum growth (21–)22–25(– 30) °C, minimum (-2–)5–12 °C and maximum (28–)33–
Botrytis cinerea.Biotechnological applications: “Noble rot” of grapes by B. cinerea. These grapes are subsequently used for the production of specific wine.
Botrytis cinerea.Biodeterioration and pathology: Botrytis cinerea is capable to spoil various types of fruits. The genus Botrytis comprises one generalist, B. cinerea, and this species is able to infect weakened or wounded plants. Other species are serious plant pathogens. Botrytis cinerea on grapes might also cause “winegrower’s lung”, a rare form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (a respiratory allergic reaction in predisposed individuals).

Cadophora.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 20 °C attaining a diameter of 23–30 mm in 10 days, more or less velvety, often with an almost hyaline margin, olivaceous-brown. Reverse dark brown to black.
Cadophora.Micromorphology: Hyphae brownish, walls usually becoming distinctly encrusted with age. Phialides borne singly, laterally or terminally on the hyphae or in clusters, flask-shaped, brownish with a collarette, 6–10(– 30) × 2.2–3(–4.2) µm. Conidia subglobose, obovoid to ellipsoidal, often apiculate at base, sometimes slightly curved, 3–6(–7) × (1.5–)2–3(–3.8) µm, subhyaline to light brown.
Cadophora.Morphs: Phialophora-like asexual morph, basipetal, phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Cadophora.Molecular markers: Cadophora fastigiata, ITS: AY249073; elongation factor 1?: KM497087. Cadop- hora malorum, ITS: AY249059; elongation factor 1?: KM497090.
Cadophora.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor envi- ronments. This species is reported throughout Europe, North America, Uganda, Russia, New Zealand and Aus- tralia. Isolated from wood and wood pulp, soil, wheat, seeds of cultivated grasses.

Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Macromorphology: Colonies attaining a diameter of (20–)25–30(–35) mm on OA after 7 days at 25 °C; similar colony diameters on MEA and smaller colonies on DG18, 4–11 mm. Colony colour in sporulating areas brown to blackish brown. Typical synnemata are lacking in young cultures (less than 7 days). Synnemata produced after prolonged incubation, and readily visible for the naked eye. Reverse on MEA uncoloured, on OA uncoloured or having a brown centre.
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Micromorphology: Synnemata up to 3 mm tall, grey-brown, with a well-developed stipe and having an ellipsoidal or cylindrical sporulation portion. The ultimate synnematal branches bear the annellides and may give rise to curled sterile setae. Sterile setae subhyaline or brown, unbranched, coiled once or twice, even in diameter, variable in length and abundance, 150
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Similar species: Five Cephalotrichum spp. are common in the built environment: C. domesticum, C. gorgonifer, C. microsporum, C. purpureofuscum and C. verrucisporum. A key to species is given on p. 44 of this book; C. domesti- cum phenotypically resembles C. purpureofuscum.
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Habitats and distribution: Occurring worldwide in indoor environment (air, plaster, wood), cultivated soils, decaying vegetable material.
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Physiology: Cephalotrichum gorgonifer is able to grow at 37°C.
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.Biodeterioration and pathology: Cephalotrichum gorgonifer has been isolated from human clinical samples and can grow at human body temperature.
Cephalotrichum gorgonifer.References: Domsch et al. (2007), Sandoval-Denis et al

Cephalotrichum microsporum.Macromorphology: Colonies attaining a diameter of (10–)20–25(–30) mm on OA after 7 days at 25 °C; similar colony diameters on MEA and smaller colonies on DG18, 3–10 mm. Colony colour in sporulating areas green-brown or grey. Typical synnemata are lacking in young cultures (less than 7 days). Synnemata produced after prolonged incubation, and readily visible for the naked eye.
Cephalotrichum microsporum.Micromorphology: Synnemata up to 1 mm tall, grey, with a slender sporulating portion, pointed when young, more rounded when sporulating to the tip. Annellides 4–9 × 3–4 µm in length. Conidia ovoid, truncated at one end, with a slightly pointed tip, smooth-walled, 3.5–5 × 2–3 µm.
Cephalotrichum microsporum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Cephalotrichum microsporum.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Cephalotrichum mi- crosporum has a worldwide distribution and is related to wet cellulose containing substrates, like wood. However, they can also occur on rotting plants, soil or dung.
Cephalotrichum microsporum.Physiology: The optimum growth temperature is around 25 °C. No growth at 5 °C, reduced growth at 30 °C and no growth 37 °C.
Cephalotrichum microsporum.References: Morton & Smith (1963), Sandoval-Denis (2016), Woudenberg et al. (2017)
Cephalotrichum microsporum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Chaetomium cochlioides.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA and MEA reach diameters of 70+ mm at 25 °C in 7 days, appearing yellowish green with darker brownish green centre due to dense ascomata production. Ascomata (perithecia) are formed after 1 week in a dense layer on OA and MEA giving the colony an olive-greyish to brownish green appearance, but ascospores are first fully mature after 2 weeks. Colonies on PCA are 52–58 mm after 7 days with thin and yellowish mycelium and well separated olive grey perithecia. Colonies on DG18 reach a diameter of 19–25 mm in 7 days at 25 °C and have a greyish to yellowish white colour. No ascomata production on DG18.
Chaetomium cochlioides.Micromorphology: Perithecia on PCA are superficial, brownish green to dull green sometimes with a yellow hue when viewed in reflective light. They are subglobose to ellipsoid, 200–440 µm in high and 140–420 µm in diameter excluding perithecial hair. Perithecial hairs are numerous, unbranched, septate, flexuous, loosely curled at the lower part and spirally coiled, which decrease in diameter towards the tip. They are dark brown and rough,
Chaetomium cochlioides.Morphs: Asexual morph absent; sexual morph readily produced on OA, homothallic.
Chaetomium cochlioides.Similar species: Chaetomium coarctatum resembles C. cochliodes, especially the ascospore shape and the coiled hair, but the colonies of C. coarctatum are paler, the
Chaetomium cochlioides.Molecular markers: RNA-polymerase II second largest subunit (rpb2): KX976829; ?-tubulin (tub2): KX976949.
Chaetomium cochlioides.Chemical markers: Chaetochalasin A, chaetosin A, chaetocochin C, chaetomin, chaetoviridins A to E, che- toseminudin A cochliodinol B, prochaetoglobosins I-IV, rotiorinol. Some strains produce geosmin, which has a mouldy, sewer-like earthy odour.
Chaetomium cochlioides.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Chaetomium cochliodes is less widespread that C. globosum, but more common in USA. It is frequently detected on cellulose containing materials, such as gypsum wallboard, plywood, wallpaper, books, textile and cardboard, after severe water damage. It has also been isolated from herbivorous dung.
Chaetomium cochlioides.Physiology: The optimum temperature for the production of ascomata is 18–24 °C. The ascospores are not heat resistant, but thermotolerant and can be very resistant to dry circumstances and UV irradiation. Growth and ascomata production, on the other hand, requires a high water activity.
Chaetomium cochlioides.Biodeterioration and pathology: Chaetomium cochlio- des is able to deteriorate cellulosic materials, such as wet cardboard and cotton fabric and cause soft-rot in wood.

Chaetomium elatum.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA and MEA reach diameters of 70+ mm at 25 °C in 7 days, appearing yellowish to olive green, sometimes with honey coloured exudate and reverse on OA. Ascomata (perithecia) are formed after 1 week in a dense layer on OA and MEA giving the colony an olive-greyish to yellow green appearance, but ascospores are first fully mature after 2 weeks. Colonies on PCA are 52–61 mm after 7 days with thin and greenish yellow mycelium and well separated olive grey perithecia. Colonies on DG18 reach a diameter of 18–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C and have a pale yellow to pinkish white colour. No ascomata production on DG18.
Chaetomium elatum.Micromorphology: Perithecia on PCA are superficial, olive grey sometimes with a yellow hue when viewed in reflective light. They are subglobose to obovoid, 280–440 µm in height and 255–380 µm in diameter excluding perithecial hair. Perithecial hairs are numerous, branched, septate, erect, flexuous and sometimes undulate. They are dark brown and verrucose, 3–5 µm at the base, repeatedly and dichotomously branched and tapering and fading towards the tip. Asci are clavate or fusiform, 36–49 × 12.5–16.5 µm with a 24–55 µm stalk and contain 8 ascospores. The asci disappear as the ascospores mature. The ascospores are brown when mature, broadly fusiform or lemoniform, usually apiculate in both ends. They are bilaterally flattened (10–)11.5–13.5(–16) × (8–)8.5–10(–11) × (6.5–)7–8
Chaetomium elatum.Morphs: Asexual morph produced, acremonium-like; sexual morph readily produced on OA, homothallic.
Chaetomium elatum.Similar species: Dichotomopilus indicus (= Chaetomium indicum) resembles C. elatum, especially the dichotomous hairs, but the colonies of D. indicus are more yellow, the ascospores are smaller and more globose and the colony diameters are also smaller on OA (20–48 mm), MEA (36–55 mm) and on DG18 (8–15 mm).
Chaetomium elatum.Molecular markers: RNA-polymerase II second largest subunit (rpb2): KX976831; ?-tubulin (tub2): KX976952.
Chaetomium elatum.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Chaetomium elatum is mainly found in the temperate zone and is less common than C. globosum, but found in in Australia, Denmark and USA. It is frequently detected on cellulose containing materials, such as gypsum wallboard, plywood, wallpaper, books, textile and cardboard, after severe water damage. It has also been isolated from herbivorous dung and straw.
Chaetomium elatum.Physiology: The optimum temperature for the production of ascomata is 18–24 °C and favoured by neutral pH and darkness. The ascospores are not heat resistant, but thermotolerant and can be very resistant to dry circumstances and UV irradiation. Growth and ascomata production, on the other hand, requires a high wateractivity.
Chaetomium elatum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Chaetomium elatum is able to deteriorate cellulosic materials, such as wet cardboard and plant material and can cause soft-rot in maple wood strips.
Chaetomium elatum.References: Domsch et al. (2007), Dosen et al. (2016), Wang et al. (2016, 2017)
Chaetomium elatum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Chaetomium globosum.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA, MEA and V8 at 25 °C reach diameters of 70+ mm in 7 days, appearing olive-grey or malachite green, sometimes with an orange extracellular pigment on OA. Ascomata (perithecia) are formed after 1 week in a dense layer on OA and MEA giving the colony an olive-greyish to bluish green appearance, but ascospores are first fully mature after 2 weeks. Colonies on PCA are 39–48 mm after 7 days with thin and yellowish mycelium and well separated olive grey perithecia. Colonies on DG18 reach a diameter of 10–17 mm in 7 days at 25 °C and have a pale yellow to pinkish cream colour. No ascomata production on DG18.
Chaetomium globosum.Micromorphology: Perithecia on PCA are superficial, greyish green to dull green sometimes with a yellow hue when viewed in reflective light. They are subglobose to ovoid, 140–270 µm in high and 100–240 µm in diameter excluding perithecial hair. Perithecial hairs are numerous, unbranched, septate, flexuous, undulate to loosely curled. They are greenish brown and finely warty, 2–5 µm at the base and tapering and fading towards the tip. Asci are clavate, 19–40 × 12–17 µm with a 22–48 µm stalk and contain 8 ascospores. The asci disappear as the ascospores mature. The ascospores are reddish brown when mature, fusiform, 8.5–11(–12) × 7–8.5(–9.5) µm in size and with one apical germ pore.
Chaetomium globosum.Morphs: Asexual morph absent; sexual morph readily produced on OA, homothallic.
Chaetomium globosum.Similar species: Chaetomium coarctatum resembles C. globosum, especially the curly hair, but the colonies of
Chaetomium globosum.Molecular markers: RNA-polymerase II second largest subunit (rpb2): KX976835; ?-tubulin (tub2): KX976969.
Chaetomium globosum.Chemical markers: Chaetoglobosins A and C, chaetmu- gilin D, chaetoviridins A and E, cochliodinol A, cochlio- dones 1-3, prenisatin, prochaetoglobosins I-IV, rotiori- nol.
Chaetomium globosum.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Chaetomium globosum has a worldwide distribution and is frequently detected on cellulose containing materials, such as gypsum wallboard, plywood, wallpaper, books, textile and cardboard, after severe water damage. Furthermore, it has been isolated from hay, bird feathers, herbivorous dung, and known as a soft-rot fungus from softwood and hardwood timber.
Chaetomium globosum.Physiology: The optimum temperature for the production of ascomata is 18–24 °C. The ascospores are not heat resistant, but thermotolerant and can be very resistant to dry circumstances and UV irradiation. Growth and ascomata production, on the other hand, requires a high wateractivity.
Chaetomium globosum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Chaetomium globosum is able to deteriorate cellulosic materials, such as wet cardboard and plant material. It has infrequently been encountered in skin and nail infections in humans.
Chaetomium globosum.References: Domsch et al. (2007), Dosen et al. (2016), Wang et al. (2016, 2017), Andersen et al. (2017)

Chaetomium globosum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Cladosporium allicinum.Species description: Cladosporium allicinum (Fr. : Fr.) Bensch et al.
Cladosporium allicinum.Synonym: Cladosporium bruhnei Davidiella allicina Mycosphae- rella allicina
Cladosporium allicinum.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diame- ter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing extremely folded and raised in the middle, velvety and dull spinach green to greyish green with a thin white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 17–19 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing leaf green to greyish green also with a thin white rim, sulcate and downy.
Cladosporium allicinum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 350 µm long, but are normally 20–330 µm and 3–5 µm wide with 5–8 µm wide swellings. Conidiophores are pale olive brown and smooth to slightly verrucose. They are straight sometimes with intercalary and terminal swellings and often with lateral or terminal branched. The ramoconidia are 34–40 × 3–4 µm with 0–2 septa. They are smooth and light brown in colour. The secondary ramoconidia are 10–24 × 3.5–5 µm and often aseptate. They are ellipsoid to subcylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–2 distal hila carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary conidia in the chains are ovoid to ellipsoid with a basal and a distal hilum, aseptate and 6–11 × 3–4 µm in size. The terminal conidia are ovoid to obovoid with a basal hilum, aseptate and 4–7 × 2.5–3.5 µm. All conidial types are pale brown in coloured and minutely verruculose to verrucose.
Cladosporium allicinum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture.
Cladosporium allicinum.Similar species: Cladosporium allicinum belongs in the C. herbarum complex together with several similar species: C. herbaroides, C. herbarum and C. macrocarpum. Cladosporium herbaroides has similar conidial sizes, but more knotty conidiophores, C. herbarum has a looser terminal branching pattern, and C. macrocarpum has larger and more ornamented conidia.
Cladosporium allicinum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladospo- rium allicinum is a common air-borne saprotroph, both indoors and outside, and is frequently encountered as a contaminant. It has been isolated from food sources such as cereal grain, living and decaying plant material, hypersaline and industrial waste water, from indoor environment sources such as water damaged wood and glass fibre and from human sputum and skin. Reported from most parts of the world.
Cladosporium allicinum.Physiology: Cladosporium allicinum grows well in environments with fluctuating humidity.

Cladosporium cladosporioides.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diame- ter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing extremely folded and raised in the middle, velvety and dull spinach green to greyish green with a thin white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 17–19 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing leaf green to greyish green also with a thin white rim, sulcate and downy.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 350 µm long, but are normally 50–135 µm and 3–4 µm wide having 2–4 septa. Conidiophores are olive brown and verrucose at the basal end turning light brown and smooth at the top. They are straight without intercalary or terminal swellings and often branched. The first ramoconidia have a truncate base with no basal hilum. They are 20–30 × 3–3.5 µm with 1–3 distal hila and often aseptate. They are smooth and light brown in colour. The secondary ramoconidia are 12–45 × 3–3.5 µm and often aseptate. They are cylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–2 distal hila carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary conidia in the chains are fusiform with a basal and a distal hilum, aseptate and 4–4.5 ×
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Similar species: Cladosporium cladosporioides is a complex and contains several species. Cladosporium pseudocladosporioides, which is very similar morphologically, has narrower ramo- and terminal conidia.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1?: HM148244, HM148490; actin: HM148521.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladosporium cladosporioides is a common air- and soil- borne saprotroph and is frequently encountered as a contaminant. It has been isolated from food sources such as cereal grain, coffee and peas and from indoor environment sources such as water-damaged wood, wallpaper and plaster. Reported from most parts of the world, but most often in temperate regions.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Physiology: Cladosporium cladosporioides grows very well in environments with fluctuating humidity.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.Biodeterioration and pathology: Cladosporium cla- dosporioides has been reported as a human pathogen in skin and nails.
Cladosporium cladosporioides.References: Domsch et al. (2007), Bensch et al. (2010)

Cladosporium halotolerans.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing extremely folded and raised in the middle, velvety and dull spinach green to greyish green with a thin white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 17–19 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing leaf green to greyish green also with a thin white rim, sulcate and downy.
Cladosporium halotolerans.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 300 µm long, but are normally 20–50 µm long and 2.5–3 µm wide without swellings. Conidiophores are pale olive brown and smooth to slightly verruculose. They are straight sometimes with short lateral denticulate branching sites. Septa, which are sporadic, appear darker than the cell walls. True ramoconidia are rare. The secondary ramoconidia are (5–)7–12(–37) × (2–)2.5–3.5(–6.5) µm with 0(–1) septa. They are smooth to slightly verruculose and pale olive brown in colour. They are ellipsoid to subcylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–4 distal conidiogenous loci carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary and terminal conidia in the chains are globose to subglobose with a basal and a distal hilum, aseptate and (2–)3–4(–6) × (2–)2.5–3(–5) µm in size. They are dark brown, verrucose and aseptate.
Cladosporium halotolerans.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph no known.
Cladosporium halotolerans.Similar species: Cladosporium halotolerans belongs in the C. sphaerospermum complex together with several similar species. Cladosporium halotolerans and C. sphaero-
Cladosporium halotolerans.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Cladosporium halo- tolerans is the most common Cladosporium in the indoor environment and very often isolated from house dust. It is found both indoors and outside and is frequently encountered as a contaminant. It has been isolated from hypersaline water, from indoor environment sources such as water damaged bathroom and basement walls, gypsum wallboard, inner roofing in attics and from hu- man sputum and skin. It has also been found in gypsum sediment in Arctic ice and in rocks. Reported from all parts of the world.
Cladosporium halotolerans.Physiology: Cladosporium halotolerans is halophilic and can grow on MEA with 17 % NaCl. Its optimal growth temperature is 25 °C, but not at 4 or 37 °C. It can tolerate transient and fluctuating humidity and UV light.
Cladosporium halotolerans.References: Zalar et al. (2007), Bensch et al. (2012, 2018)
Cladosporium halotolerans.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Cladosporium herbarum.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 27–30 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing folded, velvety and olive grey to lavender green with a white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 9–18 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 22–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing dull greyish green (cactus green) with a white rim, slightly folded and downy.
Cladosporium herbarum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They are straight and sometimes branched. They are pale and smooth at the base turning greyish brown and minutely verrucose at the top. Conidiophores are up to 350 µm long, but mostly 70–150 × 3.5–4.5 µm and 3–5 µm wide, often geniculate with intercalary and terminal swellings 6–9 µm wide. The primary ramoconidia are straight or geniculate, 20–70 × 3.5–4 µm in size, several intercalary and distal conidiogenous loci. They are greyish brown and minutely verrucose with 3–6 septa. Their terminal swelling often holds 1–4 secondary ramoconidia that are aseptate, sometime having 1 septum, cylindrical with a truncate base and 15–25 × 5–7 µm in size. The intercalary conidia are 6–9 × 3–5 µm, cylindrical to fusiform and have up to 3 distal conidiogenous loci. Terminal conidia are aseptate, ellipsoid to obovoid, 4–6 × 3–4 µm in size. Ramo-, intercalary and terminal conidia are forming branched chains of 8–12 conidia giving a loose structure. All types of conidia are greyish brown and verrucose to verruculose.
Cladosporium herbarum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture. Ascomata produce mature ascospores on axenic culture on water agar with nettle stems after a few months at 5–7 °C.
Cladosporium herbarum.Similar species: Cladosporium herbarum belongs in the C. herbarum complex together with several similar species: C. allicinum, C. herbaroides and C. macrocarpum. Cladosporium allicinum has straight conidiophores and a looser terminal branching pattern, C. herbaroides has similar knotty conidiophores, but smaller conidial sizes and C. macrocarpum has larger and more ornamented conidia.
Cladosporium herbarum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladosporium herbarum has been isolated from food sources such as weathered cereal grain, mouldy fruit and vegetables, living and decaying plant material, cheeses, butter and margarine and from indoor environment sources such as water-damaged wood, wallpaper and plaster. It is possible that C. allicinum is more associated to indoor environments and C. herbarum to cereals and other food items. Reported from most parts of the world.
Cladosporium herbarum.Physiology: Cladosporium herbarum is tolerant of environments and products with low water activity and can tolerate transient and fluctuating humidity and UV light.
Cladosporium herbarum.References: Schubert et al. (2007), Bensch et al. (2012)
Cladosporium herbarum.Fig: 131. Cladosporium herbarum. Conidiophore and conidia; modified from Schubert et al. (2007).
Cladosporium herbarum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Cladosporium macrocarpum.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 27–29 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing sulcate, velvety and greyish white. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 13–14 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing leather brown, inverted and velvety.
Cladosporium macrocarpum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They are straight and sometimes branched. They are smooth to minutely verruculose and pale greyish brown turning paler at the top. The conidiophores are up to 250 µm long and 3–6 µm wide, geniculate, nodose with intercalary and terminal swellings 6–10 µm wide. True primary ramoconidia are rare. The lateral and terminal swellings of the conidiophore often holds 1–2 secondary ramoconidia each that are aseptate, sometimes having one septum, ellipsoidal to subcylindrical and 15–25 × 5–7 µm in size. They have 1 basal hilum and 2–4 distal conidiogenous loci. The intercalary conidia are 9–15 × 3–5 µm, cylindrical to fusiform and mostly aseptate. They sometimes have 1 septum and up to 3 distal conidiogenous loci. Terminal conidia are ellipsoid to obovoid, 4–10 × 3–5 µm in size, aseptate with 1 basal hilum. Ramo-, intercalary and terminal conidia are forming branched chains giving a loose structure and all types of conidia are greyish brown, verrucose to echinulate and have darker and thickened walls and septa.
Cladosporium macrocarpum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture.
Cladosporium macrocarpum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladosporium macrocarpum is less common than its close relatives C. herbarum and C. variabile. It has been isolated from food sources such as cereal grain, mouldy fruit and vegetables and from indoor environment sources such as water-damaged wood. Reported from temperate parts of the world. Common in nature on dead herbaceous plants and shrubs in temperate regions.
Cladosporium macrocarpum.Fig: 133. Cladosporium macrocarpum. Conidiophore and conidia; modified from Schubert et al. (2007).
Cladosporium macrocarpum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing sulcate, velvety and olive green to olive yellow. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 8–18 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 19–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing greyish green to dull green, slightly folded and downy.
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 300 µm long, but are normally 45–130 µm and 3–4 µm wide. Conidiophores are light brown and smooth at the basal end turning olive brown and finely verrucose at the top. They are straight without intercalary or terminal swellings. The first ramoconidia have a truncate base with no basal hilum. They are 20–45 × 3–3.5 µm with 2–6 septa and 1–3 distal hila. The secondary ramoconidia are 16–25 × 3 µm with 1–5 dark and pronounced septa. They are cylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–2 distal hila carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary conidia in the chains are dark brown fusiform with 1 basal and 1–2 distal hila, aseptate and 5–5.5 × 3–3.5 µm in size. The terminal conidia are globose to subglobose, aseptate and 3–4 × 3–3.5 µm. Intercalary and terminal conidia are dark olive brown in coloured and verrucose.
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Similar species: Cladosporium sphaerospermum belongs in the C. sphaerospermum complex together with several similar species. C. sphaerospermum and C. halotolerans have very similar micromorphology, but C. sphaerosper- mum has ramoconidia with thick dark septa.
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladospo- rium sphaerospermum has occasionally been isolated from fruit and grain, but it is very commonly isolated from in- door environment sources such as water-damaged wood, plaster, paint, textiles and gypsum wallboard. Reported from most parts of the world.
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Physiology: Cladosporium sphaerospermum is tolerant of environments with low water activity and can tolerate transient and fluctuating humidity and UV light.
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.References: Zalar et al. (2007); Bensch et al. (2012; 2018)
Cladosporium sphaerospermum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Species description: Coniochaeta hoffmannii (J.F.H. Beyma) Z.U. Khan et al.
Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Macromorphology: Colony on MEA and OA at 25 °C attaining a diameter of 15–30 mm in 7 days, velvety or fasciculate, flat (often with a leathery appearance), with a central tuft, yellow or pinkish. Reverse pinkish buff.
Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Micromorphology: Hyphae more or less hyaline, smooth- and thin walled, often fasciculate. Phialides either single on hyphae or in dense clusters on short lateral branches, or intercalary along undifferentiated hyphae, hyaline, cylindrical to flask–shaped, sometimes elongate, 7–20 µm long, or subglobose to ovoid, 3–7 × 2–3 µm; intercalary phialides cylindrical with one or several scattered collarettes. Conidia ellipsoidal to cylindrical, sometimes somewhat curved, commonly 3–3.5 × 1.5–
Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, isolated from moist indoor environments (near window frames, wood- en construction), cereals, soil, decaying wood and man.
Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Biodeterioration and pathology: Rarely encountered as a pathogen and associated with subcutaneous infecti- ons, keratitis, sinusitis, and peritonitis.
Coniochaeta hoffmannii.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Curvularia geniculata.Macromorphology: Colonies, PCA and OA moderately fast growing, reaching a diameter of 30–40 mm within a week at 25 °C, brownish black, velvety sometimes becoming somewhat cottony. Reverse brown.
Curvularia geniculata.Micromorphology: Conidiophores erect, pigmented becoming paler near the tip, sometimes geniculate up to 600 µm long, septate. (Poro)conidia usually 4-septate, mostly curved unilaterally at the broadest and most pigmented central cell, adjacent cells less pigmented and the end cells subhyaline, 18–35(–37) × 8–14 µm. Heterothallic.
Curvularia geniculata.Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic conidio- genesis (poroconidia); sexual morph known but rarely produced in culture.
Curvularia geniculata.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Curvularia species have a world-wide distribution. They have been isolated from soil and plant materials with a preference for the tropics and warmer climates. Curvularia geniculata is also frequently isolated from cellulosic materials, e.g. paper, archives.
Curvularia geniculata.Physiology: Sporulation is enhanced by incubation under near-UV light.
Curvularia geniculata.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Didymella glomerata.Species description: Didymella glomerata (Corda) Q. Chen & L. Cai
Didymella glomerata.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA at 20–22 °C attai- ning a diameter of 50–57 mm in 7 days, aerial mycelium usually sparse, (sometimes in greyish woolly sectors), with abundant pycnidia, olivacous buff to dull green, be- coming darker due to dictyochlamydospore production. Colonies can show variation in formation of pycnidia, aerial mycelium and chlamydospores; isolates often de- generate in culture.
Didymella glomerata.Micromorphology: Pycnidia superficial on or immersed in agar, usually with one ostiole (sometimes 2–3), more or less globose (20–)30–180(–300) × (40–)60–200(–600)
Didymella glomerata.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Didymella glomerata.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor environments. Worldwide distribution; isolated from a wide variety of plants and plant material, from soil, butter, rice grain, cement, litter, paint, paper and wool. This species is also encountered in moist environments, such as bathrooms, pipelines.
Didymella glomerata.Biodeterioration and pathology: The fungus can be pathogenic to humans and attack different kinds of fruit,
Didymella glomerata.References: Aveskamp et al. (2010), Chen et al. (2015)
Didymella glomerata.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Didymella macrostoma.Species description: Didymella macrostoma (Mont.) Q. Chen & L. Cai
Didymella macrostoma.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA at 20–22 °C at- taining a diameter of 40–60 mm in 7 days, mycelial mat variable from sparse to dense and woolly. The hyphae contain a red to violet pigment which gives the colony a reddish appearance. The colonies are characterised by reddish appearance (turning bluish with additon of NaOH) in var. macrostoma. Strains without the red co- lour are distinguished as var. incolorata.
Didymella macrostoma.Micromorphology: Pycnidia superficial on or immersed in agar, globose-oval, 80–260 µm diam, blackish brown, with one (occasionally two) distinct ostiole of 10–30 µm in diam. Conidial slime pinkish, conidia one- or two-cel- led (occasionally 3-celled in vitro) septate mostly ovoid to ellipsoidal, slightly curved or straight, one-celled coni- dia: 5–8 × 2–4 µm; two-celled conidia 8.5–14 µm, hyaline to brownish coloured in old cultures.
Didymella macrostoma.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Didymella macrostoma.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor environ- ment. Widespread occurrence: isolated from a wide vari- ety of plants and plant material, from soil. Also isolated from surfaces in indoor environments, but not as com- mon as Didymella glomerata.
Didymella macrostoma.References: Aveskamp et al. (2010), Chen et al. (2015)
Didymella macrostoma.Fig: 141. Didymella macrostoma. Pycnidia with detail of outer wall, conidia, and innerwall with phialides.
Didymella macrostoma.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Epicoccum nigrum.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or OA at 20 °C attaining a diameter of at least 60 mm in 10 days, lanose to felty, yellow-orange, red or brown, sometimes greenish. Reverse similar, often more intensely coloured.
Epicoccum nigrum.Micromorphology: Pulvinate sporodochia appearing in 8–10 days on SNA, visible as black spots, 100–2000 µm in diam. Conidiophores in clusters, straight or more or less flexuous, terminating in more or less isodiametric conidiogenous cells, colourless to pale brown, short, 5–15 × 3–6 µm. (Blasto)conidia formed singly, globose to pyriform, commonly 15–25 µm in diam, with funnel- shaped base and broad attachment scar, often with pale protuberant basal stalk cell, dark golden brown, verrucose, obscuring the septa which divide the conidia into up to 15 cells.
Epicoccum nigrum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic conidioge- nesis; sexual morph not known.
Epicoccum nigrum.Physiology: Temperature: optimum 23–28 °C; minimum (-3–)4 °C; maximum 45 °C. Cultures often remaining sterile, sporulation, can be induced by exposure to near- UV (“black”) light.
Epicoccum nigrum.Fig: 143. Epicoccum nigrum. Sporodochia, clustered conidiophores with multi-celled conidia.
Epicoccum nigrum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Exophiala.Macromorphology: Colonies mosty restricted, slimy at the centre due to yeast-like growth, smooth near the margin, later often becoming velvety or lanose, olivaceous black.
Exophiala.Micromorphology: The so-called “black yeasts” have melanin deposits in their cell wall, and many of them are capable of forming a synanamorph consisting of abundant septate mycelium. Exophiala is the main genus of blackyeasts, characterisedbyannellidic conidiogenesis. Conidiogenous cells intercalary, cylindrical, or free, flask shaped or acicular, with relatively narrow, short or very short annellated zones. Conidia formed percurrently in slimy heads, (sub)hyaline, smooth-walled, 1–4 celled. Often chains of spherical cells are formed which bud profusely. Chains of barrel-shaped hyphal cells may be present. Chlamydospores or sclerotial bodies occassionally formed.
Exophiala.Morphs: Asexual morph present, combination of acropetal and basipetal annellidic conidogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced.
Exophiala.Habitats and distribution: Exophiala is commonly occurring and has previously been isolated from water (both tap and bottled), wet indoor environments, soil, plants and decaying wood material. Multiple species are related to tap and bottled water, and these include E. angulospora, E. aff. pisciphila, E. oligosperma and E. xenobiota. Members of the resembling genus Cladophialophora are encountered in sugared drinks (e.g. C. potulentorum, C. australiensis and C. subtilis).
Exophiala.Physiology: Intolerant to 10 % NaCl and benomyl; lac- tate, inulin and citrate mosly not assimilated.
Exophiala.Biodeterioration and pathology: Exophiala is the causative agent of various human infections.
Exophiala.References: de Hoog et al. (2000), Baldadi et al. (2008)
Exophiala.Fig: 145. Exophiala salmonis. Conidiophores with annellidic conidiogenous cells and conidia; redrawn from Seifert et al. (2011).
Exophiala.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium avenaceum.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 30–60 mm in 4 days. This species can be extremely variable in appearance and colour, commonly yellowish or reddish with a whitish floccose overgrowth of aerial mycelium. The latter becomes peach-coloured or reddish-brown and velvety with age. Reverse is yellowish or brownish often with reddish shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 30–60 mm after 4 days with a velvety light-brownish or reddish mycelium, often with dark brownish to black sclerotium-like structures. The reverse is light to dark brown sometimes with a reddish shade.
Fusarium avenaceum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are simple or branched, arising from the aerial mycelium often in orange sporodochia with simple or proliferated monophialides. Microconidia from polyblastic conidiogenous cells are fusiform, 0–3-septate, variable in size, 6–30 × 2.5–4.5(–6) µm. Macroconidia borne on phialides are narrowly fusiform, slender or sickle-shaped to almost straight having 4–7 septa with an elongated apical cell and a distinct foot cell, mostly 35–90 × 3.5–4(– 6) µm. Conidia in mass are more or less orange coloured. Chlamydospores are absent in mycelium, but sometimes present in conidia.
Fusarium avenaceum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced.
Fusarium avenaceum.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium tricinctum species complex”. Fusarium arthrosporioides has a similar colony appearance on PDA and YES but does also produce pyriform microconidia. The PDA and YES colonies of F. tricinctum may resemble F. avenaceum, but F. tricinctum has much shorter macroconidia and lacks  the  septated  fusiform  microconidia.  Fusarium
Fusarium avenaceum.Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF405461. ITS: U26738. Elongation factor 1?: AY337423. Strains of this species have been full genome sequenced (Lysøe et al. 2014).
Fusarium avenaceum.Chemical markers: 2-amino-14,16-dimethyloctade- can-3-ol, antibiotic Y, aurofusarin, chlamydosporol, chrysogine, enniatins, fusarin C, gibepyrone A, monili- formin.
Fusarium avenaceum.Habitats and distribution: Frequently occurring on cereal grains, vegetables and many other food items as well as in agricultural soils. World-wide distribution, mainly in temperate zones, but also reported from warmer or subtropical regions.
Fusarium avenaceum.Biotechnological applications: Has been evaluated as a potential bio-control agent of knapweed, and to control wild raspberry and related invasive Rubus species.
Fusarium avenaceum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Causes root rots in cereal plants (e.g. wheat, rye, barley, maize), clover, lucernes. Damage vegetables and fruits such as peaches, apples, pears as well as stored seeds of oats, barley, and wheat.
Fusarium avenaceum.Fig: 147. Fusarium avenaceum. A. Conidiophores with simple and polyblastic conidiogenous cells. B. Microconidia, 1–3 septate, more or less fusiform; macroconidia, 4–7 septate, slender, sickle-shaped to almost straight (orig. partly after E.J. Hermanides-Nijhof).
Fusarium avenaceum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium culmorum.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 75–90 mm in 4 days with a floccose aerial mycelium. At first the mycelium is white to yellowish turning into pinkish, red ochraceous to brownish- red. Reverse and agar surface is reddish to purple or brownish. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 75–90 mm after 4 days with a sparse aerial mycelium. Colonies are velvety in ochre to brownish-red shades. Reverse is yellowish brown to dark brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge.
Fusarium culmorum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are usually branched with short and wide phialides from which rather thick-walled macroconidia are borne in the aerial mycelium often in sporodochia or in pionnotes with a red- brown slime. Microconidia are absent. Macroconidia are fusiform to sickle-shaped, usually 5-septate (sometimes 3–4- or 6–8-septate), with a more or less pointed apex and a distinct footcell, 3-septate: 26–36 × 4–6 µm, 4-septate: 30–46 × 5–7 µm, 5-septate: 34–50 × 5–7 µm. Chlamydospores are brownish, smooth to rough-walled and present in mycelium or in conidia. Sometimes they are present in chains or in clumps. Some cultures do not form chlamydospores.
Fusarium culmorum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Fusarium culmorum.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium sambucinum species complex”. Colonies on PDA and YES
Fusarium culmorum.Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF212779. ITS: AY260958. Elongation factor 1?: AF212463 .
Fusarium culmorum.Chemical markers: 2-acetylquinazolinone, aurofu- sarin, butenolide, chrysogine, culmorin, fusarin C, rubrofusarin, trichothecenes (deoxynivalenol, 3- and 15-acetyldeoxynivalenol, fusarenon X, nivalenol and de- rivatives hereof.), zearalenone.
Fusarium culmorum.Important mycotoxins: Deoxynivalenol and other tri- chothecenes, fusarin C, zearalenone.
Fusarium culmorum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor environments. World-wide distribution with a preference for the temperate zones. Occurring on grains and stems of oats, barley, wheat, and other cereals, agricultural soils.
Fusarium culmorum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Causes foot and root rot and head blight in cereals. Attacks maize plants and cobs and causes storage rot of apples, potatoes, sugar beet.
