Fusarium culmorum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium equiseti.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 45–70 mm in 4 days with floccose aerial cream to yellowish-brown mycelium. A tendency towards pionnotes and sporodochia can be observed in some isolates. Reverse is peach-coloured, changing to light- brown or dark-brown. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 40–65 mm after 4 days. The mycelium is flat and velvety in cream to light brown shades. Reverse is light, yellowish to brownish.
Fusarium equiseti.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are often branched and monophialidic. Microconidia absent or rare, spindle-shaped or ovoid, 0–2-septate, 6–24 × 2.5–4 µm. Macroconidia sparse at first and borne from simple lateral phialides on the aerial mycelium. Macroconidia are sickle-shaped with a distinct foot cell and in some isolates an elongated curved apical cell, 3–5(–7)-septate, typically 5-septate. 3-septate: (15–)22–45 × (2.5–)3–5 µm, 5-septate: (30–)40–60 × (3–)3.7–5 µm, 7-septate: 42–60 × 4–6 µm. Chlamydospores are abundantly pro- duced intercalary, solitary, in chains or clumps, in the hyphae or in conidia. They are pale brown at maturity and often with a rough cell wall.
Fusarium equiseti.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph has been observed, but are very unlikely to be observed in culture.
Fusarium equiseti.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium incarnatum-equiseti species complex”, which is poorly resolved with many undescribed phylogenetic species (O’Donnell et al. 2013, Villani et al. 2016). The conidium morphology is quite variable. Isolates from temperate area tend to have conidia with a short bended tip, whereas
Fusarium equiseti.Chemical markers: Chrysogine, equisetin, fusarochro- manone, trichothecenes (mono- and diacetoxyscirpenol, nivalenol and derivatives hereof.), zearalenone.
Fusarium equiseti.Habitats and distribution: World-wide distribution in food, soils and damaged plant tissues.
Fusarium equiseti.Biotechnological applications: Possible biotechno- logical productions of linamarase, ursodeoxycholic acid and polyunsaturated fatty acids have been explored. So far no commercial productions have been established.
Fusarium equiseti.Biodeterioration and pathology: Reported from seeds and fruits which have been in contact with soil, but verified cases as a true pathogen have not been seen.
Fusarium equiseti.Fig: 151. Fusarium equiseti. A. Conidiophores. B. Macroconidia. C. Chlamydospores.
Fusarium equiseti.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium graminearum.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C are growing fast with a diameter of 75–90 mm after 4 days. The colony is greyish rose, red to bluish-red, becoming brownish at age. The aerial mycelium is floccose and whitish becoming brownish to rose. Reverse in red to reddish brown shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 75–90 mm after 4 days with a sparse aerial mycelium. Colonies are velvety in ochre to brownish- red shades. Reverse is yellowish brown to dark brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge.
Fusarium graminearum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are at first simple monophialides on the hyphae later strongly branched. Microconidia are absent. Macroconidia are slender, sickle-shaped, curved with pointed and curved apical and pedicellate cells, mostly (3–)5–6(–9)-septate, 41–60 (–80) × 4–5.5 µm. Chlamydospores are sometimes present, mostly intercalary and in chains, but often absent. Sporulation is often sparse (induction by near UV-light). Perithecia are often formed of SNA, especially in fresh isolates. They are about 150–250 µm in diameter, dark purple to black, with 3-septate ascospores ca. 20– 30 × 3–5 µm.
Fusarium graminearum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph has been observed and may occur in cultures.
Fusarium graminearum.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium graminearum species complex” that contains morphological indistinguishable species. Based on molecular data 15 phylogenetic species morphologically similar to F. graminearum have been described: F. acaciae- mearnsii, F. aethiopicum, F. asiaticum, F. austroamericanum,
Fusarium graminearum.Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF212776. Elongation factor 1?: AF212459 . Several strains of this species have been full genome sequenced.
Fusarium graminearum.Chemical markers: 2-acetylquinazolinone, aurofusa- rin, butenolide, chrysogine, culmorin, fusarin C, rubrofusarin, trichothecenes (deoxynivalenol, 3- and 15-acetyldeoxynivalenol, fusarenon X, nivalenol and derivatives hereof), zearalenone.
Fusarium graminearum.Habitats and distribution: Food. World-wide distri- bution, and is a colonizer and sometimes a parasite of mainly graminaceous plants. Reported from soil, cereal grains and seeds of grasses.
Fusarium graminearum.Biotechnological applications: A strain designated A 3/5 used for production of Quorn® mycoprotein was originally identified as F. graminearum, but has been reidentified as F. venenatum. This strain has been used as a host for heterologous protein production using the misapplied name F. graminearum.
Fusarium graminearum.Biodeterioration and pathology: F. graminearum causes foot and root rot and head blight in cereals. It often attacks maize plants and cobs.
Fusarium graminearum.Fig: 153. Fusarium graminearum. A. Conidiophores and phialides. B. Macroconidia.
Fusarium graminearum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium oxysporum.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 30–55 mm in 4 days. The aerial mycelium is sparse or floccose to velvety, whitish or peach, usually with a purple tinge. In some strains orange sporodochia may occur. The reverse is yellowish or in purple shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 30–60 mm after 4 days with a velvety appearance. The mycelium is whitish to light yellowish, some colonies dark rose to purple. The reverse is yellowish or in purple shades.
Fusarium oxysporum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are often branched bearing monophialides. Microconidia are generally abundant, 0(–2)-septate, borne in false heads on simple phialides or on phialides on short branched conidiophores. Conidia are variable in shape and size, ovoid-ellipsoidal to cylindrical, straight or slightly curved, 5–12 × 2.2–3.5 µm. Macroconidia are sparse in some strains, borne on phialides on branched conidiophores or in sporodochia, 3(–5)-septate, fusiform, more or less curved, pointed at both ends with a pedicellate basal cell, usually 3-septate, (20–)27–46(–50) × 3–4.5(–5) µm. Chlamydospores occur in hyphae or in conidia, hyaline, smooth- or rough-walled, (sub)globose, 5–15 µm in diameter, terminal or intercalary, in chains, pairs or single.
Fusarium oxysporum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Fusarium oxysporum.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium oxysporum species complex” that is poorly resolved with many undescribed phylogentic species. F. oxysporum is very variable in culture and morphology and may also be confused with F. subglutinans and Neocosmospora solani. Several species has been proposed based on phylogenetic
Fusarium oxysporum.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1?: MH485044; DNA-dependent RNA polymerase subunit II: MH484953.
Fusarium oxysporum.Chemical markers: Beauvericin, bikaverin, enniatins, fusaric acid, fumonisins, moniliformin, naphthoquinone pigments, nectriafurone.
Fusarium oxysporum.Important mycotoxins: Enniatins, fumonisins (a few strains from Korea), moniliformin.
Fusarium oxysporum.Habitats and distribution: World-wide distribution in food, plants and indoor environments, as well as in soils.
Fusarium oxysporum.Physiology: The species can grow under anaerobic conditions. Some strains may grow at 37 °C or slightly higher.
Fusarium oxysporum.Biotechnological applications: Fusarium oxysporum is a useful producer of enzymes used for bio-ethanol pro- duction, and is also used as a bio-control agent in agri- culture.
Fusarium oxysporum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Occurring mainly as a soil saprophyte but can be pathogenic to numerous plants causing wilt. Causes storage rot (e.g. in maize, beet). Pathogenic to humans (keratitis).
Fusarium oxysporum.References: Di Pietro et al. (2003), Leslie & Summerell (2006), O’Donnell et al. (2013)
Fusarium oxysporum.Fig: 155. Fusarium oxysporum. A. Macroconidia. B. Conidiophores and phialides with microconidia. C. Chlamydospores.
Fusarium oxysporum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium poae.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 55–80 mm in 4 days. The aerial mycelium is cottony, white or pale pinkish to peach, near the agar surface red to violet. Reverse in yellowish to reddish shades. Colonies on YES reach a diameter of 50–80 mm after 4 days at 25 °C. The mycelium is velvety white or pale pinkish to vinaceous red. Reverse in yellowish to reddish shades. Both PDA and YES cultures have a fruity peach-like odour.
Fusarium poae.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA is at first unbranched later usually branched with short and broad monophialides, not in sporodochia. Microconidia are abundantly produced, mostly one-celled, napiform, pyriform, 6–10 × 5.5–7.5 µm. Macroconidia sparsely produced, slightly curved, mostly 2–3-septate, 18–38 ×
Fusarium poae.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Fusarium poae.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium sambucinum species complex” (O’Donnell et al. 2013). Fusarium langsethiae and F. sibiricum (Yli-Mattila et al. 2011) do produce napiform conidia, but hardly any other types of conidia and their colonies lack the floccose aerial mycelium on PDA. In addition to the pyriform conidia,
Fusarium poae.Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF404237. ITS: AY188915. Elongation factor 1? AF337446.
Fusarium poae.Chemical markers: Aurofusarin, beauvericin, culmo- rins, fusarin C, gamma-lactones, trichothecenes (mono- and diacetoxyscirpenol, nivalenol and their derivatives). Fruity, peach-like odour.
Fusarium poae.Habitats and distribution: Common on gramineous plants, cereal seeds and in agricultural soils from temperate regions. Occasionally also found in the sub-tropics.
Fusarium poae.Biotechnological applications: Production of flavouring agent for the dairy industry has been explored.
Fusarium poae.Biodeterioration and pathology: Despite the frequent detection of F. poae from cereal grains it is only considered a weak pathogen.

Fusarium poae.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Fusarium verticillioides.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C have a diameter of 35–55 mm in 4 days peach and are pale cream, violet to lilac. The aerial mycelium is dense, delicately floccose to velvety or with a powdery appearance due to microconidia production and often in white, rose to vinaceous colours. Sporodochia are rarely formed. The reverse in dark violet, lilac, vinaceous or in light shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 30–60 mm after 4 days with a velvety appearance, typically in dark rose to purple shades. Some colonies are light cream to yellow. The reverse is yellowish or in purple shades.
Fusarium verticillioides.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are mostly unbranched, formed on aerial mycelium, with 1–3 simple elongated phialides. Microconidia are produced in long chains (can be observed in Petri-dish under low power), rarely in false heads, mostly one-celled, clavate with a truncate base, 4.3–20 × 1.5–4.5 µm. Macroconidium formation in many strains is rare and their conidiophores are formed as lateral branches on hyphae and may consist of a single basal cell, bearing 2–3 phialides or consisting of 2–3 metulae. Macroconidia are slender, 3–5-septate, straight or slightly curved, fusiform, thin-walled with elongated often curved apical cell and pedicellate basal cell, 3-septate mostly 30–46 × 2.7–3.6 µm; 5-septate mostly 47–58 × 3.1–3.6 µm. Chlamydospores are absent. When present sclerotia are blackish-blue and probably perithecial initials.
Fusarium verticillioides.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph has been been observed and usually occur only on dead plant material.
Fusarium verticillioides.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium fujikuroi species complex” (O’Donnell et al. 2013) and previously the collective name F. moniliforme has been used; however, due to updated taxonomy this epithet is invalid and should not be used. Many morphological
Fusarium verticillioides.Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: U34468. ITS: X94166. Elongation factor 1?: AY337450. This species have been full genome sequenced.
Fusarium verticillioides.Chemical markers: Bikaverins, fumonisins, fusaric acid, fusarin C, gibberellins, moniliformin, naphthoqui- none pigments.
Fusarium verticillioides.Habitats and distribution: World-wide distribution and very frequent in the tropics and subtropics on maize, rice, sugar-cane, bananas, asparagus, and cotton. In the temperate zones often on maize and in green houses.
Fusarium verticillioides.Physiology: Some isolates can grow under anaerobic conditions and some tolerate >15 % NaCl in the medium.
Fusarium verticillioides.Biotechnological applications: Strains of F. fujikuroi produce gibberellins in an industrial scale. Specific enzymes for production of pure hydroxyl acid for the pharmaceutical industry has been explored.
Fusarium verticillioides.Biodeterioration and pathology: Pathogenic to many plants. Causes keratitis in man, toxic to animals fed with contaminated foodstuff.
Fusarium verticillioides.References: Seifert et al. (2003), Leslie & Summerell (2006), O’Donnell et al. (2013)
Fusarium verticillioides.Fig: 159. Fusarium verticillioides. Conidiophores, phialides, macro- and microconidia, the latter formed in long chains from phialides (orig. partly after E.J. Hermanides-Nijhof).
Fusarium verticillioides.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Geotrichum candidum.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA attaining a dia- meter of 70 mm in 7 days at 24 °C, white, smooth, often butyrous or membranous, odour often sweet. Colonies very restricted on DG18.
Geotrichum candidum.Micromorphology: Advancing hyphae septate, dicho- tomously branched (forked), 7–11 µm wide. Conidia cylindrical, barrel-shaped or ellipsoidal, mostly 6–12(– 20) × 3–6(–9) µm, formed by breaking up fertile hyphae, chains mostly aerial, erect or decumbent.
Geotrichum candidum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, thallic conidiogenesis, sexual form sometimes present.
Geotrichum candidum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. This species has a worldwide distribution, and has been isolated from various substrates, such as soil, water, air, corn and other cereals, rice, grain, rotting paper, textiles, grapes, citrus, bananas, tomatoes, cucumber, frozen fruitcake, fruit juices, bread, milk and milk products, animals and man. This species is also known as the “white milk fungus” or “machinery mould”.
Geotrichum candidum.Physiology: Geotrichum candidum has, like many types of yeast, a preference for moist or wet environments. Growth occurs at a water activity of 0.95, and no growth is observed at 0.90. The optimum growth temperature is 25–27 ° and the maximum is between 35–38 °C.
Geotrichum candidum.Biotechnological applications: Recent surveys indicate that G. candidum can play an important role in the ripening of many soft and semi-hard cheeses and make a positive contribution to the development of taste and aroma. It may also influence the growth of other microorganisms, both valuable and detrimental.
Geotrichum candidum.Fig: 161. Geotrichum candidum. Hyphae dichotomously branched, conidia formed by breaking up fertile, mostly aerial hyphae.
Geotrichum candidum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Gliomastix murorum.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA attaining a diameter of 12–22 mm after 7 days at 25 °C; on MEA slightly smaller, 8–18 mm, on DG18 3–9 mm. Colonies of young cultures (less than 7 days) on MEA are white with some floccose mycelium and becoming olivaceous- black with age due to sporulation; usually with extensive feathery mycelial ropes, especially in fresh isolates. Reverse on MEA pink-brown or brown.
Gliomastix murorum.Micromorphology: Hyphae bearing phialides are often aggregated into ropes. Conidiophores are poorly defined, consisting of 1–3 cells. Phialides hyaline and smooth below, becoming subhyaline to olivaceous brown and sometimes roughened with discrete granules towards the apex, 10–35 × 1.5–3.5 µm, below tapering slightly to 0.7–1.5 µm at the apex, which very occasionally has a tiny flared collarette. Conidia produced in slime and forming readily seceding chains, often with conspicuous separators between the spores, non-septate, subglobose to ellipsoidal, thick-walled, usually markedly roughened, dark olivaceous brown to black, 2.3–5.5 × 2.0–4.5 µm wide, mostly 3.0–3.5 µm.
Gliomastix murorum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Gliomastix murorum.Similar species: The difference between G. murorum var. murorum having catenate conidia and G. murorum var. felina having conidia in slimy heads does not appear to be supported by phylogenetic analysis. Therefore these varieties are considered under G. murorum (Summerbell et al. 2011) Gliomastix polychroma also occurs in indoor environments and produces conidia in dry chains.
Gliomastix murorum.Habitats and distribution: Worldwide, isolated from soil and various plant materials, but also from cellar wall, swimming pool floor, cereals, fruit (apple, banana).
Gliomastix murorum.References: Domsch et al. (2007) under Acremonium murorum, Summerbell et al. (2011)
Gliomastix murorum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Hyphopichia burtonii.Species description: Hyphopichia burtonii (Boidin et al.) von Arx & Van der Walt
Hyphopichia burtonii.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA and DG18 10–25 mm diam., white, grey-white or cream coloured with a somewhat raised center; texture powdery usually fringed by a broad hyphal band, sometimes butyrous; margin entire or lobate; reverse pale, off white or very pale yellow.
Hyphopichia burtonii.Micromorphology: Cells are oval, elongate to cylindrical, 2–6 × 3–9 µm, and occur singly, in pairs and in small clumps. Pseudohyphae and true hyphae may be present. Conidia may be borne on denticles and denticles occur on conidia as well as on hyphae and pseudohyphae. Arthroconidia present. Formation of ascospores in a heterothallic manner. Asci may form directly from diploid cells or result from the pairing of complementary mating types. Each ascus contains one to four hat- shaped ascospores which are readily released at maturity, globose to ellipsoidal and rough.
Hyphopichia burtonii.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic and thallic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, heterothallic.
Hyphopichia burtonii.Similar species: Saccharomycopsis fibuligera also spoils modified atmosphere packaged bread as well and resembles Hyphopichia burtonii in culture. Arthroconidia
Hyphopichia burtonii.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, isolated from cereals (corn, wheat) and cereal products. Hyphopichia burtonii is one of the species causing chalk mould defects on modified atmosphere packaged bread.
Hyphopichia burtonii.Physiology: The minimum growth temperature is slightly above 5 °C, the optimum around 27 °C and the maximum around 37 °C. Growth is possible at water activities above 0.78. Optimum growth at pH 5.
Hyphopichia burtonii.References: Kurtzman et al. (2011), Burgain et al
Hyphopichia burtonii.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Lichtheimia corymbifera.Macromorphology: Colonies growing rapidly, covering the whole Petridish within one week. Fast growth at both 25 and 37 °C. Colonies light greyish, 5–7 mm high (up to 15 mm).
Lichtheimia corymbifera.Micromorphology: Stolons 5–20 µm in diameter, often with adhering droplets, hyaline to brownish, smooth- walled, with an occasional septum, often terminating in a large sporangium. Rhizoids borne on a swollen area of the stolon, up to 370 µm long, infrequently branched. Sporangiophores (40–)80–450(–500) × (3–)4–8(–13) µm, hyaline to faintly pigmented, smooth to slightly roughened, simple or sometimes branched, arising solitarily from the stolons, in groups of three or up to 7 in a whorl below the large terminal sporangium at some distance from the rhizoids (smaller sporangiophores also bent or circinnate). Sporangia more or less pyriform, 10–40 µm in diam, up to 80 µm when terminating a stolon, many-spored, hyaline at first, becoming grey to greyish-brown when mature; wall transparent, smooth to slightly roughened. Columella hyaline to greyish, with or without a collar, (7–)10–30 µm in diam, up to 60 µm when terminating a stolon, globose to short ovoid (especially larger ones). The apex of smaller columellae often with one to several projections. Sporangiospores varying from subglobose to oblong-ellipsoidal, (2.5–)3– 6(–7) × 2.5–4.5 µm, hyaline to light grey, smooth-walled.
Lichtheimia corymbifera.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. World- wide distribution with a preference for (sub)tropical regions. This species has been isolated from soil, stored grain, decaying vegetables, fruit, air, compost, animals and man.
Lichtheimia corymbifera.Biodeterioration and pathology: Lichtheimia corym- bifera is an uncommon agent of human (sub)cutaneous mycosis and several cases of invasive infections in AIDS patients have been published. It is the most frequent agent of bovine mycotic abortion (de Hoog et al. 2000).
Lichtheimia corymbifera.Fig: 166. Lichtheimia corymbifera. Sporangiophores, sporangia and sporangiospores.
Lichtheimia corymbifera.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Memnoniella echinata.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 22 mm in 7 days, appearing blackish-green with a white rim and powdery due to the conidial masses. Reverse is black. Colonies on MEA have a diameter of 23 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, appearing blackish-green with white aerial mycelium. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 5 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, appearing white. Reverse is white too. Colonies on SNA reach diameters of 8–12 mm in 7 days with thin white mycelium and sporulation in the centre.
Memnoniella echinata.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are simple and erect, up to 80 µm long and 3–4 µm wide. They are hyaline and smooth at the base and slightly rougher and darker towards the apex. Phialides, which are formed in clusters of 4–8 on each conidiophore, are 7–9 µm long and 3–4 µm wide. They are smooth, obovoid and hyaline at the base and darker towards the apex. Conidia are aseptate and subglobose, 3–4 µm, and produced in dry chains. They are first hyaline and smooth but becoming coarsely roug- hened to heavily tuberculate and black opaque with age.
Memnoniella echinata.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Memnoniella echinata.Similar species: Stachybotrys chartarum and S. chloro- halonata resemble M. echinata, but these species produced
Memnoniella echinata.Chemical markers: Griseofulvins, spiriocyclic drima- nes, trichodermin and trichodermol.
Memnoniella echinata.Important mycotoxins: Griseofulvin, spirocyclic dri- manes (different than the ones from Stachybotrys), tri- chodermin and trichodermol.
Memnoniella echinata.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Isolated from cardboard, grain, gypsum board, paper, textile and soil. Reported from Europe, the Middle East and North America.
Memnoniella echinata.Physiology: Grows poorly and do not sporulate on media with low water activity, such as DG18 and DRYES and sporulates sparingly on MEA.
Memnoniella echinata.Biodeterioration and pathology: Exposure to M. echinata on natural substrates or in culture should be avoided.
Memnoniella echinata.Fig: 168. Memnoniella echinata. Conidiophores and conidia in chains.
Memnoniella echinata.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Microascus melanosporus.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA attaining a diameter of 19–23 mm at 25 °C (7 days), convex or crateriform, pale olivaceous grey to olivaceous grey, margin undulate. On OA attaining a diameter of 21– 25 mm after 14 d at 25 °C, low convex, white to cream coloured with olivaceous grey to iron grey zones, margin crenated. On DG18 attaining a diameter of 20–24 mm, crateriform, white to cream-coloured with grey olivaceous to greyish sepia and vinaceous grey zones, margin undulate.
Microascus melanosporus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores arising from substrate mycelium, simple or indistinctive, bearing one to multiple annellides. Annellides ampulliform, (5.5–)7.5–11(–13) µm long, (2–)2.5–3.5(–4) µm broad
Microascus melanosporus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Microascus melanosporus.Similar species: Microascus melanosporus is morphologically and phylogenetically closely related to
Microascus melanosporus.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: LM652572; ?-tubulin: KX924311; ITS: KX923876.
Microascus melanosporus.Habitats and distribution: Indoor environment (air, plaster, carpet, oriented strand board), archives, food factories (cheese warehouses, bakery).
Microascus melanosporus.Physiology: Growth at 37 °C absent or very slow in some isolates.
Microascus melanosporus.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 24 °C growing rather slowly, 10–16 mm in diameter in 7 days. At first the colonies are white, with a central floccose tuft, becoming grayish in 2–3 weeks. Reverse grey, becoming sepia to fuscous-black.
Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Micromorphology: Mycelial hyphae hyaline at first, darkening in age; sporing structures mostly as single annellides borne on the aerial hyphae or ropes of hyphae, occasionally in groups of 2–3, rarely 4, on very short, single celled or rarely 2-celled conidiophores. Annellides 4–10 µm long. Conidia ovate, with a basal truncation, which is very narrow and often difficult to detect, smooth or slightly rough, 4–5.5 × 3.5–4.5 µm, black or dark brown in mass.
Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: LM652569, ?-tubulin: LM652647; ITS: LM652434.
Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Habitats and distribution: This species has a world- wide distribution and isolated from vaccination serum, air (compost) soil and indoor environments.
Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Physiology: No growth at 5 °C; the optimum temperature is 30 °C and the maximum is around 37 °C.
Microascus paisii (Pollacci).Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Mucor circinelloides.Macromorphology: Colonies covering the Petri dish within one week at 25 °C. Good growth and sporulation at 5–30 °C (length and number of tall sporangiophores decreasing at lower temperatures); maximum 37 °C. Colonies greyish-green, up to 6(–7) mm in height.
Mucor circinelloides.Micromorphology: Colonies composed of tall and short sporangiophores, when tall, then often sympodially branched with long and short branches, the latter seldom circinnate; when short, then often circinnate branches, with slightly encrusted walls, up to 17 µm in diam. Sporangiophores filled with droplets in younger parts. Sporangia whitish to yellowish at first becoming brownish-grey when mature, up to 80 µm in diam (rarely 100 µm), walls slightly roughened (spinulose), walls of larger sporangia leaving small collars after breaking up, walls of smaller ones persistent and leaving large basal membranes. Columella obovoid to ellipsoidal in larger sporangia and globose in smaller sporangia, up to 50 µm greyish-brown. Sporangiospores ellipsoidal,
Mucor circinelloides.Similar species: Mucor circinelloides differs from M. racemosus by the absence of chlamydospores.
Mucor circinelloides.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. World- wide distribution, mostly in soil, on dung, decaying potatoes, in animals and human.
Mucor circinelloides.Physiology: Maximum growth temperature 36 °C. Growth, sporulation, and presence of few or many tall and short sporangiophores can be influenced by temperature. However shape, size and uniformity (or variability) of sporangiophores are strain characteristics not influenced by temperature.
Mucor circinelloides.Biotechnological applications: Mucor circinelloides has been detected, together with Mucor indicus and Amylomyces rouxii, in various fungal fermented food products from the Orient.
Mucor circinelloides.Fig: 174. Mucor circinelloides. A. Sporangiophores and columellae. B. Sporangiospores. C. Zygospore.
Mucor circinelloides.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Mucor plumbeus.Macromorphology: Colonies fast growing, covering the Petri dish within one week, grey or light olive-grey coloured, variable in height (between 2–20 mm), due to strain properties and to external conditions (media, temperature).
Mucor plumbeus.Micromorphology: Sporangiophores with slightly encrusted walls, branching (sympodial and monopodial) up to 20(21) µm in diam, constricted and somewhat recurved below the sporangium. Sporangia hyaline becoming dark-brown to brownish-grey with age, up to 80(–100) µm in diam with spinulose walls. Columellae pyriform, obovoid with a truncate base or ellipsoidal to cylindrical-ellipsoidal; smaller columellae often pointed- conical, up to 25–50 µm (seldom up to 50–70 µm), hyaline becoming brown to grey, smooth or roughened often with several projections, collar present. Sporangiospores globose, sometimes more or less ellipsoidal or irregularly shaped, (5–)7–8(–10) µm in diam, yellowish-brown, slightly rough-walled. Chlamydospores present, especially in older cultures. Heterothallic. Zygospores rare.
Mucor plumbeus.Similar species: Mucor plumbeus is easily recognisable by its columellae with projections.
Mucor plumbeus.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor, often as air contaminant. World-wide distribution, e.g. soils, hay, dung, stored seeds of wheat, oats. This species is dimor- phic and can grow,under anaerobic conditions in a yeast phase (e.g. in juices).
Mucor plumbeus.Physiology: Growth and sporulation at 5–20 °C (at 5 °C slow); growth but poor sporulation between 20–30 °C and no growth at 37 °C.
Mucor plumbeus.Fig: 176. Mucor plumbeus. Sporangiophores, sporangia, columellae with projections and sporangiospores.
Mucor plumbeus.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Mucor racemosus.Macromorphology: Colonies fast growing, covering the Petri dish within one week, white, becoming brownish- grey with age, 2–20(–30) mm in height, consisting of tall and short sporangiophores.
Mucor racemosus.Micromorphology: Sporangiophores branched (in a mixed sympodial and monopodial way), the short branches sometimes recurved, with encrusted walls. Sporangia hyaline becoming brownish to grey with age, up to 80(90) µm in diam but mostly 70 µm in diam, wall spinulose (small sporangia up to 20 µm in diam with persistent walls). Columella obovoid, ellipsoidal, cylindrical-ellipsoidal, slightly pyriform, usually with truncate base, up to 37–55 µm, light brown with collar. Sporangiospores broadly ellipsoidal to subglobose, 5.5– 8.5(–10) × 4–7 µm or 5.5–7 µm in diam, smooth walled, greyish. Chlamydospores numerous, in sporangiophores and sometimes in columellae, barrel-shaped when young, subglobose in older cultures, yellowish. Heterothallic. Zygospores (after 10 days on cherry agar at 10 °C) in aerial mycelium, reddish-brown to bright-brown, globose or subglobose, up to 110 µm in diam, roughened by short spines (5 µm in length); suspensors equal or subequal, up to 33 µm long and 35 µm wide; zygospores slightly roughened. Chlamydospores can be present in zygophores and suspensors.
Mucor racemosus.Similar species: Mucor racemosus is similar to M. circinelloides, but the former is characterised by the formation of numerous chlamydospores in sporangiophores (and sometimes columellae).
Mucor racemosus.Physiology: Good growth and sporulation between 5–30 °C; optimum 20–25 °C and maximum around 37 °C.
Mucor racemosus.Biodeterioration and pathology: Mucor racemosus is responsible for a spongy soft rot of cool stored (sweet) potatoes and citrus.
Mucor racemosus.Fig: 178. Mucor racemosus. A. Sporangiophores with sporangium and columellae. B. Columellae. C. Sporangiospores. D. Chlamydospores.
Mucor racemosus.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Neocosmospora solani.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 25–50 mm after 4 days. Aerial mycelium sparse or dense and floccose, sometimes leathery, greyish-white, cream to buff, conidial slime formed in sporodochia or pionnotes. Agar surface sometimes green to bluish-brown. Reverse often in greenish or brownish shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 20–55 mm after 4 days with velvety dense mycelium often in dark rose to brownish-red colours. Some strains have a yellowish shade. The reverse is bright yellow with a red to brownish-red tinge.
Neocosmospora solani.Micromorphology: onidiophoreson SNA areunbranched or branched bearing monophialides. Microconidia are usually abundant, ovoid or oblong, 0–1-septate, 8–16(– 24) × 2–4(–5) µm, formed from elongated (up to 90 µm) and sometimes verticillate conidiophores. Macroconidia formed after 4–7 days from short branched conidiophores which may form sporodochia, 3–5(–7)-septate (usually 3-septate), fusiform, cylindrical, often moderately curved, 27–52(–65) × 4.4–6.8 µm, with an indistinctly pedicellate footcell and a short blunt apical cell. Chlamydospores are hyaline, smooth- or rough walled, globose to ovoid, in hyphae or in conidial cells, either terminal, on lateral branches, intercalary or in chains.
Neocosmospora solani.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph has been observed and may occur in some strains.
Neocosmospora solani.Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium solani species complex” (O’Donnell et al. 2013) that contains numerous undescribed phylogenetic species. It has been proposed to reclassify the species as Neocosmospora species (Lombard et al. 2015). In the broad sense N, solani includes a number of species with very similar morphology, and more than 40 varieties and pathogenic forms have been described based on the pathogenicity towards different plants and mammals. Recently many have been described at species level supported by phylogenetic analyses e.g. Fusarium azukicola, F. brasiliense, F. crassistipitatum, F. cuneirostrum,
Neocosmospora solani.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: KT313611; DNA-dependent RNA polymerase subunit II: KT313623.
Neocosmospora solani.Chemical markers: Cyclosporine A, fusaric acid, napht- hoquinone pigments, nectriafurone.
Neocosmospora solani.Habitats and distribution: Neocosmospora solani is common world-wide in food and indoor environments. Occurring in soils and on a wide range of plants and animals.
Neocosmospora solani.Biotechnological applications: Strains have been found to degrade many organic pollutants and pesticides. Production of enzymes, e.g. cutinases, has been investigated.
Neocosmospora solani.Biodeterioration and pathology: Causes root and stem rot and spoilage of many different plants. Often found in wounds and damaged organisms as secondary infections. Some strains are pathogenic to humans and animals and can cause keratitis in man.
Neocosmospora solani.Fig: 180. Neocosmospora solani. A. Macroconidia and conidiophores. B–C. Microconidia formed from elongated conidiophores. D. Chlamyd- ospores (orig. partly after E.J. Hermanides-Nijhof).
Neocosmospora solani.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Neurospora sitophila.Macromorphology: Colonies are growing fast on most media, attaining a diameter of 25 mm in one day at 24 °C. Colonies are floccose with irregular tufts, especially at the margin of the Petri-dish, initially colourless, becoming pinkish to orange. Mycelium, conidiogenous hyphae and conidia often grow out of the Petri-dish and are able to lift the lid. Because of the explosive growth of this fungus, spoilage of products can occur within a few days.
Neurospora sitophila.Micromorphology: Conidiogenous hyphae are more or less ascending, smooth-walled, septate, with lateral branches, which form chains of conidia. Conidia are one- celled, produced in chains and connected by a narrow hyaline strand. Conidia become separated quickly and are dispersed as a powdery mass under dry conditions. They are ellipsoidal, more or less cylindrical or globose to subglobose and often also irregular in shape and size, (7–)10–15 × 5–10(–11)µm. Conidia are hyaline, pinkish to orange in mass and have smooth walls.
Neurospora sitophila.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal and thallic conidiogenesis; sexual morph may occur in culture.
Neurospora sitophila.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Neurospora sitophila is reported from Europe, USA, Japan, Surinam and Indonesia. Neurospora sitophila is also known as the “red bread mould”, occurring on bread and related products, silage, meat, sometimes in connection with harvest, transportation and storage rot of fruit (e.g. apples, strawberries, raspberries). This fungus is able to grow into slants or Petri dishes of other cultures so that contamination in the laboratory and hospitals easily can occur. Sometimes it is also occurring as a contaminant in indoor environments.
Neurospora sitophila.Physiology: Neurospora sitophila has good growth between 25–35 °C and is capable of grow at a water activity of 0.88–0.90. Neurospora sitophila is capable of spoiling mycologial media stored at 2 °C.
Neurospora sitophila.Biotechnological applications: Neurospora sitophila is used for the production of oncom merah, a fermented food product made from peanut press cake in Indonesia.
Neurospora sitophila.Fig: 182. A. Neurospora sitophila; branched conidiophores forming chains of conidia. B. Neurospora crassa; branched conidiophores forming chains of conidia.
Neurospora sitophila.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Oidiodendron griseum.Macromorphology: Colonies are slow-growing reaching about up to 15 mm in 14 days on most media. They are greyish to olivaceous brown, velvety often with tufts towards the central part of the colonies. Reverse dark brown.
Oidiodendron griseum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores erect, pigmented, up to 100 µm long and 1.5–2.0 µm wide, apically branched. Branches, consisting of chains of arthroconidia. The arthroconidiamayalsobeproducedfromundifferentiated hyphae. Between the arthroconidia which are produced basipetally often empty cells are present. Arthroconidia pale grey-green in mass, smooth-walled or nearly so, 2.0–3.5 × 1.5–2.0 µm, ovoid to short cylindrical.
Oidiodendron griseum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Oidiodendron griseum.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Isolated from soils in forests in Scandinavia, Britain, France, Africa, New Zealand, North America and Canada, Trinidad. Also from humus, garden compost, decaying wood, pine lit- ter, cedar and peat bogs, hay. Frequently isolated from paper, archives, and timber.
Oidiodendron griseum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Parengyodontium album.Species description: Parengyodontium album (Limber) C.C. Tsang et al.
Parengyodontium album.Macromorphology: Colonies attaining a diameter of 14–16 mm in 8 days on MEA, appearing lanose to floccose, up to 2 mm high, sometimes zonate, purely hyaline. Reverse ochraceous buff or uncoloured.
Parengyodontium album.Micromorphology: Submerged hyphae and hyphae of the aerial mycelium hyaline, smooth–walled, 1–2.5 µm wide. Fertile hyphae mostly slightly differentiated, 2–4 µm wide, ascendent to procumbent, somewhat stiff, apically dichotomously branched, bearing conidiogenous cells in whorls of 1–3 at wide, often right angles; conidiogenous cells occasionally scattered or with two on a lateral stalk cell which is cylindrical, 6–12 × 2–3 µm, or rarely swollen up to 5 µm. Conidiogenous cells consisting of an elongate to subcylindrical tapering basal part, (7–)10–24(–30) × 1.5–2.5 µm, sometimes slightly swollen up to 3.5 µm, and a well developed rachis, up to 3 5 µm long and rather constantly 1 µm wide, geniculate, denticulate, denticles as wide as the rachis and up to 1 µm long. Conidia hyaline, smooth, globose to subglobose, sometimes with an apiculate base, (1.5–)2–3(–3.5) × (1.5–)2–2.5(–3) µm. No chlamydospores were observed.
Parengyodontium album.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic, sympodi- al, denticulate conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Parengyodontium album.Molecular markers: Three potential cryptic species within the Parengyodontium album species complex are revealed. The ITS and BenA sequences of the type of P. album (CBS 504.83) are given: ITS: LC092880; ?-tubulin: LC092918.
Parengyodontium album.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. This species has a worldwide distribution and has been isolated from air, humid frescos, water damaged and moist walls in buildings, caves and crawlspaces. Often found on dead insects in cellars.
Parengyodontium album.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species has long been utilized for the mass production of proteinase K. Parengyodontium album is a opportunistic human pathogen (Tsang et al. 2016).
Parengyodontium album.References: de Hoog et al. (2000), Tsang et al. (2016)
Parengyodontium album.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Pleurostoma richardsiae.Macromorphology: Colonies reaching 20–30 mm in diameter in 10 days at 20 °C on MEA, floccose, or woolly. Colony surface on MEA olive-brown, in reverse a darker shade of olive-brown.
Pleurostoma richardsiae.Micromorphology: Phialides arising singly or in sparsely branching divergent conidiophores. Pleurostoma richardsiae produces two very distinct types of conidia: brown, (sub)globose conidia, 2.5–3.5 µm; and hyaline, ellipsoidal conidia, 2–6 × 1.0–3.0. Phialides of P. richardsiae are 10–35 µm long with prominently flaring collarettes, particularly those producing the pigmented conidia.
Pleurostoma richardsiae.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Pleurostoma richardsiae.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide distribution. It has been reported from margarine, CIP tanks, soil and wood.
Pleurostoma richardsiae.Physiology: Minimum temperature for growth is below 10 °C, optimum 30 °C and maximum 35 °C.
Pleurostoma richardsiae.Biodeterioration and pathology: Pleurostomophora richardsiae can also infect humans, usually through traumatic implantation, and also cause subcutaneous phaeo-hyphomycotic cysts.
Pleurostoma richardsiae.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Macromorphology: Colonies slow growing, initially white becoming greyish, buff or brownish with age, velvety often tufted. Reverse creamish, yellowish with a reddish brown center.
Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Micromorphology: Alternate arthroconidia produ- ced from fertile hyaline hyphae, in short chains of 2–4, in terminal or lateral position, barrel-shaped, obovoid, cuneiform, often with a truncate base, 3–6 × 2–4 µm subhyaline, initially thin- and smooth-walled, becoming rough-walled and thicker walled with age. Intercalary conidia, barrel-shaped, 3–6 × 2–5 µm, smooth-walled at first, later rough-walled.
Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic, acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. This species has a preference for temperate regions. Pseudogymnoascus pannorum has been isolated from wood, leaves, compost, archives and soils (especially Arctic permafrost soils).
Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Physiology: The optimum temperature for this species is 18 °C and the maximum 25–30 °C. Strains of Pseudo- gymnoascus pannorum have been reported to show some growth below 0 °C. Furthermore, P. pannorum is a xero- philic species and is able to grow at a water activity of 0.89.
Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species has been implicated in the biodeterioration of antique and optical glass, which might lead to etching. Furthermore, it has been reported as an agent of superficial infection of skin and nails in humans.
Pseudogymnoascus pannorum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Purpureocillium lilacinum.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA moderately to fast growing and attaining a diameter of 25–35 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, consisting of a basal felt with or without floccose aerial overgrowth, sometimes strongly floccose, white at first, becoming vinaceous; reverse mostly in shades of purple or sometimes uncoloured.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores arising from submerged hyphae 4–6 mm in length, occasionally forming loose synnemata up to 2 mm high; stalks with roughened thick walls, 3–4 mm wide consisting of verticillate branches with whorls of two to four phialides. Phialides 6–9 × 2.5–3 µm, having a swollen basal portion tapering into a short distinct neck about 1 mm wide. Conidia in divergent chains, ellipsoidal to fusiform, smooth-walled to slightly roughened, hyaline, purple en masse, 2–3 × 2–4 µm.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Similar species: Purpureocillium lilacinum was previously classified in the genus Paecilomyces based on the production of paecilomyces-type phialides.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: FR734156; ?-tubulin: JQ965114; ITS: FR734101.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide; isolated from wet environments including water from water tanks, bottled water, sinks, showers (including drains) and toi- lets. This species can thrive on wet and moist surfaces of water distribution systems and form a biofilm, together with other species such as Aspergillus, Fusarium and Sa- rocladium. Purpureocillium lilacinum is also isolated from other substrates, such as decaying vegetation, insects, nematodes, wood (pulp), man and other vertebrates.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Physiology: No or very slow growth at 37 °C (0–10(–20) mm).
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Biotechnological applications: Purpureocillium lilaci- num is used for the control of nematode pests.
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species is occasionally associated with human infections (most frequent manifestation is keratitis, but other sites of the body can be affected).
Purpureocillium lilacinum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Rhizomucor miehei.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA growing attaining a diameter of 30–70 mm after 7 days at 25 °C. Growth at 37 °C faster, covering the Petri-dish in one week. Colonies 1 mm in height, grayish coloured.
Rhizomucor miehei.Micromorphology: Stolons up to 9 µm in diameter with roughened walls; rhizoids weakly developed; sporangiophores sympodially branched, up to 7 µm in diameter, with slightly encrusted, brownish walls; sporangia grey, glittering, up to 50(–60) µm in diameter, with encrusted walls which rupture at maturity; columellae obovoid to slightly pyriform, up to 28 × 25 µm, rarely larger, brownish to mouse grey, with small protrusions; collars poorly defined to none; sporangiospores subglobose, a few ellipsoidal, 3–4 µm in diameter, rarely larger; zygospores (homothallic) formed in the aerial mycelium, globose to slightly compressed, up to 50 µm, but mostly approx. 35 µm in diameter reddish brown when young becoming blackish brown.
Rhizomucor miehei.Habitats and distribution: Cosmopolitan, isolated from soil, compost and stored barley. This species is thermophilic and therefore occurs in warmer environments. Rhizomucor is significant for foods in (sub)tropical regions.
Rhizomucor miehei.Physiology: This species is thermophilic and has an optimum growth temperature between 42 and 45 °C. Minimum and maximum temperatures are 21 and 62 °C, respectively.
Rhizomucor miehei.Biotechnological applications: Used for the production of proteolytic and lipase enzymes; production of milk- coagulating enzymes for milk clotting in the cheese production.
Rhizomucor miehei.Fig: Rhizomucor miehei. Sporangiophores, columella spores and zygospores; redrawn from Schipper (1978).
Rhizomucor miehei.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Rhizopus oligosporus.Macromorphology: Colonies fast growing, covering the Petri dish within one week. Colony pale brownish- grey, up to 1 mm high.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Micromorphology: Sporangiophores solitary or in groups of up to 4(–6), arising as subhyaline to brownish hyphae opposite very short rhizoids, smooth or slightly rough-walled, up to 1000 µm long and 10–18 µm in diameter. Sporangia globose, brownish-black at maturity, (50–)100–180 µm in diam. Columella globose to subglobose with funnel-shaped apophysis. Sporangiospores irregularly shaped, globose, ellipsoidal, 7–10(–24) µm in length, brownish in mass, single, subhyaline, smooth-walled. Chlamydospores abundant, single or in short chains, colourless, with granular contents, occurring in hyphae, sporangiophores and sporangia, globose, ellipsoidal, cylindrical, (7–)12–45 × 7–35 µm.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Similar species: Rhizopus oligosporus is considered to be the domesticated form of R. microsporus.This species has typical shorter sporangiophores and smaller ornamented spores. Spores of R. oligospores are irregularly shaped, large (7–24 µm) and smooth-walled. Rhizopus oligosporus is used for the fermentation of soybeans e.g. tempe.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Habitats and distribution: Food. Known from Japan, China, and Indonesia; isolated from tempe.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Physiology: Optimum between 30–35 °C; minimum at 12 °C and maximum around 42 °C.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Biotechnological applications: Rhizopus oligosporus is used in food fermentations, especially for the production of tempe.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Fig: 259. Rhizopus oligosporus. A. Sporangiophores and sporangium. B. Columellae and apophysis. C. Sporangiospores. D. Chlamydospores.
Rhizopus oligosporus.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Rhizopus oryzae.Macromorphology: Colony white becoming brownish- grey with age, about 10 mm high.
Rhizopus oryzae.Micromorphology: Stolons smooth or slightly rough, almost colourless to yellowish-brown. Rhizoids brownish, opposite the sporangiophores that also can arise directly from stolons without rhizoids. Sporangiophores solitary or in groups of up to 5, sometimes forked, smooth-walled, 150–2000 µm long and 6–14 µm in diam. Sporangia globose or subglobose with spinulose wall, becoming dark- brown to black-brown, 50–200 µm in diam. Columella ovoid or globose, 30–120 µm in diameter, smooth- or slightly rough-walled. Sporangiospores globose, ovoid or irregularly shaped, often polygonal, striate, 4–10 µm long. Chlamydospores globose, 10–35 µm in diam, ellipsoidal or cylindrical, 8–13 × 16–24 µm in diameter.
Rhizopus oryzae.Habitats and distribution: Food. Worldwide distribu- tion, though mainly in tropical and subtropical zones. Isolated from soils, grains, groundnuts, polluted water, vegetables, decaying fruit.
Rhizopus oryzae.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species is associated with Rhizopus rot of fruits. Furthermore, it is an important agent of human mucormycosis.
Rhizopus oryzae.Fig: 261. Rhizopus oryzae. A. Sporangiophores. B. Columellae and apophysis. C. Sporangium. D. Sporangiospores. E. Chlamydospores.
Rhizopus oryzae.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Rhizopus stolonifer.Macromorphology: Colony whitish becoming greyish- brown due to brownish sporangiophores and brown- black sporangia, often over 20 mm high. Mycelium, sporangiophores and spores can grow outside the Petri dish and therefore contamination of the laboratory can easily occur.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Micromorphology: Sporangiophores 1.5–3(–4) mm tall, solitary or in groups of 2–7 (usually 3–4) from the almost colourless to dark-brown, smooth or slightly rough-walled stolons opposite the branched rhizoids. Sporangia globose to subglobose, (50–)150–360 µm in diam, blackish-brown at maturity. Columella globose, subglobose, ovoid (40–) 70–160(–250) µm in diam. Sporangiospores irregular in shape often polygonal or ovoid, globose, elliptical, striate, (4–)7–15 × 6–8(–12) µm. Chlamydospores absent in stolons, sometimes present in submerged hyphae. Heterothallic. Zygospores brownish-black, warted, with unequal suspensors, (75–)150–200 µm in diam.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Similar species: Rhizopus stolonifer can be distinguished from R. oryzae and R. oligosporus by its inability to grow at 37 °C.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor (commonly air-borne). Worldwide distribution but more often occurring in warmer zones. Isolated from soil, grain, vegetables, fruit and nuts.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Physiology: The optimum temperature is 25–26 °C, minimum about 5 °C and maximum 32–33 °C.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Biodeterioration and pathology: Rhizopus rot of various fruits, such as strawberries, peaches, avocados etc., is mostly caused by R. stolonifer.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Fig: 263. Rhizopus stolonifer. A. Sporangiophores. B. Columellae and apophysis. C. Sporangiospores. D. Zygospore.
Rhizopus stolonifer.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA and DG18 15– 25 mm diameter, dull and gray-white with a somewhat raised center. Tufts of hyphal outgrowths on the colony surface give a diagnostic roughness; reverse pale, off- white or very pale yellow.
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Micromorphology: Abundant production of true hyphae with varying numbers of blastoconidia, as well as some pseudohyphae. Conidia arise on denticles (small projections) along the length of undifferentiated hyphae, yeast-like, spherical, ellipsoidal or pyriform, 2–6 µm long, with thin smooth walls. Budding cells are ovoid to elongate, 2–5 × 3–12.5 µm, sometimes tapered. Asci are, when present, spherical to ovoid and may be free, having formed from a single budded cell, or attached to the ends or sides of hyphae. Occasionally, asci arise on protuberances from two adjacent hyphal cells, but generally asci are unconjugated. Each ascus forms two to four hat-shaped ascospores that are liberated at maturity; 7–8 µm long, including the flange.
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic and thallic conidiogenesis; sexual morph present, homothallic.
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Similar species: Hyphopichia burtonii also spoils modified atmosphere packaged bread and resembles S. fibuligera in culture. Arthroconidia are produced by H. burtonii and this feature can be used to differentiate both
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, isolated from cereals and cereal products. Saccharomycopsis fibuligera is one of the species causing chalk mold defects on modified atmosphere packaged bread. This species is also present in traditional Asian alcoholic starters for rice wine production (e.g. Daqu, Ragi, Nuruk).
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Physiology: The minimum growth temperature is around 5 °C, the optimum around 26 °C and the maximum around 38 °C. Growth is possible at water activities above 0.82. Optimum growth at pH 5.
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Biotechnological applications: This species is present in Asian alcoholic starters and has potential in biofuel production using biomass. It is a common spoilage orga- nism of modified atmosphere packaged bread.
Saccharomycopsis fibuligera.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Sarocladium strictum.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA are slow-growing, generally less than 20 mm in diameter in 7 days. The colonies of S. strictum are pale pink with cylindrical conidia. Colonies are very inhibited on DG18.
Sarocladium strictum.Micromorphology: Vegetative mycelium is mostly hyaline. Phialides are awl-shaped, simple, erect, arising from the substrate mycelium or from bundled aerial hyphae (fasciculate). If compound conidiophores occur, branches are only restricted to the basal part (basitonous). Conidia are usually one-celled, hyaline or pigmented, mostly in slimy heads.
Sarocladium strictum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not present in culture.
Sarocladium strictum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Saro- cladium has a world-wide distribution. Most species are saprophytic and have been isolated from dead plant material and soil and some species are pathogenic to plants and humans. Sarocladium strictum has been isolated from wet or water-damaged indoor environments, e.g. bathrooms, humidifier water, wet wallpaper and woodwork.
Sarocladium strictum.Physiology: A coarse overview of different physiological characters for several Acremonium species can be found in Domsch et al. (2007). Sarocladium strictum is here listed under Acremonium strictum.
Sarocladium strictum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Several Sarocladium species are related to infections in humans and animals and are (weakly) pathogenic for plants.
Sarocladium strictum.Fig: 266. Sarocladium strictum. Conidiophores, phialides and conidia.
Sarocladium strictum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Scopulariopsis asperula.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 24 °C attaining a diameter of 19–25 mm, light rose-brown at first with a whitish velvety margin and a central tuft, becoming brown to brownish-black and floccose to funiculose all over. Reverse light brownish-rose becoming dark brown.
Scopulariopsis asperula.Micromorphology: Conidiogenous cells annellate, borne singly on aerial hyphae or in groups of 2–10 on short conidiophores, cylindrical often with a slightly swollen base, 2–27 µm long. Conidia globose to broadly ovate with a truncate base and occasionally a more or less pointed apex, 5–8 × 5–7 µm, smooth-walled, olive to brown in mass.
Scopulariopsis asperula.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Scopulariopsis asperula.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: KX924182; ?-tubulin: KX924392; ITS: LM652463.
Scopulariopsis asperula.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. This species is isolated from mouldy straw, cheese, hen’s eggs, cacao leaves from Ghana, paper, rabbit liver, man (onychomycosis, dermatomycosis), soil from Hong Kong, Central Africa, Peru, Germany, UK.
Scopulariopsis asperula.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species can be involved in onychomycoses (Hoog et al. 2000).
Scopulariopsis asperula.Fig: 268. Scopulariopsis asperula. Annellate conidiogenous cells, single or on short conidiophores and smooth walled conidia.

Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 24 °C attaining a diameter of 32–55 mm in 7 days, whitish becoming brownish-rose (vinaceous-buff), more or less funiculose at first, becoming powdery with a prominent central tuft. Reverse in cream to brownish shades.
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Micromorphology: Conidiogenous cells annellate, borne singly on aerial hyphae or terminally on once or twice branched conidiophores, in groups of 2–3(–4), cylindrical, often with a more or less swollen base, 9–25
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, microascus-type.
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Similar species: Morphologically, S. brevicaulis resembles Scopulariopsis flava (Sopp) Morton & Smith. The only difference is that in S. flava the colony is whitish to creamish instead of brownish. Abbott et al. (1998) found several isolates of S. brevicaulis to form perithecia
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: HG380363; ?-tubulin: KX924423; ITS: LM652465.
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Worldwide distribution, isolated from soil, wood, stems, straw, grains (e.g. wheat), fruit (apples), soy-beans, groundnuts, dead insects, dung, paper, animals, human (e.g. skin lesions, lungs), animal products like meat, cheese, milk, butter. Its presence can be recognized by a characteristic ammoniac odour.
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Physiology: The optimum temperature is 24–30 °C; minimum 5 °C; maximum 37 °C.
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species is involved in onychomycoses; see also Pérez-Cantero A, Guarro J (2019).
Scopulariopsis brevicaulis.Fig: 270. Scopulariopsis brevicaulis. Conidiophores with annellate conidiogenous cells and rough-walled conidia.

Scopulariopsis candida.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 24 °C attaining a diameter of 30–40 mm in 7 days, white (darkening after about two weeks), velvety to powdery with a central tuft. Occasionally the powdery appearance of the colony is disturbed by small white sterile overgrowths. Reverse in creamish to light brown shades.
Scopulariopsis candida.Micromorphology: Conidiogenous cells annellate, borne singly on aerial hyphae or terminally in groups of 2–3 short conidiophores, cylindrical, often with a slightly swollen base, 10–25 µm in diam. Conidia subglobose to broadly ovate with a truncate base and more or less rounded apex, 5–8 × 4–7 µm, smooth-walled, whitish to cream in mass. Small black sclerotial bodies can be formed after 1–2 weeks, especially at 17–19 °C.
Scopulariopsis candida.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Scopulariopsis candida.Similar species: Scopulariopsis brevicaulis is related but differs in conidial colour and has rough walled conidia;
Scopulariopsis candida.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Isolated from soils, milled rice, paper, cheese, human (nails, skin).
Scopulariopsis candida.Fig: 272. Scopulariopsis candida. Annellate conidiogenous cells, single or on conidiophores, and smooth-walled conidia.
Scopulariopsis candida.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Stachybotrys chartarum.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 28 mm in 7 days, appearing blackish green with a white rim and powdery due to the conidial masses. Sometimes producing an orange-brown extracellular pigment. Reverse is black. Colonies on SNA have a diameter of 30 mm after 7 days at 25 °C in the dark, mycelium appearing thread-like with blackish green centre of conidia. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 7 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, appearing beige. Reverse is also beige. Colonies on MEA are 22 mm in diameter with a greyish appearance and feather-like synnemata.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are simple or branched, up to 100 µm long and 3–6 µm wide. They are hyaline and smooth at the base and rough and dark towards the apex. Phialides, which are formed in clus- ters of 4–10 on each conidiophore, are 9–13 µm long and 4–6 µm wide. They are smooth, obovoid and hyaline at the base and dark towards the apex. Conidia are borne in slime heads, ellipsoidal and hyaline. Mature conidia are aseptate, ellipsoidal, 8–12 × 4–5 µm, coarsely roughened (tuberculate to striate) and black opaque.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Similar species: Stachybotrys chlorohalonata has a simi- lar morphology, but differs from S. chartarum by having broadly ellipsoidal conidia and producing a green extra- cellular pigment on PDA and CYA. For a key see page 83.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: KU847003; ?-tubulin: KU847115; ITS: KU846679.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Chemical markers: Stachybotryschartarum contains two chemotypes (S and A) that share the same morphology, but produce different metabolites. Stachybotrys chartarum (S) produces satratoxins and roridins, while
Stachybotrys chartarum.Typical cultures: Stachybotrys chartarum (S): CBS 109209, 109288. S. chartarum (A): CBS 109287, 109289,
Stachybotrys chartarum.Important mycotoxins: Stachybotrys chartarum (S) produces satratoxins and roridins.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Isolated from cardboard, grain, gypsum board, paper, textile and soil. Reported from Belgium, Denmark, England, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, USA.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Physiology: Grows poorly and does not sporulate on media with low water activity, such as DG18 and DRYES and sporulates sparsely on MEA. Sporulates best in the dark. Conidia are sensitive and loose their viability after recurring transferral.
Stachybotrys chartarum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Exposure to Stachy- botrys on natural substrates or in culture can cause ra- shes and mucosal irritation or bleeding.

Stachybotrys chartarum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 18 mm in 7 days, appearing blackish-green with a halo of green extracellular pigment. Colonies appear powdery due to the conidial masses. Reverse is black. Colonies on SNA have a diameter of 20 mm after 7 days at 25 °C in the dark, also appearing blackish-green. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 6 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, appearing beige. Reverse is beige too. Colonies on MEA are 18 mm in diameter with a greyish feather- like appearance and a dark reverse.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are simple or branched, 40–70 µm long and 3–6 µm wide. They are hyaline and smooth at the base and rough and dark towards the apex. Phialides, which are formed in clusters of 3–5 on each conidiophore, are 8–11 µm long and 4–6 µm wide. They are smooth, and clavate to obovoid, hyaline at the base and dark towards the apex. Conidia are borne in slime heads. They are first ellipsoidal and yellow-green, becoming broadly ellipsoidal to ovoid, often inconspicuously papillate at the base. Mature conidia are aseptate, 8–11 × 5–7 µm and opaque, blackish-green. The surface texture of the mature conidia depend on the medium: they are smooth to finely granular on cornmeal agar, verruculose to granular on SNA and PDA, and heavily verrucose on MEA.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Similar species: Stachybotrys chartarum has a similar morphology, but differs from S. chlorohalonata by having narrow ellipsoidal conidia and either producing no or yellow extracellular pigment on PDA and CYA.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: KU847053; ?-tubulin: KU847164; ITS: KU846729.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Chemical markers: Stachybotrys chlorohalonata produ- ces atranones, dolabellanes and trichodermin.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Isolated from textile, hay, seaweed, grain, paper, wallpaper, gypsum board and soil. Reported from Europe, The Middle East and North America.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Physiology: Grows poorly and do not sporulate on media with low water activity, such as DG18 and DRYES and sporulates sparingly on MEA. Sporulates best in the dark. Conidia are sensitive and loose their viability after recurring transferral.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.Biodeterioration and pathology: Exposure to Stachy- botrys on natural substrates or in culture can cause rashes and mucosal irritation or bleeding.
Stachybotrys chlorohalonata.References: Jong & Davis (1976), Andersen et al. (2002b), Cruse et al. (2002), Andersen et al. (2003)

Stemphylium eturmiunum.Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 38–40 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing folded, lavender green with a white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on PCA are 63–67 mm in diameter after 7 days at 22–23 °C in alternating cool white fluorescent light/ darkness, producing ascomata after a week in culture. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 19–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing greyish white and downy. Ascomata produce mature ascospores in axenic culture after 3–6 months at 5–7 °C.
Stemphylium eturmiunum.Micromorphology: Primary conidiophores on PCA are annellidic and simple, 30–90 × 3–4 µm, arising from the agar surface. They are smooth and golden brown with an inflated, 6–7 µm, darker conidiogenous locus. Conidia are solitary, ovoid to ellipsoid, 20–35 × 13–17 µm, with a length/width ratio in the range of 1.6–2.1. They have 1–6 transverse and 0–3 longitudinal septa, where 2–3 of the transverse septa are constricted. They are densely verru- cose and golden to brown in colour with darker septa and outer wall.
Stemphylium eturmiunum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic conidio- genesis (poroconidia); sexual morph known, but rarely produced in culture.
Stemphylium eturmiunum.Similar species: Stemphylium vesicarium (sexual morph Pleospora sp. indet.) has a similar morphology
Stemphylium eturmiunum.Molecular markers: ITS: AY329230; Glyceraldehyde- 3-phosphate dehydrogenase gene: AY317034.
Stemphylium eturmiunum.Chemical markers: Stemphylium eturmiunum produces infectopyrone and macrosporin.
Stemphylium eturmiunum.Habitats and distribution: Food. Stemphylium eturmi- unum has been isolated from tomato, pomaceaous and stone fruit, especially pear and cherry. Reported from Europe, the Middle East, South Africa and North and South America.
Stemphylium eturmiunum.References: Andersen & Frisvad (2004), Inderbitzin et al. (2009), Simmons (1969, 2001), Olsen et al. (2018)

Syncephalastrum racemosum.Macromorphology: Colony white becoming grey with age, growing rapidly, covering the Petri-dish within a week, about 4–5(–15) mm high.
Syncephalastrum racemosum.Micromorphology: Vegetative hyphae hyaline, branched, septa produced in old cultures to delimit reproductive structures. Main sporangiophores (with rhizoids) and their often strongly curved lateral branches each bearing a terminal vesicle, which forms merosporangia all over its surface. Vesicles brownish, globose or subglobose to ovoid; terminal vesicles 30–80 µm, lateral 10–40 µm in diam, with or without a septum. Merosporangia grey, cylindrical, 15–33 µm long and 4 µm wide, breaking up into 5–10(–18) merospores. Merosporangium wall thin and disappearing. Merospores globose or ovoid, 2.5–5(–6.5) µm in diam, usually faintly roughened, pale brown. Chlamydospore-like swellings more or less spherical, 12–13 µm in diam. Heterothallic. Zygospores (after 10 days on MEA at 20–24 °C) mainly in substrate mycelium, orange-brown, with conical projections, 50–90 µm in diam. Suspensors hyaline, smooth, subequal.
Syncephalastrum racemosum.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Main distribution in tropical and subtropical regions; isolated from soil, dung and as a storage organism from grains.
Syncephalastrum racemosum.Physiology: Good growth occurs between 17 and 40 °C. Most Zygomycetes require high water activities for their growth, but S. racemosum is an exception and can grow at a low water activity down to 0.84. Its capability to grow at lower water activities makes this species an important storage organism.
Syncephalastrum racemosum.Fig: 278. Syncephalastrum racemosum. A. Sporangiophores bearing vesicles which produce merosporangia all over their surface. B. Merosporangia and merospores.
Syncephalastrum racemosum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Talaromyces purpurogenus.Synonym: Penicillium purpurogenum P. crateriforme P. sanguine- um
Talaromyces purpurogenus.Macromorphology: Colonies growing restrictedly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 15–22(–33) mm after 7 days), consisting of a dense felt of often yellow vegetative mycelium intermixed with grey to yellow green conidiophores. Conidiophores arising from the agar surface or from bundles. Reverse pink to deep red, or orange-brown. Exudate mostly absent, collected in yellow droplets when present. On MEA the conidia are grey green, with distinctly funiculose colonies having a pale reverse, diameter 19–30 mm. On YES agar the degree of sporulation is strong, reverse colour red brown. The colonies are growing rather rapidly (diameter 19–32 mm after 7 days). On CREA, poor growth and no acid production.
Talaromyces purpurogenus.Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, biverticil- late, consisting of smooth-walled stipes, 150–240 × 3.5–
Talaromyces purpurogenus.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Talaromyces purpurogenus.Chemical markers: Chlororugulovasine A and B, rubra- toxin A and B, rugulovasine A and B, spiculisporic acid.
Talaromyces purpurogenus.Habitats and distribution: Food. Talaromyces purpu- rogenus is common in subtropical and tropical regions especially in tropical cereals, fruits and nuts.
Talaromyces purpurogenus.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Trichoderma harzianum.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA or MEA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 80–90 mm in four days, appearing hyaline, whitish green to olive green depending on the conidium production. The conidiophores form tufts, which are scattered around often in rings relating to alternating light conditions. The reverse is whitish with a yellowish tinge.
Trichoderma harzianum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores are branched in a pyramidal structure, i.e. long repeatedly branched lateral branches below with short branches near the apex. The bottle shaped phialides are often more slender and longer at the apex of the branches measuring up to 18
Trichoderma harzianum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogensis; sexual morphs of the hypocrea-type known but not produced in culture.
Trichoderma harzianum.Similar species: The T. harzianum complex contains many species that are different to delimitate by their morphology, e.g. T. aggresivum which is an aggressive
Trichoderma harzianum.Chemical markers: Peptaibols, anthraquinone pig- ments, harzianopyridone, harzianolide, 6-n-pentyl-alfa- pyrone (6PP), siderophores, isonitrin A-D, koninginin A-E.
Trichoderma harzianum.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species has been reported from patients who have had major surgeries. May be a causal agent in allergies.
