Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Macromorphology: Colonies on OA and MEA at 25
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores forming along the scant aerial mycelium or in continuous, confluent aggregates. Fertile axes bear phialides to the tip and often plumose with phialides arising singly over an average distance of ca. 60 µm before the first branch occurs, typically not held in whorls or multiples, although both occasionally occur. Phialides typically cylindrical, 5.5–9.0 µm in length, width 2.0–3.5 µm. Conidia cylindrical to ellipsoidal, 3.5–5.0 × 2.0–3.0 µm, smooth. Chlamydospores present.
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morphs of the hypocrea-type known but not produced in culture.
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Similar species: Trichoderma longibrachiatum is genetically closely related to T. orientale (= Hypocrea orientalis).
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Molecular markers: ITS: EU401511; calmoduline: EU401459; EF1-?: EU401591.
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Habitats and distribution: Worldwide distribution and commonly occurring in indoor air, also isolated from soil, wood, tree roots, herbaceous tissue and humans.
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Biotechnological applications: Strains of T. longibrachiatum have been used as agents of biological control against phytopathogenic fungi.
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Biodeterioration and pathology: Trichoderma longibrachiatum is an emerging opportunistic human pathogen (Kredics et al. 2003).
Trichoderma longibrachiatum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Trichothecium roseum.Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 25 °C attaining a diameter of about 60 mm in 7 days, pink, powdery due to abundant sporulation.
Trichothecium roseum.Micromorphology: Conidiophores are pinkish, erect, up to 2 mm long and 4–5 µm wide. They are unbranched, often septate near the base and more or less rough-walled. They produce the conidia in retrogressive basipetal zig- zag chains, with the oldest conidium at the apex. The younger conidia are formed below the apical conidium. Conidia are aseptate when young and one-septate when they are mature. They are ellipsoidal to pyriform, 12– 23(–35) × 8–10(–13) µm, with an obliquely truncate basal scar, hyaline, smooth to delicately roughened and thick-walled.
Trichothecium roseum.Morphs: Asexual morph present, sympodial retrogressive conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Trichothecium roseum.Habitats and distribution: Food. This species has a world-wide distribution and has been isolated from fresh cereal grain, decaying plant substrates, soil and flour products. Occasionally isolated from indoor air.
Trichothecium roseum.Fig: 296. Trichothecium roseum. A. Unbranched conidiophores bearing basipetal zig-zag chains of conidia. B. Conidia with obliquely basal scars.
Trichothecium roseum.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Tritirachium oryzae.Macromorphology: Colonies in vitro growing slowly, attaining a diameter of 3–5 mm in 8 days, appearing vel- vety to lanose, at first rosy vinaceous to rosy buff, when older lilac or cinnamon. Reverse dark brick and towards the margin lighter, or brown vinaceous.
Tritirachium oryzae.Micromorphology: Submerged hyphae hyaline to pale brownish, smooth walled, 1–2 µm wide, often somewhat stromatic. Conidiophores reddish brown, lighter towards the base, smooth- and somewhat thick-walled, 200– 1500 µm long, 1.5–3 µm wide, slightly tapering towards the tip, bearing mainly on the upper part (3–)5–12(–30) whorls of 1–3(–5) conidiogenous cells and occasionally a side branch which bears 1–3 conidiogenous cells. Conidiogenous cells consisting of an elongate basal part, slightly swollen below the middle, tapering towards the tip, (7–)9–20(–25) × 1.5–3 µm and a well developed, geniculate (intervals 1–2 µm cicatrized rachis, mostly 25 µm long, up to 165 µm, and 1 µm wide. Conidia hyaline, smooth, thin-walled, globose to ellipsoidal, rarely with a slightly apiculate base, (1.5–)2–3(–3.5) × 1.5–3 µm. No chlamydospores were observed.
Tritirachium oryzae.Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic, sympodial conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Tritirachium oryzae.Habitats and distribution: Tritirachium oryzae has a world-wide distribution in indoor environments and has previously been isolated from air, soil and nylon.
Tritirachium oryzae.Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.

Wallemia sebi.Macromorphology: Colonies are small on DG18, M20 or MY50g attaining a diameter of about 4–6 mm in 10 days at 25 °C. Colonies are pale orange-brown to cocoa-brown on most media with a fan-like or stellate appearance and often powdery due to heavy conidium production. No growth on V8 and very restricted growth on most media. Xerophilic.
Wallemia sebi.Micromorphology: Conidiophores on DG18 varying in  length,  cylindrical,  smooth-walled,  pale-brown,
Wallemia sebi.Morphs: Asexual morph present, basauxic conidiogenesis resembling thallic development; sexual morph not known.
Wallemia sebi.Similar species: Five other species are accepted in Wallemia: W. canadensis, W. ichthyophaga, W. mellicola, W. muriae and W. tropicalis. A dichotomous key to Wallemia species using the growth characteristics on various media (MY50G, MEA supplemented with NaCl (28%) and MgCl2 (15% and 17%) is presented in Jan?i? et al. (2016). For molecular identification we recommend
Wallemia sebi.Molecular markers: Pre-rRNA processing protein (TSR1): KM035026; ITS: AY328915.
Wallemia sebi.Chemical markers: Wallemia sebi can produce wallimidione, walleminol and walleminone.
Wallemia sebi.Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. This species has a worldwide distribution and has been isolated from food with a low water activity, such as jams, syrups, marzipan, dates, bread, cakes, salted fish, bacon, salted beans, but also from fruit, hay and textiles. Wallemia sebi is found on moist plaster and brick walls and is occasionally found in high concentrations in indoor air.
Wallemia sebi.Physiology: The optimum temperature of W. sebi is 23–25 °C; no growth at 5 °C; maximum 36 °C. Wallemia sebi grows best on low water activity media (e.g. M20 or MY50G).
Wallemia sebi.Biodeterioration and pathology: This species can cause subcutaneous infections in humans and probably also allergological problems resulting in farmer’s lung disease.
Wallemia sebi.References: Zalar et al. (2005), Deroches et al. (2014), Jan?i? et al. (2016), Díaz-Valderrama et al. (2017)

Aspergillus filifer.Colony characters: CYA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderately deep,slightly sulcate; margins entire; mycelium white and pale olive;texture ﬂoccose; sporulation absent; soluble pigments absent;exudates clear to light brown droplets; reverse greyish brown atcentre, buff at edge; Ascomata present after 1 wk. MEA 25 °C, 7 d:Colonies moderately deep, plane to slightly sulcate;margins entire;mycelium white and light yellow; texture ﬂoccose; sporulation ab-sent; soluble pigments absent; exudates clear to light brown droplets; reverse dark brown at centre, yellowish brown at edge.Ascomata present after 1 wk. YES 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderatelydeep to deep, sulcate; margins entire; mycelium white and lightyellow; texture velvety; sporulation sparse to moderately dense,conidia en masse yellow green; soluble pigments absent; exudatesclear droplets; reverse light brown to cream yellow. DG18 25 °C, 7d: Colonies moderately deep, plane; margins entire; myceliumwhite; texture velvety; sporulation dense, conidia en masse yellowgreen; soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse paleyellow green. OA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies low, plane; margins entire;mycelium white; texture granular due to ascomata production;sporulation absent; soluble pigments absent; exudates cleardroplets; reverse pale brownish green. Ascomata present after 1wk. CREA 25 °C, 7 d: Acid production absent.
Aspergillus filifer.Micromorphology: Ascomata cleistothecial, superﬁcial, greyishgreen to brown, globose to subglobose 220–660 μm, sur-rounded by numerous Hülle cells; Hülle cells hyaline to paleyellowish brown, globose to ovoid, 13–24 μm. Asci 8 spored,stellate, globose to subglobose. Asci 8-spored, globose to subglobose 12–14 µm, evanescent at maturity. Ascospores lensshaped, 4.5–7.5 µm, with two equatorial crests, convex surfaces smooth to microtuberculate. Neosartorya warcupii.Species description: Neosartorya warcupii Peterson, Varga & Samson, sp. nov. (Fig. 38) – MycoBank MB505572.
Neosartorya warcupii.Holotype: Holotype of Neosartorya warcupii, here designated as NRRL 35723T (dried culture), isolated from soil, Finders Range, Australia. Homothallic, cleistothecia superficial, yellowish white to pale yellow, globose to subglobose, 180–350 µm in diam., surrounded by a loose covering of hyaline to yellowish white hyphae. Asci 8-spored, globose to subglobose 10–16 µm, evanescent at maturity. Ascospores lens shapedm 4.5–7 µm, with two prominent equatorial crests, convex surface smooth to microtuberculate. Mycelium composed of hyaline, branched, septate, smooth-walled hyphae. Conidial heads short, columnar. Conidiophores arising from aerial hyphae, uniseriate, stipes 100–150 × 4–6 µm; vesicles subclavate to subglobose, 12–18 µm in diam; phialides 7.5–9 x 2–3 µm, covering the upper half of vesicle. Conidia globose to subglobose, smooth, 1.8–2.5 µm. Colonies on MEA growing rapidly, 35–40 mm in 7 d at 25 °C. Colonies on CYA, 18–22 mm in 7 d at 25 °C, creamish white, sectors frequently produced. Conidial heads few in number. Reverse bluish in colour.
Neosartorya warcupii.Etymology: named after Prof. J. H. Warcup, eminent mycologist, who isolated this culture.
Neosartorya warcupii.Morphological characteristics: Homothallica; cleistothecia superficialia, alba vel dilute lutea, globosa vel subglobosa, 200–350 μm diam, in hyphis hyalinis vel luteoalbis laxe obtextis. Asci octospori, globosi vel subglobosi, 4.5–7 μm diam, evanescentes. Ascosporae 5.5–7 μm diam, cristis angustis, aequatoriis binis, pagina convexa sublaevigata. Mycelium ex hyphis hyalinis, ramosis, septatis, laeviparietinis constans. Capitula conidialia curta, columnaria. Conidiophora ex hyphis aeriis exorientia, uniseriata, stipitibus 100–150 x 4–5 μm; vesiculae ampulliformes, 10–25 μm diam; phialides 7.5–9 x 2–3 μm, dimidium supernum vesiculae obtegentes. Conidia subglobosa vel ellipsoidea, laevia, 1.8–1.5 μm diam. Coloniae in agaro MEA in 7 dieibus et 25 °C celeriter crescentes, 35–40 mm diam, albae, capitulis conidialibus paucis. Coloniae in agaro CYA in 7 dieibus et 25 °C 20–30 mm diam, cremeoalbae, centro ab hyphis aerialibus laxe obtecto; capitula conidialia pauca; colonia reversa luteobrunnea vel atrobrunne.
